sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka's own replication keeps copies within one cluster but does not span regions, because stretching the in-sync replica set across a high-latency link would cripple write latency. So for multi-datacenter I use a separate copying layer, typically MirrorMaker 2, which is built on Kafka Connect. It replicates topic data and, importantly, consumer group offsets, and it emits checkpoints so a consumer can resume in the other region near where it left off. It also prefixes mirrored topics with the source cluster alias, which prevents infinite replication loops in a bidirectional setup.

The topology choice is active-passive versus active-active. Active-passive is simpler: one region takes all writes and the other is a warm standby that I fail over to during a disaster. The tradeoffs are that the standby capacity sits idle, failover is a deliberate operation, and the possible data-loss window equals the replication lag, so I monitor that lag and I rehearse failover regularly.

Active-active lets both regions accept writes, which gives local users lower latency and uses all capacity, but it introduces three hard problems: loop prevention, solved by the cluster-alias prefix; offset translation, solved by the checkpoint map since offsets differ per cluster; and conflicting writes to the same key, which is the dangerous one. For money, I never allow true multi-master writes to the same account, so I pin each account's write ownership to a home region. That gives me active-active for locality and read scaling while behaving like active-passive per account to avoid conflicts.

In my National Bank of India project across Mumbai and Chennai, we ran active-active with home-region ownership. Rajesh's account was written only in Mumbai and Priya's only in Chennai, both regions mirrored to each other with MirrorMaker 2, and our recovery point objective was the mirror lag of a second or two. On failover we translated offsets through the checkpoints so consumers resumed cleanly, and we drilled the failover quarterly so it actually worked when regulators asked.

answers.question: When would you deliberately choose NOT to use Kafka?
answers.shortTitle: When would you deliberately choose NOT to use Kafka?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log optimized for high-throughput streaming, replayable event history, and many consumers. You deliberately avoid it when its strengths do not match the problem: for simple request-reply where a synchronous call is clearer, for low-volume workloads where a managed queue is cheaper and simpler to operate, for strict priority or per-message scheduling and complex routing that a traditional broker handles natively, for tiny teams without the operational capacity to run a stateful cluster, and for workloads needing transactional joins across business tables where a database is the right tool.
s1_definition.analogy: Kafka is like building a dedicated high-speed conveyor system through National Bank of India that keeps a permanent record of every item and lets many departments read it at their own pace. That is fantastic for a flood of transactions feeding many systems. But if a teller just needs a yes-or-no answer from the credit desk right now, you do not build a conveyor, you make a phone call. And if the mailroom only handles a few letters a day, buying and maintaining an industrial conveyor is wasteful.
s1_definition.oneliner: Skip Kafka for simple request-reply, for low-volume or tiny-team workloads where a managed queue is cheaper, for priority or complex routing that a classic broker does natively, and when a database transaction is actually the right tool.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log optimized for high-throughput streaming, replayable event history, and many consumers. You deliberately avoid it when its strengths do not match the problem: for simple request-reply where a synchronous call is clearer, for low-volume workloads where a managed queue is cheaper and simpler to operate, for strict priority or per-message scheduling and complex routing that a traditional broker handles natively, for tiny teams without the operational capacity to run a stateful cluster, and for workloads needing transactional joins across business tables where a database is the right tool.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Kafka is like building a dedicated high-speed conveyor system through National Bank of India that keeps a permanent record of every item and lets many departments read it at their own pace. That is fantastic for a flood of transactions feeding many systems. But if a teller just needs a yes-or-no answer from the credit desk right now, you do not build a conveyor, you make a phone call. And if the mailroom only handles a few letters a day, buying and maintaining an industrial conveyor is wasteful.

**One line to remember:** Skip Kafka for simple request-reply, for low-volume or tiny-team workloads where a managed queue is cheaper, for priority or complex routing that a classic broker does natively, and when a database transaction is actually the right tool.

sections.s2_technical:
The first case is synchronous request-reply. If a caller needs an immediate answer, such as a fraud check that must return approve or decline before a transaction proceeds, a direct REST or gRPC call is simpler and clearer than publishing a request and correlating a reply through Kafka. You can do request-reply over Kafka, but it adds correlation ids, reply topics, and latency for no benefit when a simple call suffices.

The second case is low volume. Kafka is a stateful distributed system with brokers, replication, and now the KRaft controller quorum to operate, patch, and monitor. If you move a few hundred or a few thousand messages a day, the operational cost dwarfs the benefit, and a managed queue such as Amazon SQS or a lightweight broker gives you the same decoupling with almost no operations. Choosing Kafka here is over-engineering.

The third case is rich messaging features that traditional brokers provide natively. If you need per-message priority, where urgent messages jump ahead, or complex routing by headers and patterns, or per-message time-to-live and delayed delivery, RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ handle these out of the box. Kafka has no native priority queue and no native per-message TTL; you would simulate them with multiple topics and custom logic, which is awkward.

The fourth case is small teams and limited operational maturity. Running Kafka well means understanding partitions, replication, in-sync replicas, consumer groups, rebalancing, retention, and monitoring lag. A small team without that capacity is better served by a fully managed queue or even a database-backed job table, because an poorly operated Kafka cluster causes more incidents than it prevents. If you do need Kafka's model, a fully managed Kafka service removes most of the operational burden and changes this calculus.

The fifth case is when the real need is transactional data operations, not streaming. If you need to atomically update several business tables, run ad-hoc queries, enforce foreign keys, or join across entities, that is a database job. Kafka is a log, not a query engine, so forcing relational, transactional work through it is the wrong tool.

A senior nuance is that these are not absolutes. Kafka shines for high-throughput ingestion, event sourcing, replayable history, stream processing, and fan-out to many independent consumers, so the decision is about matching the tool to the access pattern. Another nuance is cost and latency: Kafka adds an asynchronous hop and at-least-once semantics that force you to design for idempotency and out-of-order delivery, which is unnecessary complexity when the interaction is naturally synchronous and exactly one caller cares about the result.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India has several integration needs, and an architect must decide which belong on Kafka and which do not. Blindly putting everything on Kafka would add cost and complexity where a simpler tool fits better.

Problem 1 — a point-of-sale terminal needs an instant approve or decline for Rajesh's card swipe. This is synchronous request-reply, so a direct call is right, not Kafka.

Problem 2 — the branch sends a handful of end-of-day summary emails. This is low volume, so a managed queue or even a scheduled job is right, not a Kafka cluster.

Problem 3 — a VIP customer's urgent wire must jump ahead of ordinary transfers. This needs message priority, which a classic broker does natively and Kafka does not.

Problem 4 — the transaction firehose feeds analytics, fraud, and ledger consumers that read independently and sometimes replay history. This is exactly where Kafka fits.

The code will implement a small decision helper that, given a workload's characteristics, recommends Kafka or an alternative and explains why, logging the recommendation for each banking workload.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka is a distributed commit log optimized for high throughput, replayable history, stream processing, and fanning out to many independent consumers. I choose not to use it when the problem does not match those strengths. The clearest case is synchronous request-reply. If a caller needs an immediate answer, like a fraud check that must approve or decline a card swipe before it proceeds, a direct REST or gRPC call is simpler and faster than publishing a request and correlating a reply through Kafka.

The second case is low volume. Kafka is a stateful distributed system that you have to operate, patch, and monitor, so for a trickle of messages a day a managed queue gives the same decoupling with almost no operations, and choosing Kafka there is over-engineering. The third case is rich messaging features that traditional brokers provide natively, like per-message priority, complex routing, or per-message time-to-live. Kafka has no native priority queue, so if a VIP wire must jump ahead of ordinary transfers, RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ is the better fit.

The fourth case is a small team without the operational maturity to run a cluster well, because a poorly operated Kafka causes more incidents than it prevents, though a fully managed Kafka service changes that calculus. And the fifth case is when the real need is transactional, relational work across business tables, which is a database job, not a log.

In my National Bank of India work, I made exactly these calls. The card authorization path was synchronous REST because the terminal needed an instant decision. The handful of end-of-day emails went on a managed queue. A priority-sensitive wire path used a classic broker. And the transaction firehose, which ran at tens of thousands of messages a second and fed analytics, fraud, and the ledger with replay, was the workload that genuinely belonged on Kafka. Matching the tool to the access pattern kept the architecture simple and cheap where it could be and powerful where it needed to be.

answers.question: What is tiered storage (KIP-405), and what problem does it solve?
answers.shortTitle: What is tiered storage (KIP-405), and what problem does it solve?

s1_definition.profdef: Tiered storage, introduced by KIP-405, lets a Kafka broker keep only recent log segments on its local disk and offload older, closed segments to cheaper remote storage such as Amazon S3, while they still appear as part of the same topic. This decouples storage from compute, so you can retain data for months or years without buying huge local disks, and it makes brokers faster to scale and recover because they hold far less local data. Consumers reading old offsets transparently fetch from the remote tier.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps this month's transaction ledgers on the clerk's desk for instant access, but moves last year's ledgers to a cheap off-site warehouse. The ledgers are still part of the official records and anyone can request an old one, it just comes from the warehouse instead of the desk. The desk stays small and tidy, the bank keeps seven years of history cheaply, and a new clerk can start work immediately because the desk has very little on it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Tiered storage keeps hot recent segments on local disk and offloads cold segments to cheap remote object storage, so Kafka retains data for years cheaply and brokers scale and recover fast.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Tiered storage, introduced by KIP-405, lets a Kafka broker keep only recent log segments on its local disk and offload older, closed segments to cheaper remote storage such as Amazon S3, while they still appear as part of the same topic. This decouples storage from compute, so you can retain data for months or years without buying huge local disks, and it makes brokers faster to scale and recover because they hold far less local data. Consumers reading old offsets transparently fetch from the remote tier.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps this month's transaction ledgers on the clerk's desk for instant access, but moves last year's ledgers to a cheap off-site warehouse. The ledgers are still part of the official records and anyone can request an old one, it just comes from the warehouse instead of the desk. The desk stays small and tidy, the bank keeps seven years of history cheaply, and a new clerk can start work immediately because the desk has very little on it.

**One line to remember:** Tiered storage keeps hot recent segments on local disk and offloads cold segments to cheap remote object storage, so Kafka retains data for years cheaply and brokers scale and recover fast.

sections.s2_technical:
A Kafka partition is stored as a sequence of log segment files on a broker's local disk. Traditionally, every byte you retain lives on that local disk, so if you want ninety days of retention for a high-volume topic, you must provision and pay for a lot of fast local disk on every broker, and that disk is coupled to the compute. This coupling is the core problem tiered storage attacks.

With tiered storage enabled, a broker keeps only the most recent segments locally, controlled by a local retention setting, and once a segment is closed and older than the local retention, it is uploaded to the configured remote store and removed from local disk, subject to the overall remote retention. You enable it per topic with configs like `remote.storage.enable=true`, and you set `local.retention.ms` or `local.retention.bytes` for how much stays local while `retention.ms` governs the total including remote. For example, you might keep one day locally and one year in S3.

The remote store is pluggable through a RemoteStorageManager interface, with implementations for object stores like S3, Google Cloud Storage, and Azure Blob. The broker tracks which segments live remotely in remote log metadata. When a consumer requests an offset that is only in the remote tier, the broker fetches that segment from the remote store and serves it, so from the consumer's point of view nothing changes; it is the same topic and the same offsets, just a slightly higher latency for very old data.

The problems this solves are several. First, cost: object storage is far cheaper per gigabyte than fast local disk, so long retention becomes affordable. Second, elasticity: because brokers hold far less local data, adding or removing a broker and rebalancing partitions moves much less data, so scaling is faster and cheaper. Third, recovery: when a broker fails and a replica must catch up, it has less local data to replicate, so recovery is faster. Fourth, retention flexibility: you can keep data for compliance or reprocessing for months or years without sizing local disks for the worst case.

A senior nuance is the latency tradeoff. Reads of recent data stay fast from local disk, but reads of very old data pay the remote fetch latency, so tiered storage suits workloads where most reads are recent and only occasional backfills or audits touch old data. Another nuance is that the remote store becomes part of your durability and security surface, so you encrypt it, control access with policies, and account for remote-store availability. A final nuance is that tiered storage matured across Kafka versions and is production-ready in recent releases, and some managed Kafka offerings provide it transparently.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India must retain transaction event history for seven years to satisfy regulators, but the live analytics and fraud systems almost always read only the last few days. Keeping seven years on local broker disk would be enormously expensive and would make brokers slow to scale and recover.

Problem 1 — seven years of high-volume transaction data on local disks costs a fortune and forces huge brokers. This is exactly what tiered storage solves by offloading old segments to cheap object storage.

Problem 2 — when traffic spikes, adding a broker and rebalancing takes hours because each broker holds terabytes locally. This is exactly what tiered storage solves by keeping local data small so rebalancing moves little.

Problem 3 — an auditor occasionally requests transactions from three years ago, which must still be readable through the same topic. This is exactly what tiered storage provides: old offsets are fetched transparently from the remote tier.

The code will model a tiered-retention planner that, given a message's age, decides whether it is served from local disk or remote storage, and computes local versus remote footprint to show the cost benefit, logged for Rajesh's and Priya's transaction history.

Input data: reads of transaction records of various ages, and a daily ingest of five hundred gigabytes.

Step 1 — Rajesh's swipe from two hours ago is younger than the one-day local retention, so the planner says it is served from local disk, fast and hot.

Step 3 — the auditor's request for a transaction three years ago is also within the seven-year window, so it is fetched from remote storage as the same topic and offset, satisfying the audit.

Step 4 — a record from eight years ago is beyond the total retention, so it has been deleted everywhere and is reported as expired.

Step 5 — the footprint calculation shows that with one day local, the brokers only need about five hundred gigabytes of fast local disk, while roughly one and a quarter petabytes of cold history lives cheaply in object storage, demonstrating the cost benefit.

Tiered storage, introduced by KIP-405, lets a Kafka broker keep only recent log segments on its local disk and offload older closed segments to cheaper remote object storage such as S3, while they remain part of the same topic. From a consumer's point of view nothing changes, because the broker fetches old segments from the remote store transparently, serving the same topic and the same offsets, just with a little more latency for very old data. The tradeoffs I keep in mind are that remote reads are slower, so it suits workloads where most reads are recent, and that the remote store becomes part of my durability and security surface, so I encrypt it and lock down access.

In my National Bank of India project, regulators required seven years of transaction history, but the fraud and analytics systems almost always read only the last few days. Keeping seven years on local disk would have been enormously expensive and would have made brokers slow to scale. We enabled tiered storage with one day local and seven years in S3, so the brokers stayed small and fast, we scaled out quickly during surges, and an auditor could still pull a three-year-old transaction through the same topic.

answers.question: How do you secure a Kafka cluster in a regulated environment (mTLS/SASL, ACLs, TLS, encryption at rest, network segmentation)?
answers.shortTitle: How do you secure a Kafka cluster in a regulated environment?

s1_definition.profdef: Securing Kafka in a regulated environment layers several controls. Encryption in transit with TLS protects data on the wire between clients and brokers and between brokers. Authentication, using mutual TLS or SASL mechanisms such as SCRAM, GSSAPI/Kerberos, or OAuth, proves who each client is. Authorization with ACLs controls which authenticated principals may produce, consume, or administer which topics and groups. Encryption at rest protects the data on disk and in any remote tier. Network segmentation isolates the cluster in private subnets with tight firewall and security-group rules. Together these enforce confidentiality, integrity, and least privilege, with audit logging for compliance.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India's vault. TLS is the armored, sealed pipe that moves cash so no one can see or tamper with it in transit. Authentication is checking each person's verified ID badge at the door. ACLs are the rule that a teller may open drawer five but not the main vault. Encryption at rest is keeping the cash itself in locked, tamper-proof boxes even inside the vault. Network segmentation is building the vault in a restricted wing that only authorized corridors reach. And every entry is written in a logbook for auditors.
s1_definition.oneliner: Encrypt in transit with TLS, authenticate with mTLS or SASL, authorize with ACLs for least privilege, encrypt at rest, segment the network, and log everything for audit.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Securing Kafka in a regulated environment layers several controls. Encryption in transit with TLS protects data on the wire between clients and brokers and between brokers. Authentication, using mutual TLS or SASL mechanisms such as SCRAM, GSSAPI/Kerberos, or OAuth, proves who each client is. Authorization with ACLs controls which authenticated principals may produce, consume, or administer which topics and groups. Encryption at rest protects the data on disk and in any remote tier. Network segmentation isolates the cluster in private subnets with tight firewall and security-group rules. Together these enforce confidentiality, integrity, and least privilege, with audit logging for compliance.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India's vault. TLS is the armored, sealed pipe that moves cash so no one can see or tamper with it in transit. Authentication is checking each person's verified ID badge at the door. ACLs are the rule that a teller may open drawer five but not the main vault. Encryption at rest is keeping the cash itself in locked, tamper-proof boxes even inside the vault. Network segmentation is building the vault in a restricted wing that only authorized corridors reach. And every entry is written in a logbook for auditors.

**One line to remember:** Encrypt in transit with TLS, authenticate with mTLS or SASL, authorize with ACLs for least privilege, encrypt at rest, segment the network, and log everything for audit.

sections.s2_technical:
Encryption in transit is the first layer. You configure brokers to use TLS on their listeners so every client-to-broker and broker-to-broker connection is encrypted, preventing eavesdropping and tampering. You set `security.protocol=SSL` or `SASL_SSL` on clients and provide a truststore so the client verifies the broker's certificate. Without TLS, transaction data crosses the network in plaintext, which no regulated bank can accept.

Authentication proves identity. Mutual TLS, or mTLS, means both sides present certificates, so the broker verifies the client's certificate and the client verifies the broker's, giving strong certificate-based identity. The alternative is SASL, which supports several mechanisms: SCRAM for username and password hashed with a salted challenge, GSSAPI for Kerberos integration common in enterprises, and OAUTHBEARER for OAuth tokens from an identity provider. You pick based on your environment; banks often use mTLS for service-to-service and Kerberos or OAuth where they already have that infrastructure. You never use the PLAINTEXT listener in production.

Authorization with ACLs enforces least privilege. Kafka's authorizer checks, for each operation, whether the authenticated principal is allowed. You grant specific rights, such as letting the settlement service principal only read the transfers topic and write the results topic, with a command like `kafka-acls --add --allow-principal User:settlement --operation Read --topic transfers`. You deny everything by default by setting the broker so that a resource with no matching allow ACL is denied, which is the secure default. This stops a compromised analytics service from, say, producing fake transfers.

Encryption at rest protects data on disk. Kafka itself does not encrypt its log files, so you rely on the storage layer: encrypted volumes such as LUKS or cloud-provider disk encryption, and for tiered storage the object store's server-side encryption with managed keys. You also protect the keys themselves with a key management service and rotate them. This ensures a stolen disk or backup is useless without the keys.

Network segmentation limits exposure. You place brokers in private subnets with no public addresses, allow only the required ports from only the required client subnets using security groups or firewall rules, and often front access through a controlled gateway or VPC peering. You separate the control plane, the KRaft controllers, from general access. This means even an attacker inside the broader network cannot reach the brokers without passing the segmentation controls.

A senior nuance is that these layers compose and you need all of them, because TLS without ACLs lets any authenticated client read everything, and ACLs without TLS send credentials and data in clear. Another nuance is audit and compliance: you enable authorizer logging so every allowed and denied operation is recorded, you monitor for anomalies, and you keep certificates and credentials in a secrets manager with rotation. A final nuance is operational: certificate expiry is a common outage cause, so you automate certificate issuance and renewal.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India must pass a regulatory audit of its Kafka platform. The auditors require encrypted transport, authenticated clients, least-privilege authorization, encryption at rest, network isolation, and an audit trail.

Problem 1 — transaction data currently crosses the network in plaintext and clients connect anonymously. This is exactly what TLS and mTLS or SASL authentication solve: encrypt the wire and verify every client's identity.

Problem 2 — every service can read and write every topic, so a compromised reporting service could forge transfers. This is exactly what ACLs with deny-by-default solve: each principal gets only the rights it needs.

Problem 3 — a stolen backup disk would expose years of transactions, and anyone on the corporate network can reach the brokers. This is exactly what encryption at rest and network segmentation solve.

The code will model a security policy engine that validates a client connection: it checks the protocol is encrypted, the principal is authenticated, and the requested operation is permitted by an ACL, logging allow or deny decisions for the settlement and reporting services.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four connection requests representing different clients and conditions.

Step 1 — the settlement service connects over TLS with a client certificate from the private subnet and asks to read the transfers topic. The engine checks network segmentation (trusted subnet, pass), encryption (SSL, pass), authentication (authenticated principal, pass), and the ACL (settlement may read transfers, pass), so it is allowed.

Step 2 — the reporting service, authenticated over TLS, tries to write to the transfers topic. All layers pass until the ACL check, where reporting has no write grant on transfers, so it is denied by default. This blocks a compromised reporting service from forging transfers.

Step 3 — an anonymous client connects over plaintext. The engine denies it at the encryption layer because the transport is not encrypted, and it would also fail authentication. Transaction data never flows in clear.

Step 4 — the settlement service, properly authenticated, connects from outside the segmented network. The engine denies it at the segmentation layer, because even a valid identity may only connect from approved subnets.

```
2026-10-24 22:50:01 [INFO] ALLOW User:settlement READ:transfers
2026-10-24 22:50:01 [WARNING] DENY  User:reporting WRITE:transfers — no ACL grants WRITE:transfers to User:reporting
2026-10-24 22:50:01 [WARNING] DENY  ANONYMOUS READ:transfers — transport not encrypted (TLS required)
2026-10-24 22:50:01 [WARNING] DENY  User:settlement READ:transfers — connection not from a trusted segmented subnet
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Securing Kafka in a regulated environment means layering several controls that together enforce confidentiality, integrity, and least privilege. The first layer is encryption in transit with TLS, so every client-to-broker and broker-to-broker connection is encrypted and transaction data never crosses the network in plaintext. The second layer is authentication, where I prove each client's identity with mutual TLS, in which both sides present certificates, or with SASL mechanisms like SCRAM, Kerberos, or OAuth, and I never expose a plaintext listener in production.

The third layer is authorization with ACLs for least privilege. The broker's authorizer checks every operation against the authenticated principal, and I configure deny-by-default so that a resource with no matching allow rule is refused. That way the settlement service can only read the transfers topic and write the results topic, and a compromised reporting service cannot forge transfers. The fourth layer is encryption at rest, because Kafka does not encrypt its own log files, so I use encrypted volumes and, for any remote tier, server-side encryption, with keys held in a key management service and rotated.

The fifth layer is network segmentation. I place brokers in private subnets with no public addresses, allow only the required ports from only the required client subnets, and isolate the controller control plane. On top of all this I enable authorizer audit logging so every allowed and denied operation is recorded for the regulators, and I automate certificate renewal because certificate expiry is a classic cause of outages.

In my National Bank of India project, we had to pass a regulatory audit, so we ran mutual TLS between services, deny-by-default ACLs scoped tightly per service, encrypted disks with a managed key service, brokers locked into a segmented private subnet, and a full audit trail into our SIEM. The key point I always make is that these layers only work together: TLS without ACLs lets any authenticated client read everything, and ACLs without TLS send credentials in the clear, so a regulated bank needs all of them.

answers.question: What happens if a Kafka broker runs out of disk space?
answers.shortTitle: What happens if a Kafka broker runs out of disk space?

s1_definition.profdef: When a Kafka broker's log directory fills up, the broker cannot append new records or write index entries, so it logs IO errors, marks the affected log directory offline, and the partitions whose leaders are on that broker become unavailable for writes. Producers to those partitions fail or block, replication stalls so those partitions can fall out of the in-sync replica set, and if the whole broker is affected it may shut down. You prevent and recover from this with retention and cleanup policies, disk monitoring and alerts, quotas, adding capacity or brokers, and in modern versions tiered storage to keep local disk small.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the clerk's desk at National Bank of India is completely covered in ledgers with no room left to write. The clerk cannot record any new transaction, so new entries get rejected and pile up at the counter. The backup clerks who copy the ledgers also cannot keep up, so their copies fall behind. The fix is to archive old ledgers off the desk regularly, watch the desk's fullness and get warned before it overflows, and get a bigger desk or more clerks before the rush.
s1_definition.oneliner: A full broker disk takes its partitions offline for writes and stalls replication, so you prevent it with retention, monitoring, quotas, and capacity, and recover by freeing space or adding disk.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When a Kafka broker's log directory fills up, the broker cannot append new records or write index entries, so it logs IO errors, marks the affected log directory offline, and the partitions whose leaders are on that broker become unavailable for writes. Producers to those partitions fail or block, replication stalls so those partitions can fall out of the in-sync replica set, and if the whole broker is affected it may shut down. You prevent and recover from this with retention and cleanup policies, disk monitoring and alerts, quotas, adding capacity or brokers, and in modern versions tiered storage to keep local disk small.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the clerk's desk at National Bank of India is completely covered in ledgers with no room left to write. The clerk cannot record any new transaction, so new entries get rejected and pile up at the counter. The backup clerks who copy the ledgers also cannot keep up, so their copies fall behind. The fix is to archive old ledgers off the desk regularly, watch the desk's fullness and get warned before it overflows, and get a bigger desk or more clerks before the rush.

**One line to remember:** A full broker disk takes its partitions offline for writes and stalls replication, so you prevent it with retention, monitoring, quotas, and capacity, and recover by freeing space or adding disk.

sections.s2_technical:
Kafka stores each partition replica as log segment files plus index files in a configured log directory on local disk. When that directory's filesystem runs out of space, any attempt to append a record or extend an index fails with an IO exception. Kafka treats IO errors on a log directory seriously: it marks that log directory offline, takes the partitions hosted there out of service on that broker, and may shut the broker down if it cannot function.

For the partitions whose leader was on the full broker, writes fail. Producers trying to send to those partitions get errors such as NotEnoughReplicas or timeouts, and with `acks=all` and a sensible `min.insync.replicas`, a write that cannot be safely replicated is rejected rather than silently lost, which is the safe behaviour. If other brokers hold healthy replicas, Kafka elects a new leader from the in-sync replicas, so the partition can recover on another broker, but only if those replicas were in sync; a replica on the full broker falls behind and drops out of the in-sync set.

Replication is also affected because a follower on the full broker cannot write the data it fetches, so it stops making progress and is removed from the in-sync replica set. This reduces the redundancy of every partition that had a replica there, so a second failure becomes more dangerous. This is why a disk-full condition is not just a local problem; it erodes the durability guarantees across the cluster.

Prevention is mostly about retention and monitoring. You set `retention.ms` or `retention.bytes` per topic so old data is deleted on a schedule, and `log.retention.check.interval.ms` controls how often the cleaner runs. For keyed topics you may use compaction, but note that compaction still needs working space. You monitor disk usage per log directory and alert well before full, commonly at seventy or eighty percent, so operators can act. You can set producer and client quotas to stop a runaway producer from filling disks faster than cleanup frees space.

Recovery, once it happens, means freeing space or adding it. You can reduce retention temporarily so the cleaner deletes more, delete or move data for non-critical topics, add disk capacity to the volume, or add brokers and reassign partitions to spread the load. You must be careful that manual deletion of segment files is risky and best avoided; changing retention and letting Kafka clean up is safer. Once space is available, you bring the log directory back online and the affected replicas catch up and rejoin the in-sync set.

A senior nuance is that tiered storage largely prevents this class of incident for high-retention topics by keeping only recent segments locally, so local disk stays small. Another nuance is to spread partitions and data evenly, because an unbalanced cluster can fill one broker while others are near empty, so you monitor per-broker balance and rebalance proactively. A final nuance is that you should separate the Kafka data volume from the operating-system volume, so a full data disk does not also crash the OS and logging.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs a transactions topic. One night a surge, plus a retention misconfiguration, fills one broker's data disk. The platform team needs to understand the impact and respond safely.

Problem 1 — the full broker can no longer append records, so transfers routed to its leader partitions start failing. This is exactly the disk-full behaviour: the log directory goes offline and writes to those partitions fail.

Problem 2 — the follower replicas on that broker fall behind and drop out of the in-sync set, reducing redundancy for several partitions. This is exactly how a disk-full condition erodes durability cluster-wide.

Problem 3 — the team must decide a safe recovery: not manual file deletion, but reducing retention, adding capacity, and rebalancing, while monitoring alerts to prevent recurrence. This is exactly the prevention-and-recovery playbook.

The code will model a disk monitor that classifies a broker's disk state, decides whether writes to its partitions are accepted, simulates a follower dropping out of the in-sync set, and recommends a safe recovery action, logged for the transactions topic.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a broker whose disk usage climbs from fifty-five to one hundred percent.

Step 1 — at fifty-five percent the guard classifies the broker as healthy and writes to its leader partitions are accepted normally.

Step 2 — at seventy-five percent the guard raises a warning, telling operators to clean up or add capacity soon. Writes still succeed, but this is the moment to act.

Step 3 — at ninety-two percent the guard classifies it as critical. Operators should act immediately, for example reducing retention so the cleaner deletes old segments.

Step 4 — at one hundred percent the disk is full. The log directory goes offline, so writes to that broker's leader partitions are rejected, producers see errors, and a new leader is elected from in-sync replicas on healthy brokers if available.

Step 5 — the follower replica on the full broker cannot write fetched data, so it falls out of the in-sync replica set, reducing redundancy for the transactions partitions. The guard logs the safe recovery: reduce retention, add disk or brokers, and reassign partitions, explicitly avoiding manual segment deletion.

```
2026-10-24 23:00:01 [INFO] broker-2 disk 55% → HEALTHY | writes ACCEPTED
2026-10-24 23:00:01 [INFO] broker-2 disk 75% → WARNING (clean up / add capacity soon) | writes ACCEPTED
2026-10-24 23:00:01 [INFO] broker-2 disk 92% → CRITICAL (act now) | writes ACCEPTED
2026-10-24 23:00:01 [INFO] broker-2 disk 100% → FULL (log dir offline, partitions unavailable for writes) | writes REJECTED
2026-10-24 23:00:01 [WARNING] Follower on broker-2 fell out of ISR for transactions partitions
2026-10-24 23:00:01 [SEVERE] RECOVERY: reduce retention.ms, add disk/brokers, reassign partitions (do NOT hand-delete segment files)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When a Kafka broker's log directory fills up, the broker can no longer append records or write index files, so it logs IO errors, marks that log directory offline, and takes its hosted partitions out of service. For partitions whose leader was on the full broker, writes fail, and producers using all-acknowledgements with a sensible minimum in-sync replicas get rejected rather than silently losing data, which is the safe behaviour. If healthy in-sync replicas exist on other brokers, Kafka elects a new leader there so the partition can recover.

The damage is not just local. A follower replica on the full broker cannot persist the data it fetches, so it falls out of the in-sync replica set, which reduces the redundancy of every partition that had a replica there and makes a second failure more dangerous. That is why a disk-full condition erodes durability across the whole cluster, not just on one node.

I prevent it mainly with retention and monitoring. I set per-topic retention by time or size so old data is cleaned up on schedule, I monitor disk usage per log directory and alert well before full, usually at seventy or eighty percent, and I use quotas to stop a runaway producer. For recovery I never hand-delete segment files, which is risky; instead I reduce retention so the cleaner frees space, add disk or brokers, and reassign partitions to rebalance, then let the recovered replica catch up and rejoin the in-sync set.

In my National Bank of India project, a surge plus a retention misconfiguration once filled one broker. Transfers to its leader partitions started failing and its followers dropped out of the in-sync set. We recovered safely by temporarily cutting retention and adding capacity, and afterward we hardened the setup by separating the data volume from the operating-system volume, balancing partitions evenly, alerting earlier, and ultimately adopting tiered storage so local disks stayed small for our long-retention topics.

answers.question: What happens if a consumer crashes after consuming but before committing the offset, and how do you ensure at-least-once (manual offset commit)?
answers.shortTitle: What happens if a consumer crashes after consuming but before committing the offset, and how do you ensure at-least-once?

s1_definition.profdef: If a consumer reads records and crashes before committing their offsets, the committed offset still points before those records, so when the consumer or another group member resumes, it re-reads and reprocesses them. This is at-least-once delivery: no message is lost, but a message can be processed more than once. You ensure at-least-once deliberately by disabling auto-commit and committing offsets manually only after processing has succeeded, and you make the downstream processing idempotent so reprocessing a duplicate has no harmful effect.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a settlement clerk at National Bank of India who takes a stack of transfer slips off the tray, starts working, but faints before marking the tray as cleared up to that slip. When a new clerk arrives, the tray still shows those slips as not yet cleared, so the new clerk picks them up again. Nothing is lost, but a slip might get worked twice, so the ledger must be designed so that applying the same transfer twice does not double-charge Rajesh. The safe rule is: only mark the tray cleared after the work is truly done.
s1_definition.oneliner: A crash before commit means those records are reprocessed on resume, which is at-least-once, so you disable auto-commit, commit only after successful processing, and make processing idempotent.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** If a consumer reads records and crashes before committing their offsets, the committed offset still points before those records, so when the consumer or another group member resumes, it re-reads and reprocesses them. This is at-least-once delivery: no message is lost, but a message can be processed more than once. You ensure at-least-once deliberately by disabling auto-commit and committing offsets manually only after processing has succeeded, and you make the downstream processing idempotent so reprocessing a duplicate has no harmful effect.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a settlement clerk at National Bank of India who takes a stack of transfer slips off the tray, starts working, but faints before marking the tray as cleared up to that slip. When a new clerk arrives, the tray still shows those slips as not yet cleared, so the new clerk picks them up again. Nothing is lost, but a slip might get worked twice, so the ledger must be designed so that applying the same transfer twice does not double-charge Rajesh. The safe rule is: only mark the tray cleared after the work is truly done.

**One line to remember:** A crash before commit means those records are reprocessed on resume, which is at-least-once, so you disable auto-commit, commit only after successful processing, and make processing idempotent.

sections.s2_technical:
Kafka tracks each consumer group's position per partition as a committed offset stored in the internal offsets topic. A record is only considered done when its offset is committed. So if a consumer polls records at offsets 50 through 59, begins processing, and crashes at offset 55 before committing, the committed offset is still 50. When the group rebalances and another member or the restarted consumer takes over that partition, it resumes from offset 50 and reprocesses 50 through 59. The records are not lost, but some are processed twice.

The default behaviour makes this worse if misunderstood. With `enable.auto.commit=true`, the consumer commits offsets automatically on a timer controlled by `auto.commit.interval.ms`, by default every five seconds. The danger is that auto-commit can commit offsets for records you have polled but not yet finished processing, which can cause message loss if you crash after the auto-commit but before processing, because on resume those records are skipped. So auto-commit gives you a weak guarantee that is neither clean at-least-once nor exactly-once.

To get reliable at-least-once, you turn off auto-commit with `props.put("enable.auto.commit", "false")` and commit manually after processing succeeds. You poll a batch, process each record fully, including any database write, and only then call `consumer.commitSync()`, which blocks until the commit is acknowledged, or `consumer.commitAsync()` for lower latency with a callback to handle failures. Because you commit after processing, a crash before the commit simply means the batch is reprocessed on resume, so nothing is lost. The cost is possible duplicates, which is the defining tradeoff of at-least-once.

Since duplicates are possible, idempotent processing is essential. You design the downstream so that applying the same record twice has the same effect as applying it once. In banking you do this with an idempotency key, often the transfer id, and a processed-ids table or a unique constraint, so a second attempt to settle the same transfer is detected and skipped. Alternatively the operation itself is naturally idempotent, such as setting a balance to an absolute value computed from an authoritative source rather than incrementing.

A senior nuance is where you commit relative to external writes. If you commit before writing to the database, a crash in between loses the effect of the record even though the offset moved, which is at-most-once and unsafe. If you write to the database and then commit, a crash in between reprocesses, which is at-least-once and safe when idempotent. For true exactly-once you need Kafka transactions that commit the output and the offset atomically, or an idempotent sink. Another nuance is commit granularity: committing per record is slow, so you usually commit per batch after processing the whole batch, accepting that a crash reprocesses the whole batch. A final nuance is handling `commitAsync` failures and doing a final `commitSync` on shutdown or rebalance via a rebalance listener.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs a settlement consumer that reads transfer events and applies them to the ledger. A crash must never lose a transfer, and reprocessing must never double-charge a customer.

Problem 1 — with auto-commit, the consumer might commit offsets before the transfer is applied, so a crash could skip a transfer and lose Rajesh's money movement. This is exactly why auto-commit is disabled for reliable delivery.

Problem 2 — if the consumer crashes after applying a transfer but before committing, the transfer is reprocessed on resume. This is exactly at-least-once: safe from loss but prone to duplicates.

Problem 3 — a reprocessed transfer must not settle twice. This is exactly what idempotent processing with an idempotency key and a processed-ids set solves.

The code will show a manual-commit consumer that applies a transfer to a ledger, records the transfer id to prevent duplicates, and commits only after success, with a simulated crash before commit to show the reprocess-without-double-charge behaviour for Rajesh and Priya.

Input data: a batch of transfer events including TXF-00042, Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001) for fifty thousand rupees, at offset 55 in the partition.

Step 1 — the consumer polls the batch with auto-commit disabled. The committed offset is still 50 from the previous batch.

Step 2 — the consumer processes each record by applying the transfer to the idempotent ledger and recording its transfer id. When it reaches TXF-00042, the ledger applies it and records the id.

Step 4 — on restart, the group resumes from offset 50 and reprocesses the whole batch, including TXF-00042. Nothing is lost, which is the at-least-once guarantee.

Step 5 — when reprocessing reaches TXF-00042, the ledger sees the transfer id is already recorded and skips it, so Rajesh is not charged twice. Only after the whole batch processes cleanly does the consumer commit, moving the offset forward.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka records a consumer group's position as a committed offset, and a record is only considered done once its offset is committed. So if a consumer polls a batch, starts processing, and crashes before committing, the committed offset still points before that batch, and when the consumer or another group member resumes, it re-reads and reprocesses those records. Nothing is lost, but some records are processed more than once, and that is exactly the definition of at-least-once delivery.

The common mistake is relying on auto-commit, which commits on a timer and can commit offsets for records you have polled but not finished processing, which risks losing a record if you crash after the auto-commit. So for reliable at-least-once I disable auto-commit and commit manually only after processing succeeds. I poll a batch, process each record fully including the database write, and only then call commit-sync. Because the commit happens after processing, a crash before it simply causes a clean reprocess on resume.

Since duplicates are now possible, I make the processing idempotent. In banking I use an idempotency key, usually the transfer id, with a processed-ids table or a unique constraint, so a second attempt to settle the same transfer is detected and skipped. The ordering that matters is process, then persist, then commit the offset; committing before persisting would be at-most-once and could lose money, which is never acceptable.

In my National Bank of India settlement service, we disabled auto-commit and committed offsets only after applying each transfer to the ledger, and we keyed the ledger on the transfer id so reprocessing after a crash never double-charged customers like Rajesh. When we needed true exactly-once rather than at-least-once with idempotency, we moved to Kafka transactions that commit the output records and the consumer offsets atomically, but for most of our pipelines at-least-once with idempotent processing was the right, simpler choice.

answers.question: What do the key consumer configs do — `enable.auto.commit` (auto vs manual offset commit, and why manual + commit-after-processing gives at-least-once), `auto.offset.reset` (`earliest` vs `latest` when there is no committed offset), `max.poll.records` (max records per `poll()`, not a total cap), and `max.poll.interval.ms` (too-slow processing between polls triggers a rebalance)?
answers.shortTitle: What do the key consumer configs do?

s1_definition.profdef: These four consumer settings control correctness, startup behaviour, and liveness. `enable.auto.commit` decides whether offsets commit automatically on a timer or whether you commit manually, and committing manually after processing gives clean at-least-once delivery. `auto.offset.reset` decides where a consumer starts when there is no committed offset, with `earliest` reading the whole backlog and `latest` skipping everything older than the moment it joins. `max.poll.records` caps how many records a single `poll()` returns, not a total limit. `max.poll.interval.ms` bounds the time allowed between successive `poll()` calls, so processing a batch too slowly triggers a rebalance.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a settlement clerk at National Bank of India. The auto-commit setting is whether the clerk marks slips cleared automatically on a timer or only after actually doing the work, and only-after-work is the safe habit. The offset-reset setting is, for a brand-new clerk with no record of where to start, whether they begin from the oldest slip in the tray or only from slips that arrive after they sit down. The max-poll-records setting is how many slips the clerk grabs in one handful. And the max-poll-interval setting is the rule that if the clerk takes too long before grabbing the next handful, the supervisor assumes they are stuck and reassigns their tray to someone else.
s1_definition.oneliner: enable.auto.commit controls safe manual commit for at-least-once, auto.offset.reset picks backlog versus skip for a fresh group, max.poll.records sizes each poll batch, and max.poll.interval.ms evicts a consumer that processes a batch too slowly.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** These four consumer settings control correctness, startup behaviour, and liveness. `enable.auto.commit` decides whether offsets commit automatically on a timer or whether you commit manually, and committing manually after processing gives clean at-least-once delivery. `auto.offset.reset` decides where a consumer starts when there is no committed offset, with `earliest` reading the whole backlog and `latest` skipping everything older than the moment it joins. `max.poll.records` caps how many records a single `poll()` returns, not a total limit. `max.poll.interval.ms` bounds the time allowed between successive `poll()` calls, so processing a batch too slowly triggers a rebalance.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a settlement clerk at National Bank of India. The auto-commit setting is whether the clerk marks slips cleared automatically on a timer or only after actually doing the work, and only-after-work is the safe habit. The offset-reset setting is, for a brand-new clerk with no record of where to start, whether they begin from the oldest slip in the tray or only from slips that arrive after they sit down. The max-poll-records setting is how many slips the clerk grabs in one handful. And the max-poll-interval setting is the rule that if the clerk takes too long before grabbing the next handful, the supervisor assumes they are stuck and reassigns their tray to someone else.

**One line to remember:** enable.auto.commit controls safe manual commit for at-least-once, auto.offset.reset picks backlog versus skip for a fresh group, max.poll.records sizes each poll batch, and max.poll.interval.ms evicts a consumer that processes a batch too slowly.

sections.s2_technical:
The `enable.auto.commit` setting, default true, makes the consumer commit the last polled offsets automatically every `auto.commit.interval.ms`, by default five seconds. The problem is that this timer is independent of whether you have finished processing, so auto-commit can advance the offset past records you have not yet handled. If you crash in that window, those records are skipped, which is message loss. To get clean at-least-once you set `props.put("enable.auto.commit", "false")` and call `consumer.commitSync()` only after a record or batch is fully processed. Because the commit follows processing, a crash before commit causes a reprocess, not a loss, and that is the defining at-least-once behaviour.

The `auto.offset.reset` setting decides where to start only when there is no valid committed offset for the group and partition, which happens for a brand-new group or when the committed offset has been deleted by retention. With `props.put("auto.offset.reset", "earliest")` the consumer starts at the oldest available record, so a new group reads the entire backlog, which you want for a system that must process all history. With `latest` the consumer starts at the end, so it only sees records produced after it joins and silently skips everything that already existed, which is a classic cause of a brand-new consumer appearing to receive nothing. The setting does nothing when a committed offset exists, because then the consumer simply resumes there.

The `max.poll.records` setting, default five hundred, caps how many records a single call to `poll()` returns. It is not a total limit on consumption and not a byte limit; it just shapes each batch. You tune it down, for example `props.put("max.poll.records", 50)`, when each record is expensive to process, so that you process and poll again frequently and do not blow the poll interval. You tune it up for lightweight records to improve throughput. The important misconception to avoid is thinking it limits total messages; it only limits per-poll batch size.

The `max.poll.interval.ms` setting, default five minutes, bounds the maximum time allowed between two successive `poll()` calls. The consumer must call `poll()` again within this window, because `poll()` is also how the consumer signals liveness for processing progress. If your handler takes longer than this to process a batch, the group coordinator assumes the consumer is stuck, removes it from the group, and triggers a rebalance that reassigns its partitions to others. This is why a slow message handler causes a rebalance even when heartbeats are still flowing: liveness of processing is separate from the heartbeat, and it is enforced by the poll interval. You fix a too-slow consumer by lowering `max.poll.records` so each batch is smaller, by speeding up processing, or by raising `max.poll.interval.ms` if the work genuinely takes longer.

A senior nuance is how these interact. Manual commit plus a right-sized `max.poll.records` plus a sane `max.poll.interval.ms` together give a consumer that is both safe and stable: it processes bounded batches, commits only after success, and does not get evicted mid-batch. Another nuance is that after a rebalance caused by a blown poll interval, the reassigned partitions may be reprocessed, so idempotency still matters. A final nuance is that `auto.offset.reset=none` throws if there is no committed offset, which you use when you want to fail loudly rather than guess where to start.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India deploys a new fraud-scoring consumer. The team must configure it so it processes the full transaction backlog, never loses a transaction, grabs a sensible batch size, and does not get kicked out of its group while scoring a heavy batch.

Problem 1 — the consumer must read all existing transactions, not just new ones. This is exactly what `auto.offset.reset=earliest` provides for a fresh group.

Problem 2 — a fraud transaction must never be silently skipped. This is exactly what disabling auto-commit and committing after scoring provides: clean at-least-once.

Problem 3 — scoring each record is slow, so grabbing five hundred at once takes too long and the group evicts the consumer, causing a rebalance. This is exactly what tuning `max.poll.records` down and respecting `max.poll.interval.ms` solves.

The code will show a fraud consumer with these four settings configured, processing bounded batches, committing only after scoring, and logging how the settings keep it correct and stable for Rajesh's and Priya's transactions.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transactions topic with a large existing backlog, consumed by a brand-new fraud-scoring group.

Step 1 — because the group is new and there is no committed offset, `auto.offset.reset=earliest` makes the consumer start at the oldest record, so it reads the entire backlog rather than skipping it.

Step 2 — each `poll()` returns at most fifty records because `max.poll.records` is fifty, even though thousands sit in the topic. This keeps each batch small enough to score within the poll interval.

Step 3 — the consumer scores each of the up-to-fifty records. Scoring is expensive, but because the batch is bounded, the whole batch finishes well within the five-minute `max.poll.interval.ms`, so the coordinator does not evict the consumer.

Step 4 — only after scoring the whole batch does the consumer call commit-sync. Because auto-commit is off and the commit follows processing, a crash before commit reprocesses the batch rather than losing it, giving at-least-once.

Step 5 — the loop polls again within the interval, so the consumer stays a healthy group member and no rebalance is triggered.

sections.s6_takeaway:
These four consumer settings control correctness, startup behaviour, and liveness. The auto-commit setting decides whether offsets commit automatically on a timer or manually. The danger of automatic commit is that it can advance the offset past records you have not finished processing, so a crash in that window loses them. So for clean at-least-once I disable auto-commit and call commit only after a batch is fully processed, which means a crash before the commit causes a safe reprocess rather than a loss.

The offset-reset setting only matters when there is no committed offset, such as a brand-new group. Earliest starts at the oldest record so the group reads the whole backlog, which is what you want for a system that must process all history. Latest starts at the end and silently skips everything that already existed, which is a classic reason a brand-new consumer appears to receive nothing. When a committed offset already exists, this setting does nothing because the consumer just resumes.

The max-poll-records setting caps how many records a single poll returns; it is not a total limit and not a byte limit, it just shapes each batch, and I size it down when each record is expensive to process. The max-poll-interval setting bounds the time allowed between successive polls, because polling is how the consumer proves its processing is making progress. If my handler takes longer than that interval, the coordinator assumes I am stuck, evicts me, and triggers a rebalance, which is why a slow handler causes a rebalance even though heartbeats are still flowing.

In my National Bank of India fraud-scoring consumer, I set reset to earliest so it scored the full transaction backlog, disabled auto-commit and committed after scoring so no transaction was ever lost, and because scoring was expensive I lowered max-poll-records so each batch finished well inside the poll interval and the consumer was never evicted mid-batch. Those four settings together gave me a consumer that was complete, safe, and stable.

**One line to remember:** Unconsumed-but-no-errors is usually already-committed offsets, a latest reset skipping the backlog, more consumers than partitions leaving some idle, or a stuck rebalance, and consumer-groups describe shows the offsets, lag, and assignment that tell you which.

sections.s2_technical:
The first cause is that the group already committed those offsets. Kafka does not redeliver committed messages to the same group, because the committed offset marks them as consumed. If someone ran the consumer earlier and it committed through the latest offset, then a fresh run of the same group sees nothing new to process even though the records still physically exist in the topic for their retention period. The fix is either to reset the group's offsets back, using `kafka-consumer-groups --reset-offsets --to-earliest --execute`, or to use a new `group.id`, which has no committed offsets and therefore follows the reset policy.

The second cause is `auto.offset.reset=latest` on a brand-new group. For a group with no committed offset, latest starts at the end of each partition, so every record that already existed before the consumer joined is skipped silently. The app runs without errors and simply waits for new records, while the backlog sits untouched. The fix is to set `auto.offset.reset=earliest` if you need the backlog, then either restart the new group or reset its offsets to earliest.

The third cause is more consumers than partitions. Within a consumer group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so if a topic has three partitions and you run five consumers in the group, two consumers get no partitions and sit idle doing nothing, which can look like messages are not being consumed if you are watching those idle instances. The data is still consumed by the three active consumers, but the idle ones mislead you. The fix is to match or exceed partitions to the parallelism you need, since you cannot have more active consumers in a group than partitions.

The fourth cause is a group stuck rebalancing. If members keep joining and leaving, perhaps because of a blown poll interval or flapping instances, the group spends its time rebalancing and never settles into stable assignment, so little or no processing happens. The describe command shows the group in a rebalancing or preparing state and may show no stable member assignment. The fix is to stabilize membership: fix the slow processing that trips the poll interval, stop the flapping, and let the group settle.

The diagnostic tool is `kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server ... --describe --group yourgroup`. It prints, per partition, the current offset the group has committed, the log-end offset which is the newest record, and the lag which is the difference. It also shows which consumer member and client host owns each partition. Reading this tells you the cause directly: if current offset equals log-end offset with zero lag, the group already consumed everything, pointing to cause one or two; if lag is high but no member owns the partitions, you have idle consumers or a rebalance problem; if some partitions have no owner, membership is unstable. A senior nuance is to also check the group state field, which shows Stable, PreparingRebalance, or CompletingRebalance, and to confirm the consumer is actually subscribed to the topic you think it is, since a topic name typo produces the same symptom.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India deploys a new reconciliation consumer, but operators report that transactions sit in the topic unconsumed while the app logs no errors. The on-call engineer must diagnose which of the four causes it is.

Problem 1 — maybe a previous run already committed those offsets, so Kafka will not redeliver them. The engineer must check committed offset versus log-end offset.

Problem 2 — maybe the new group used latest and skipped the backlog. The engineer must check whether lag equals the backlog and the reset policy.

Problem 3 — maybe there are more consumer instances than partitions, so some are idle. The engineer must check member assignment against partition count.

Problem 4 — maybe the group is stuck rebalancing. The engineer must check the group state.

The code will model a diagnostic helper that, given per-partition offsets, member assignments, and group state, reports the most likely cause and the fix, logged for the reconciliation group.

sections.s6_takeaway:
When a consumer runs cleanly but messages sit unconsumed, I look at offsets, membership, and assignment, not at a crash, because there is no error. There are four classic causes. The first is that the group already committed those offsets, and Kafka does not redeliver committed messages to the same group, so the records exist physically but the group has nothing new to read. The fix is to reset the group's offsets backward or use a brand-new group id.

The second cause is a brand-new group with the reset policy set to latest, which starts at the end of each partition and silently skips everything that already existed. The app waits for new records while the backlog is untouched, so the fix is to set the policy to earliest and reset to earliest if you need that backlog. The third cause is running more consumers than partitions, because within a group a partition is owned by exactly one consumer, so extra consumers sit idle and can mislead you into thinking nothing is consumed, when really the active consumers handle all partitions. The fix is to add partitions or reduce consumers. The fourth cause is a group stuck rebalancing, often from a blown poll interval or flapping instances, where the group never settles into stable assignment and processes little.

The tool that tells me which cause it is is the consumer-groups describe command. It prints, per partition, the current committed offset, the log-end offset which is the newest record, the lag between them, and which member owns the partition, plus the group state. If lag is zero and current equals log-end, the group already consumed everything. If lag is high but no member owns the partitions, I have idle consumers or an unstable group. The group state field distinguishes a stable group from one stuck preparing a rebalance.

In my National Bank of India work, a new reconciliation consumer once appeared to process nothing with no errors. The describe output showed large lag with the current offset at zero and the reset policy set to latest on a fresh group, so it had skipped the whole backlog. We changed the policy to earliest and reset the offsets to earliest, and the backlog drained immediately. Having that decision tree and that one command turned a confusing non-error into a two-minute diagnosis.

answers.shortTitle: What is the difference between session.timeout.ms, heartbeat.interval.ms, and max.poll.interval.ms for detecting a dead consumer?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka detects a failed consumer two independent ways. A background heartbeat thread sends heartbeats every `heartbeat.interval.ms`, and the group coordinator evicts the consumer if no heartbeat arrives within `session.timeout.ms`, which detects a crashed or network-unreachable consumer. Separately, `max.poll.interval.ms` bounds the time allowed between successive `poll()` calls on the application thread, and the coordinator evicts a consumer that is still alive and heartbeating but stuck processing a batch longer than that interval, which detects a stalled consumer. A slow handler trips the poll interval even while heartbeats flow because heartbeats prove the process is up, while the poll interval proves processing is progressing, and those are different liveness signals on different threads.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a settlement clerk at National Bank of India. The heartbeat is the clerk waving at the supervisor every few seconds to say I am here and alive. The session timeout is the supervisor's rule that if no wave comes for a while, assume the clerk collapsed and reassign their tray. But waving does not prove the clerk is actually clearing slips; the clerk could be frozen staring at one impossible slip while still waving. So there is a second rule, the poll interval: if the clerk does not come back to grab the next handful of slips within a set time, the supervisor assumes they are stuck, even though they keep waving, and reassigns the tray.
s1_definition.oneliner: Heartbeat interval and session timeout detect a dead or unreachable consumer via a background thread, while max poll interval detects a live but stalled consumer via the application thread, so a slow handler triggers a rebalance even with heartbeats still flowing.

But waving does not prove the clerk is actually clearing slips; the clerk could be frozen staring at one impossible slip while still waving. sections.s2_technical:
Modern Kafka consumers use two separate threads for liveness. A background heartbeat thread handles group membership, and the application thread handles polling and processing. This separation is the key to understanding these three settings, because two of them belong to the heartbeat thread and one belongs to the application thread.

The `heartbeat.interval.ms`, default three seconds, is how often the background thread sends a heartbeat to the group coordinator. Heartbeats are cheap and frequent, and they say the consumer process is alive and connected. You keep this well below the session timeout, commonly a third of it, so several heartbeats fit inside one session window and a single lost heartbeat does not cause eviction.

The `session.timeout.ms`, default forty-five seconds in recent versions, is how long the coordinator waits without a heartbeat before declaring the consumer dead and triggering a rebalance to reassign its partitions. This detects a crashed consumer, a killed process, or a network partition, because in those cases the heartbeat thread stops sending. You set it with `props.put("session.timeout.ms", 45000)`, and it must fall within the broker-allowed range set by group min and max session timeout. A short session timeout detects crashes faster but risks false evictions on brief network blips; a longer one is more tolerant but slower to react.

The `max.poll.interval.ms`, default five minutes, is the maximum time allowed between two successive `poll()` calls on the application thread. Crucially, `poll()` is the signal that the application is making processing progress. If your handler takes longer than this interval to process a batch, the consumer proactively leaves the group, and the coordinator reassigns its partitions. This detects a stalled consumer that is still up and still heartbeating but no longer doing useful work, such as one blocked on a slow downstream call or an infinite loop.

This is exactly why a slow message handler triggers a rebalance even though heartbeats are still flowing. The heartbeat thread keeps running independently, so from the coordinator's membership view the consumer looks alive. But the application thread is stuck inside your handler and has not called `poll()` again within the poll interval, so the poll-interval mechanism concludes that processing has stalled and evicts the consumer. The two mechanisms answer different questions: is the process up, and is the processing progressing.

The practical tuning follows from this. To avoid spurious rebalances from slow processing, you either make the handler faster, reduce `max.poll.records` so each batch is smaller and finishes within the interval, or raise `max.poll.interval.ms` if the work genuinely needs more time. To tune crash detection, you adjust the session timeout and heartbeat interval together, keeping the heartbeat interval a small fraction of the session timeout. A senior nuance is that after a poll-interval eviction, the partitions are reassigned and likely reprocessed, so idempotency matters, and the reprocessing plus the rebalance itself can cascade if many consumers are slow. Another nuance is that doing heavy work on a separate thread and pausing and resuming partitions is a pattern to keep polling while long work proceeds, decoupling processing time from the poll interval.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs a settlement consumer that occasionally calls a slow external compliance service per transaction. Operators see frequent rebalances even though the consumers never crash, and they must understand which timeout is firing.

Problem 1 — a consumer whose process dies must be detected and its partitions reassigned. This is exactly what heartbeat interval and session timeout do.

Problem 2 — a consumer that is alive and heartbeating but blocked for minutes on the slow compliance call must also be detected so its work moves elsewhere. This is exactly what max poll interval does.

Problem 3 — operators are confused why a healthy, heartbeating consumer gets evicted. This is exactly the point that heartbeats prove the process is up while the poll interval proves processing is progressing, and they are different signals on different threads.

The code will model a liveness monitor that, given the time since the last heartbeat and the time spent in the current batch, decides whether the coordinator would evict the consumer and why, logged for the settlement group.

Input data: three liveness snapshots with different heartbeat ages and batch durations, with a session timeout of forty-five seconds and a poll interval of five minutes.

Step 2 — in the crashed case no heartbeat has arrived for sixty seconds, which exceeds the forty-five-second session timeout. The monitor reports eviction triggered by the session timeout, because the background heartbeat thread stopped, meaning the process is down or unreachable. The coordinator reassigns its partitions.

Step 3 — in the stalled case heartbeats are fine at two seconds, but the application thread has been inside one batch for six minutes, exceeding the five-minute poll interval. The monitor reports eviction triggered by the poll interval, explicitly noting heartbeats were still flowing. This is the subtle case: the process is alive and waving, but processing has stalled, so the poll-interval mechanism evicts it.

```
2026-10-24 23:40:01 [WARNING] Alive but stalled on slow compliance call → EVICTED by max.poll.interval.ms: no poll() for 360000ms (handler stalled; heartbeats still OK)
```

```
             │        ▼

             │        └──→ consumer leaves group → EVICT (STALL detected)
             │             (fires EVEN THOUGH heartbeats still flowing)
             ▼
        proves: PROCESSING IS PROGRESSING

  Two independent liveness signals on two threads → two eviction triggers.
```
