sections.s6_takeaway:
In a compacted topic, deleting a key does not remove a row the way a database delete does. Instead you publish a tombstone, which is a record carrying the key with a null value. Compaction then promises to keep at least the latest value per key and, over time, to remove the older values and eventually the tombstone itself. The reason you can still see old records for a key you thought you deleted is that compaction is a lazy, asynchronous background job with several timing rules, so what you are seeing is almost always expected timing rather than a failure.

There are three timing rules that cause this. First, compaction runs in the background via the log cleaner, so there is always a gap between your write and the physical removal of old values. Second, the cleaner only works on closed segments, never on the active segment that is still being appended to, and it only bothers once the stale fraction of the log crosses the cleanable dirty ratio, so recent records simply have not become eligible yet. Third, the tombstone is deliberately retained for the delete retention window, which defaults to twenty-four hours, so that consumers that are behind get a chance to actually read the delete before it vanishes. Until a cleaning pass has processed the segments holding the old values, those old values sit ahead of the tombstone in the log and are perfectly visible.

On the National Bank of India profile stream we hit this exactly. Compliance asked us to delete Rajesh's profile from the compacted account.profiles topic. We produced a tombstone for his account, immediately replayed the topic to verify, and still saw three old versions. Nothing was wrong: the cleaner had not yet run on the closed segments and would never have touched the fresh tombstone in the active segment. After a compaction pass the old versions collapsed, and the tombstone stayed for the retention window so our slower consumers could still learn about the delete.

The second half of the lesson is that tombstones only work if consumers cooperate. One of our cache services was ignoring null values, so even after compaction it kept a stale entry for Rajesh forever. The fix was to make every consumer treat a null value as an instruction to evict the key from its local view. When I need deletes to take effect faster, I tune the topic by rolling segments sooner, lowering the cleanable dirty ratio so the cleaner runs more aggressively, and shortening the delete retention window, but I never set that window so short that a slow consumer could miss the delete and hold a stale key. The one thing I always warn about is that a record with a null key cannot be compacted at all, because compaction is keyed, so a mistakenly null-keyed record will linger until ordinary retention removes it.

---

answers.question: Does the idempotent producer protect you from application-level duplicate publishes?
answers.shortTitle: Does the idempotent producer protect you from application-level duplicate publishes?

s1_definition.profdef: No. The idempotent producer, enabled with `enable.idempotence=true`, only guarantees that the Kafka client's own internal retries do not create duplicates on the broker. It works by tagging each record with a producer id, an epoch, and a monotonically increasing per-partition sequence number, so the broker can detect and discard a retransmission of a record it already persisted. It does not deduplicate two logically distinct `send()` calls that your application code made, because those carry different sequence numbers and the broker treats them as two separate records. Application-level duplicates require an application-level idempotency key and a dedup check, not the idempotent producer.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh mails a transfer instruction to National Bank of India. The post office (the Kafka client) guarantees that if it has to resend the same sealed envelope because of a delivery hiccup, the bank will only process it once, because each envelope has a tracking number and the bank ignores a tracking number it already saw. That is the idempotent producer. But if Rajesh himself, worried the first letter was lost, writes a brand new letter asking for the same transfer and mails it, those are two different envelopes with two different tracking numbers, and the bank will happily process both, debiting him twice. Stopping that requires Rajesh to write his own reference number on the request and the bank to reject a reference it already honored. That is application-level idempotency.
s1_definition.oneliner: The idempotent producer deduplicates the client's retransmissions within one producer session, not two separate sends from your code — for application-level duplicates you need your own idempotency key and a dedup store.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** No. The idempotent producer, enabled with `enable.idempotence=true`, only guarantees that the Kafka client's own internal retries do not create duplicates on the broker. It works by tagging each record with a producer id, an epoch, and a monotonically increasing per-partition sequence number, so the broker can detect and discard a retransmission of a record it already persisted. It does not deduplicate two logically distinct `send()` calls that your application code made, because those carry different sequence numbers and the broker treats them as two separate records. Application-level duplicates require an application-level idempotency key and a dedup check, not the idempotent producer.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh mails a transfer instruction to National Bank of India. The post office (the Kafka client) guarantees that if it has to resend the same sealed envelope because of a delivery hiccup, the bank will only process it once, because each envelope has a tracking number and the bank ignores a tracking number it already saw. That is the idempotent producer. But if Rajesh himself, worried the first letter was lost, writes a brand new letter asking for the same transfer and mails it, those are two different envelopes with two different tracking numbers, and the bank will happily process both, debiting him twice. Stopping that requires Rajesh to write his own reference number on the request and the bank to reject a reference it already honored. That is application-level idempotency.

**One line to remember:** The idempotent producer deduplicates the client's retransmissions within one producer session, not two separate sends from your code — for application-level duplicates you need your own idempotency key and a dedup store.

sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India exposes a transfer API. When the API publishes a settlement event, it uses an idempotent producer because the team assumed that was enough to prevent double settlements. Rajesh (SAV2001) transfers to Priya (CUR3001).

Problem 1 — Rajesh's mobile app timed out waiting for the transfer response and automatically retried the HTTP request. The API handled both requests and called the publish method twice for the same transfer id. The idempotent producer did nothing to stop this, because these were two separate sends, so two settlement events landed and Priya was credited twice. This is exactly the limit of the idempotent producer: it only catches the client's own retransmissions.

Problem 2 — we needed a fix that works even across producer restarts and across multiple API instances. This is why the real fix lives at the consumer, using the transfer id as an idempotency key against a durable store.

Our runnable demo models an `IdempotentProducer` that dedupes only its own retransmissions by sequence number, shows that two application sends still produce two records, and then a `DedupConsumer` that uses a transfer id against a processed-keys store to apply the settlement exactly once. The classes are `DuplicateDemo`, `IdempotentProducer`, `Broker`, `SettlementEvent`, and `DedupConsumer`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one logical transfer with id TXF-123 crediting Priya fifty thousand, under three scenarios.

Step 1: The idempotent producer sends the settlement for TXF-123. The broker assigns it sequence zero for this producer id and partition and persists one record.

Step 2: The acknowledgment is lost, so the client retransmits the exact same batch with the same sequence zero. The broker sees a sequence it already accepted and discards the retransmission, so the record count stays at one. This is the idempotent producer doing its job against client retries.

Step 3: Now the mobile app retried the HTTP request, so the API called the publish method twice. The producer issues two sends with two different sequence numbers. The broker treats them as two distinct records and persists both. The record count is two, a duplicate settlement, and the idempotent producer did nothing, because these were not retransmissions of the same batch.

Step 4: The consumer reads both records. On the first, the transfer id TXF-123 is not in the processed store, so it credits Priya and records the id. On the second, TXF-123 is already present, so it skips the credit and acknowledges. Priya is credited exactly once.

Step 5: This dedup store is durable and shared, so it also protects against producer restarts and multiple API instances, which the in-session idempotent producer could never do, confirming the fix must live at the application and consumer level keyed by the business id.

sections.s6_takeaway:
No, the idempotent producer does not protect you from application-level duplicate publishes, and understanding why is important. The idempotent producer, which you turn on with enable idempotence true, solves exactly one narrow problem: duplicates caused by the Kafka client's own retries. It tags every record batch with a producer id, an epoch, and a monotonically increasing per-partition sequence number, so if the producer resends a batch because an acknowledgment was lost, the broker recognizes the sequence number it already accepted and discards the retransmission. That removes duplicates from retries and also preserves ordering. But the sequence number is assigned by the client per send call, so if your application code calls send twice for the same business event, those are two different sequence numbers and the broker stores two separate records. The idempotent producer has no notion of business identity.

This is exactly the trap we hit on the National Bank of India transfer API. Rajesh's mobile app timed out and automatically retried the HTTP request, our API processed both requests and published the settlement twice for the same transfer id, and because these were two independent sends and not a client retransmission, both landed on the topic and Priya was credited twice. The idempotent producer was enabled the whole time and was powerless, because it only ever deduplicates the client's own retransmission of the same batch within a single producer session.

The correct fix is an application-level idempotency key combined with a durable dedup check, placed as close as possible to the side effect. Our events carry the transfer id as the idempotency key, and the consumer that actually applies the credit first checks a processed-transfers table with the transfer id as its primary key. If the id is already there, it skips the credit and acknowledges; if not, it credits the account and records the id in the same database transaction. Because that store is durable and shared across all consumer instances, it protects us even across producer restarts and multiple API pods, which the in-session idempotent producer could never do.

The mental model I give the team is a layered one. The idempotent producer handles the transport layer, meaning retries on the wire. Kafka transactions build on it to give atomic multi-partition writes and effectively-once consumption within Kafka, but even transactions do not know that two of your sends mean the same thing. Business-level exactly-once is your responsibility and lives in your idempotency key and dedup store, and when a publish must be exactly-once together with a database write, I reach for the transactional outbox pattern so there is a single source of truth for whether the event exists. In short, the idempotent producer is necessary but never sufficient for real-world duplicate prevention.

answers.question: Your consumer is structurally slower than your producer indefinitely — what happens, given Kafka has no built-in backpressure?
answers.shortTitle: Your consumer is structurally slower than your producer indefinitely — what happens, given Kafka has no built-in backpressure?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka decouples producers and consumers through a durable log, so a producer is never slowed down by a slow consumer; there is no end-to-end backpressure that throttles the producer. If a consumer group's aggregate processing rate is permanently below the producer's rate, the gap accumulates as ever-growing consumer lag, which is the number of messages between the latest produced offset and the committed consumer offset. Lag grows without bound, end-to-end latency grows with it, and eventually the oldest unconsumed messages are deleted by retention before the consumer ever reads them, which is silent data loss from the consumer's perspective.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has one clerk opening a mail slot and reading transfer letters, while ten branches keep dropping letters into the slot faster than the clerk can read. The mailbox (the Kafka log) is huge, so the branches never have to wait; they just keep dropping letters. But the pile the clerk has not read keeps growing every single day. Rajesh's transfer letter sinks deeper into the unread pile, so by the time the clerk reaches it, hours have passed. Worse, the mailbox has a rule that letters older than seven days are shredded. If the clerk never catches up, Rajesh's letter is shredded before it is ever read, and nobody is told.
s1_definition.oneliner: With no backpressure, a permanently slow consumer causes lag to grow forever, latency to climb, and eventually retention to delete unread messages — so you must fix the throughput imbalance, not wait for Kafka to slow the producer.

Lag grows without bound, end-to-end latency grows with it, and eventually the oldest unconsumed messages are deleted by retention before the consumer ever reads them, which is silent data loss from the consumer's perspective.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has one clerk opening a mail slot and reading transfer letters, while ten branches keep dropping letters into the slot faster than the clerk can read. **One line to remember:** With no backpressure, a permanently slow consumer causes lag to grow forever, latency to climb, and eventually retention to delete unread messages — so you must fix the throughput imbalance, not wait for Kafka to slow the producer.

sections.s2_technical:
The first thing to internalize is that Kafka deliberately has no end-to-end backpressure. A producer writes to the log and gets acknowledged based only on broker replication; it does not know or care how far behind consumers are. This decoupling is a feature, because it lets producers and consumers scale and fail independently, but it means the system will never automatically slow the producer to match a slow consumer. The consequence of a permanent rate imbalance is unbounded lag.

Lag is a concrete, measurable quantity. For each partition, lag equals the log end offset, which is the offset of the next message to be produced, minus the consumer's committed offset. You read it with the consumer group tool: `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group settlement-apply --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092` shows a LAG column per partition. If the producer rate exceeds the consumer rate indefinitely, this number climbs steadily. Two bad things follow. End-to-end latency, the time from when a message is produced to when it is processed, grows roughly in proportion to lag divided by consumer throughput. And because the log has retention, configured by `retention.ms` or `retention.bytes`, the broker eventually deletes the oldest segments. If lag grows until the committed offset points at data that has already been deleted, the consumer skips forward to the earliest available offset and those messages are lost to it, usually surfacing as an offset-out-of-range situation governed by `auto.offset.reset`.

Now the fixes, because the real answer to the interviewer is how you resolve the imbalance. The most direct lever is consumer parallelism: add consumers to the group up to the number of partitions, because the maximum useful parallelism in a group equals the partition count. If you already have one consumer per partition and still cannot keep up, you must add partitions to the topic so you can add more consumers, accepting the key-remapping caveat that comes with repartitioning. Beyond scaling out, you speed up each consumer: process records in parallel within a consumer using a worker pool while being careful about offset commit ordering, batch expensive operations such as database writes, remove per-record synchronous calls to slow dependencies, and tune `max.poll.records` and `fetch.max.bytes` so each poll does useful bulk work. You can also offload: if each message triggers heavy work, have the consumer quickly hand the work to an internal bounded queue or a separate scaled worker tier, which is how you create application-level backpressure since Kafka gives you none.

Application-level backpressure deserves emphasis because it is the real answer to "Kafka has no backpressure." You build it yourself. A common pattern is the consumer uses `pause()` and `resume()` on partitions when its internal work queue is full, so it stops fetching more until it drains, which prevents it from pulling messages it cannot yet handle and keeps memory bounded. In Spring Kafka you achieve similar control with container concurrency and by not acknowledging until work completes. Reactive frameworks like Reactor Kafka expose real backpressure to the application layer by only requesting as many records as downstream demand allows. None of this slows the producer, but it keeps the consumer stable and makes lag an explicit, managed signal rather than an unbounded memory or latency problem.

Senior-level nuances: first, if the imbalance is only bursty rather than permanent, lag is healthy and self-correcting, and the log is precisely the buffer that absorbs the burst, so do not over-engineer for a steady-state problem you do not have. Second, you must size retention so that it comfortably exceeds your worst-case recovery time, giving you room to catch up after an incident without losing data. Third, you should alert on lag trend, not just absolute lag, because a steadily rising lag is the early warning of a structural imbalance long before retention deletes anything. Fourth, watch out for a single hot partition masquerading as a global throughput problem, because one slow or oversized partition can dominate lag even when the group as a whole has spare capacity.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India ingests card-authorization events into the `card.auth` topic and a consumer group performs a fraud score on each one, which involves a slow model call. Producers emit two thousand events per second during the day. Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) generate card authorizations.

Problem 1 — the fraud scorer processes only one thousand two hundred events per second with its current setup, so it is permanently eight hundred per second behind. Because Kafka never slows the producers, the unprocessed backlog grows all day. This is the no-backpressure reality: lag climbs without bound.

Problem 2 — retention on `card.auth` is six hours. During a heavy day the lag grew to represent more than six hours of events, so the oldest authorizations were deleted before the scorer read them, meaning some fraud checks never happened. This is the silent data loss that retention causes when a slow consumer never catches up.

Our runnable demo simulates a producer rate and a consumer rate over time, tracks lag, shows lag crossing the retention horizon and causing dropped events, and then applies two fixes: scaling consumers up to the partition count, and adding application-level backpressure with a bounded queue and pause/resume so the consumer stays stable. The classes are `BackpressureDemo`, `PartitionedTopic`, `ConsumerGroup`, and `BoundedWorkQueue`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: producers emitting two thousand card authorizations per second, a fraud scorer consuming at one thousand two hundred per second, and a six-hour retention.

Step 1: Every second two thousand events are appended to the log and acknowledged to producers purely on replication. Producers never slow down, regardless of the scorer's state.

Step 2: The scorer processes one thousand two hundred events that second, so eight hundred events accumulate as new lag. Lag rises by eight hundred every second, climbing steadily through the day because the imbalance is structural, not bursty.

Step 3: End-to-end latency rises with lag. A card authorization produced now will not be fraud-scored until the scorer works through everything ahead of it, so Rajesh's authorization might be scored hours after it occurred, which for fraud is effectively useless.

Step 4: Lag eventually represents more than six hours of events. The broker deletes the oldest segments per the retention policy, and those authorizations are gone before the scorer reads them. The scorer's committed offset falls off the start of the log, so it jumps forward and those events are never scored, a silent loss of fraud checks.

Step 5: After scaling the group to process two thousand four hundred per second, each second consumes more than is produced, so lag drains and stabilizes near zero, latency returns to seconds, and nothing is dropped. Separately, the bounded work queue with pause and resume keeps the consumer's memory bounded during spikes by applying the backpressure Kafka itself does not provide.

Final output:

```
[2026-10-24 23:05:33] [INFO] === Before fix: 1 consumer group @ 1200/sec (structurally slow) ===
[2026-10-24 23:05:33] [SEVERE] Final lag=43200000 events; DROPPED by retention=19872000 (fraud checks NEVER ran — silent loss)
[2026-10-24 23:05:33] [INFO] === Fix 1: scale consumers to match (12 partitions, 2400/sec) ===
[2026-10-24 23:05:33] [INFO] Final lag=0 events; nothing dropped, consumer keeps up
[2026-10-24 23:05:33] [INFO] === Fix 2: application backpressure keeps memory bounded ===
[2026-10-24 23:05:33] [INFO] Bounded queue held at capacity 5000 (consumer paused instead of exhausting heap)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka deliberately has no end-to-end backpressure, and that is the key to this question. A producer is acknowledged based only on broker replication and never learns or cares how far behind the consumers are, which is exactly what lets producers and consumers scale and fail independently. The flip side is that if a consumer group's processing rate is permanently below the producer's rate, nothing in Kafka will slow the producer down. Instead the gap accumulates as consumer lag, which is the difference between the latest produced offset and the consumer's committed offset, and that lag grows without bound.

Three bad things follow from unbounded lag. End-to-end latency climbs roughly in proportion to lag over consumer throughput, so a message produced now might be processed hours later, which for something like fraud scoring is worthless. Memory can blow up if the consumer naively keeps fetching messages it cannot process. And most dangerously, retention eventually deletes the oldest unread segments, so if lag grows past the retention horizon, those messages are gone before the consumer ever reads them. The consumer's offset falls off the start of the log and it jumps forward, silently losing data.

On the National Bank of India card-authorization pipeline we lived this. Producers emitted two thousand events per second while the fraud scorer managed only twelve hundred, so lag grew all day and eventually crossed the six-hour retention window, which meant some authorizations were deleted before they were ever fraud-scored. The fix had three parts. First, we scaled consumer parallelism up to the partition count, and because that was still not enough we added partitions so we could add more consumers, so steady-state consumption exceeded production and lag drained to near zero. Second, we made each consumer faster by batching the database writes and parallelizing the slow model call with a worker pool. Third, we built application-level backpressure ourselves, since Kafka gives none, using a bounded internal queue and the consumer's pause and resume so that when the queue fills the consumer stops fetching and keeps its memory bounded instead of collapsing.

The principle I emphasize is that because Kafka will not throttle the producer for you, a structural throughput imbalance is an application design problem you must solve by scaling and speeding up the consumer side and by sizing retention above your worst-case recovery time. I also alert on lag trend rather than just absolute lag, because a steadily rising lag is the early warning of a structural imbalance, and I watch for a single hot partition that can make the whole group look slow even when it has spare capacity. If the imbalance is only bursty, I do nothing special, because the log is precisely the buffer designed to absorb bursts and the lag will self-correct.

answers.question: You need exactly-once across a database write and a Kafka publish — why don't Kafka transactions cover this, and what is the fix (transactional outbox)?
answers.shortTitle: You need exactly-once across a database write and a Kafka publish — why don't Kafka transactions cover this, and what is the fix (transactional outbox)?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka transactions are atomic only across Kafka itself; they coordinate writes to Kafka topics and consumer offset commits within a single Kafka transaction, but they have no visibility into or control over an external database. When you must write a row to your database and publish an event to Kafka as one atomic unit, Kafka transactions cannot span both systems because there is no shared transaction coordinator across the database and the broker, and a reliable distributed two-phase commit across them is impractical. The standard fix is the transactional outbox pattern: in one local database transaction you write both the business row and an outbox row, and a separate relay reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka, so the database is the single source of truth for whether the event exists.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India must do two things together when Rajesh transfers money: update his account ledger in the vault's ledger book, and send a notice to the central clearing house. The ledger book is the database and the clearing house is Kafka. Kafka's own "all or nothing" guarantee only covers the clearing house's internal paperwork; it knows nothing about the vault's ledger book. If the clerk updates the ledger and then the line to the clearing house drops before the notice is sent, the two are now out of sync. The outbox fix is: in the same trip to the ledger book, the clerk writes both the ledger entry and a note in an "outbox" column saying a notice must be sent, as one signature. A separate messenger later reads the outbox and sends the notice to the clearing house, and only crosses it off once it is confirmed sent. The ledger book is the one place that decides whether the notice is owed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Kafka transactions are atomic only within Kafka, so for atomicity across a database write and a Kafka publish you use the transactional outbox — write the business row and an outbox row in one local DB transaction, then a relay publishes the outbox at least once with an idempotency key.

sections.s2_technical:
To see why Kafka transactions do not cover this, you have to be precise about their scope. A Kafka transaction, driven by a transactional producer, gives atomicity over two things: records written to one or more Kafka topics and partitions, and the offsets committed for messages the same producer consumed. That is the consume-process-produce loop, and within it Kafka gives you effectively-once semantics. The transaction coordinator and the commit markers it writes are entirely inside Kafka. A relational database has its own completely separate transaction manager. There is no shared coordinator that can atomically commit both, and trying to bolt on a classic distributed two-phase commit across a database and a broker is fragile, slow, and not supported by Kafka's model. So the moment your unit of work spans both a database and Kafka, Kafka transactions alone cannot make them atomic.

The naive approaches and why they fail are worth naming. If you write to the database first and then publish to Kafka, a crash between the two leaves a committed database row with no event ever published, which is a lost event. If you publish to Kafka first and then write to the database, a crash between the two leaves an event consumers already acted on but no database row, which is a phantom event. Wrapping both in a try-catch does not help, because the failure can happen in the gap after one side has durably committed. This is the classic dual-write problem, and there is no ordering of two independent commits that makes it safe.

The transactional outbox pattern solves it by removing the dual write. You give your database an outbox table. When you perform the business operation, you write the business change and an outbox row that represents the event you want to publish, both inside the same local database transaction. Because it is one transaction in one database, it is truly atomic: either both the business row and the outbox row commit, or neither does. Now there is exactly one durable fact about whether the event should exist, and it lives in your database. A separate process, the message relay, reads unpublished outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka, marking each as published once Kafka acknowledges. If the relay crashes after publishing but before marking, it will republish on restart, so publication is at-least-once, which is why each outbox row carries a unique id used as the Kafka message key or header so downstream consumers deduplicate. The result is end-to-end exactly-once effect: the event is published if and only if the business transaction committed, and it is applied once despite at-least-once delivery.

There are two common ways to implement the relay. The polling publisher periodically queries the outbox table for unpublished rows, publishes them in order, and marks them published; it is simple and database-agnostic. The log-tailing approach, often called change data capture, uses a tool such as Debezium to tail the database's transaction log and stream outbox inserts to Kafka without polling, which is lower latency and lower load on the database. Here is the heart of the business side in Spring, showing the single local transaction:

```java
@Transactional // ONE local DB transaction — atomic for both writes
public void transfer(String from, String to, BigDecimal amount) {
    accountRepo.debit(from, amount);                 // business row
    accountRepo.credit(to, amount);                  // business row
    outboxRepo.save(new OutboxEvent(UUID.randomUUID().toString(),
            "TransferCompleted", buildPayload(from, to, amount))); // outbox row
    // No Kafka call here. If the DB commit fails, nothing is written anywhere.
}
```

Senior-level nuances: first, order and ordering keys matter, so the relay typically publishes in outbox insertion order and keys events so per-aggregate ordering is preserved. Second, because delivery is at-least-once, consumers must be idempotent using the outbox event id, which ties back to the earlier point that business-level exactly-once is the consumer's responsibility. Third, you must manage outbox growth by deleting or archiving published rows, often with a retention job, so the table does not bloat. Fourth, change data capture decouples the relay from application code entirely and survives application crashes gracefully, which is why it is the preferred relay at scale, though it adds operational components. Fifth, the inbound side has a mirror pattern called the inbox, where a consumer records processed event ids transactionally with its state change, giving the same exactly-once effect on the receiving end.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India processes transfers in a service that must both persist the ledger change and publish a TransferCompleted event so downstream systems update statements and send notifications. Rajesh (SAV2001) transfers to Priya (CUR3001).

Problem 1 — the first implementation wrote the ledger to the database and then published to Kafka. One day the broker was briefly unreachable right after the database commit, so Rajesh's balance changed but no TransferCompleted event was ever published. Priya's statement never updated and no notification went out. This is the dual-write lost-event failure, and Kafka transactions could not have prevented it because they do not cover the database.

Problem 2 — a developer proposed publishing to Kafka first and then writing the database, but we realized a crash in the gap would create a phantom event that consumers act on with no backing ledger entry. This made it clear no ordering of two independent commits is safe, so we adopted the transactional outbox.

Our runnable demo models a `Database` with a transaction boundary, an `OutboxTable`, a `TransferService` that writes the ledger and the outbox atomically, and an `OutboxRelay` that publishes to a `KafkaBroker` at least once and marks rows published, with a `DedupConsumer` that applies each event once by id. We inject a crash between the two writes in the naive version to show the lost event, then show the outbox version surviving the same crash. The classes are `OutboxDemo`, `Database`, `OutboxEvent`, `TransferService`, `OutboxRelay`, `KafkaBroker`, and `DedupConsumer`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer of fifty thousand from Rajesh to Priya that must both update the ledger and publish a TransferCompleted event.

Step 1 (naive path): The service begins a database transaction, applies the debit and credit, and commits. The ledger is now durably changed.

Step 2 (naive path): Before the separate Kafka publish runs, the process crashes or the broker is unreachable. The event is never published. Rajesh's balance changed but Priya's statement never updates and no notification is sent. Kafka transactions cannot help here because the database commit happened entirely outside Kafka's scope.

Step 3 (outbox path): The service begins one database transaction and writes the ledger rows and an outbox row carrying a unique event id, then commits. Because it is a single local transaction, either both the ledger and the outbox row commit or neither does. There is now exactly one durable fact that the event is owed.

Step 4 (outbox path): The relay reads unpublished outbox rows and publishes to Kafka. In the demo it crashes right after publishing but before marking the row as published, so on restart it republishes the same event. Publication is therefore at-least-once, and the duplicate is expected.

Step 5 (outbox path): The consumer applies each event keyed by the outbox event id. The first copy is applied, updating the statement and sending the notification; the duplicate is recognized by its id and skipped. The net effect is exactly-once: the event exists if and only if the ledger committed, and it is applied once.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka transactions do not cover a database write plus a Kafka publish because their atomicity is scoped entirely to Kafka. A Kafka transaction makes writes to Kafka topics and the consumer offset commits atomic together, all coordinated by Kafka's own transaction coordinator and commit markers. Your relational database has a completely separate transaction manager, there is no shared coordinator across the two systems, and a real distributed two-phase commit across a database and a broker is impractical and unsupported. So the instant your unit of work spans both, Kafka transactions alone cannot make them atomic.

This matters because the naive dual write is unsafe in both orderings. If you write the database first and then publish, a crash in the gap gives you a committed row with no event, a lost event. If you publish first and then write the database, a crash in the gap gives you an event consumers already acted on with no backing row, a phantom event. On the National Bank of India transfer service we actually lost events this way: the ledger committed, the broker was briefly unreachable, and the TransferCompleted event was never published, so statements and notifications silently fell out of sync.

The fix is the transactional outbox pattern, which removes the dual write. In one local database transaction I write both the business change and an outbox row that represents the event I want to publish. Because it is a single transaction in a single database it is truly atomic, so either both the ledger and the outbox row commit or neither does, and now the database is the single source of truth for whether the event is owed. A separate relay then reads unpublished outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka, marking each as published once acknowledged. If the relay crashes after publishing but before marking, it republishes on restart, so delivery is at-least-once, and that is why each outbox event carries a unique id that consumers use to deduplicate, giving an end-to-end exactly-once effect.

In production I choose between two relays. The polling publisher simply queries the outbox for unpublished rows and is dead simple and database-agnostic. At scale I prefer log-tailing with change data capture using Debezium, which tails the database transaction log and streams outbox inserts to Kafka with lower latency and no polling load, fully decoupled from application code. I preserve per-aggregate ordering by keying events on the aggregate id, I keep consumers idempotent on the event id, and I run a retention job to archive published outbox rows so the table does not bloat. The one-sentence principle I give the team is that Kafka transactions give you atomicity inside Kafka, and the outbox pattern gives you atomicity between your database and Kafka, and you need both to get real end-to-end exactly-once.

answers.question: (Scenario) A Kafka topic has a hot partition due to skewed key distribution (e.g. one enterprise customer generates 80% of traffic) — how do you fix it without downtime: increasing partitions helps spread NON-skewed traffic but the same key still maps deterministically to one partition (hash(key) % numPartitions), so the real fix is key bucketing/salting (e.g. key = customerId + "-" + hash(orderId) % 4) to split one logical key across multiple partitions — and what is the consumer-side trade-off (must read from multiple partitions and merge results for that customer)?
answers.shortTitle: (Scenario) A Kafka topic has a hot partition due to a skewed key — how do you fix it without downtime, and what is the consumer-side trade-off?

s1_definition.profdef: A hot partition occurs when one key, or a small set of keys, receives a disproportionate share of traffic, so the partition that key maps to becomes a bottleneck while other partitions sit idle. Because Kafka assigns a keyed record to a partition with the deterministic formula hash of the key modulo the number of partitions, a single high-volume key always lands on one partition, and simply adding partitions does not help that key, it only spreads the other, non-skewed keys. The real fix is key bucketing or salting: you augment the key with a bucket suffix so one logical key is split across several physical keys and therefore several partitions. The trade-off is on the consumer side, which must now read all the buckets for that logical key and merge them, giving up strict single-partition ordering for the split key.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India sorts incoming transfer slips into counters by customer, so each customer's slips always go to the same counter to keep them in order. One enterprise customer sends eighty percent of all slips, so that one counter is swamped while the others are nearly empty. Adding more counters does not help, because the rule still sends all of that giant customer's slips to the same single counter. The fix is to split that one customer into several sub-queues, for example "BigCorp line 1," "BigCorp line 2," "BigCorp line 3," and "BigCorp line 4," by tagging each slip with a sub-line number derived from the order number, so four counters now share the load. The cost is that if you later want the full picture for BigCorp, you must gather slips from all four sub-lines and merge them, because they are no longer in one neat ordered pile.
s1_definition.oneliner: Adding partitions cannot relieve a single hot key because hash(key) mod partitions is deterministic; split the hot key with a bucket suffix so it spans multiple partitions, and accept that consumers must read and merge across those buckets, losing strict per-logical-key ordering.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A hot partition occurs when one key, or a small set of keys, receives a disproportionate share of traffic, so the partition that key maps to becomes a bottleneck while other partitions sit idle. Because Kafka assigns a keyed record to a partition with the deterministic formula hash of the key modulo the number of partitions, a single high-volume key always lands on one partition, and simply adding partitions does not help that key, it only spreads the other, non-skewed keys. The real fix is key bucketing or salting: you augment the key with a bucket suffix so one logical key is split across several physical keys and therefore several partitions. The trade-off is on the consumer side, which must now read all the buckets for that logical key and merge them, giving up strict single-partition ordering for the split key.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India sorts incoming transfer slips into counters by customer, so each customer's slips always go to the same counter to keep them in order. One enterprise customer sends eighty percent of all slips, so that one counter is swamped while the others are nearly empty. Adding more counters does not help, because the rule still sends all of that giant customer's slips to the same single counter. The fix is to split that one customer into several sub-queues, for example "BigCorp line 1," "BigCorp line 2," "BigCorp line 3," and "BigCorp line 4," by tagging each slip with a sub-line number derived from the order number, so four counters now share the load. The cost is that if you later want the full picture for BigCorp, you must gather slips from all four sub-lines and merge them, because they are no longer in one neat ordered pile.

**One line to remember:** Adding partitions cannot relieve a single hot key because hash(key) mod partitions is deterministic; split the hot key with a bucket suffix so it spans multiple partitions, and accept that consumers must read and merge across those buckets, losing strict per-logical-key ordering.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with why the obvious fix fails. When you key a record, the partitioner computes hash of the key modulo the number of partitions. For one specific key, that formula yields exactly one partition number regardless of how many partitions exist. If you increase partitions from six to twelve, the hot key might move to a different single partition, but it is still confined to one partition, so its partition is still hot. Adding partitions genuinely helps the other keys, because their collective load now spreads across more partitions, but it does nothing for the concentration caused by one dominant key. This is the crux the question is testing.

The real fix is to change the key itself so the hot logical entity no longer maps to a single partition. This is key bucketing, also called salting. You pick a bucket count, say four, and derive a bucket from some varying field of the record, then append it to the key. For example the physical key becomes customerId plus a dash plus the hash of the orderId modulo four, so BigCorp's traffic is split into BigCorp-0, BigCorp-1, BigCorp-2, and BigCorp-3. Those four physical keys hash to up to four different partitions, so the load that was crushing one partition is now shared. You choose the bucket field so it varies within the hot entity, orderId or a timestamp component works well, and you choose the bucket count based on how much you need to spread; it does not need to equal the partition count, it just needs to be large enough to break the concentration.

Here is the producer-side code that implements the split:

```java
int buckets = 4; // split factor for hot customers
String physicalKey = customerId + "-" + (Integer.toString(orderId.hashCode() & 0x7fffffff)
        .hashCode() & 0x7fffffff) % buckets;
// simpler and clearer:
int bucket = Math.floorMod(orderId.hashCode(), buckets);
String key = customerId + "-" + bucket; // BigCorp-0 .. BigCorp-3
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("orders", key, payload));
```

A refinement used in practice is selective salting: you only split keys that are actually hot, leaving normal customers with their plain customerId key so you do not pay the merge cost for everyone. You maintain a small set of known hot keys, or detect them dynamically, and salt only those. This keeps ordering intact for the ninety-nine percent of customers that are not hot, and only the genuinely hot customer pays the trade-off.

Now the consumer-side trade-off, which is the second half of the question. Before salting, all of a customer's records were in one partition, so a single consumer read them in strict offset order, which gave you per-customer ordering for free. After salting, the hot customer's records are spread across several partitions, possibly handled by several consumers in the group. So you lose the automatic strict ordering for that customer, and if you need a complete or ordered view of that customer, the consumer side must read from all the relevant buckets and merge the results, for example by buffering and sorting on a sequence number or timestamp, or by having a downstream aggregation step that reassembles per-customer state. You must also decide whether strict ordering for the hot key still matters; often for a high-volume enterprise customer you only need ordering within an order, not across all their orders, in which case salting by orderId preserves exactly the ordering you actually need, because each individual order still lands in one bucket. The craft is picking the bucket field so that the ordering you must keep stays within a single bucket while the load you must spread crosses buckets.

Doing this without downtime is the final requirement. You cannot retroactively re-key existing data, so you roll it out going forward. You deploy the new partitioning logic behind a feature flag or configuration so producers start emitting salted keys for the hot entity, you update consumers first to understand both the old plain keys and the new salted keys and to merge across buckets, and then you flip producers. Because consumers already handle both key shapes, there is no gap and no downtime, and old in-flight records under the plain key drain naturally. If you also need more partitions for the non-skewed traffic, you add them as a separate, carefully planned change, mindful of the key-remapping caveat that repartitioning carries.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India publishes corporate payment orders to the `corp.orders` topic, keyed by customer id so each corporate client's orders stay ordered. One enterprise client, BigCorp, generates eighty percent of all orders. Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) are ordinary clients with light traffic.

Problem 1 — the partition that BigCorp hashes to is saturated: its consumer is perpetually behind while the partitions for ordinary clients are nearly idle. An engineer doubled the partitions and nothing improved for BigCorp. This is exactly the deterministic-mapping problem: BigCorp's single key still lands on one partition no matter how many partitions exist.

Problem 2 — we need to spread BigCorp's load without downtime and without scrambling the ordering that actually matters, which is the ordering of events within a single payment order. This is why we salt by order id, so each order stays in one bucket but BigCorp's many orders spread across buckets, and why consumers must merge across buckets for a full BigCorp view.

Our runnable demo models a `Partitioner`, publishes a skewed workload first with plain keys to show the hot partition, then with selective salting on the hot key to show the balanced spread, and finally a `MergingConsumer` that reads all BigCorp buckets and reassembles per-order ordering. The classes are `HotPartitionDemo`, `Partitioner`, `SaltingKeyStrategy`, `PartitionLoad`, and `MergingConsumer`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: ten thousand corporate orders where BigCorp produces eight thousand and fifty ordinary customers share two thousand, on a six-partition topic.

Step 1: With plain keys, every BigCorp order is keyed BIGCORP, which hashes to exactly one partition. That partition receives roughly eight thousand records while the other five partitions share only two thousand. The BigCorp partition is hot and its consumer falls behind.

Step 2: An engineer adds partitions. BigCorp's single key now hashes to some single partition out of the larger set, but it is still just one partition, so the hot spot moves but does not disappear. Only the non-skewed customers benefit from the extra partitions.

Step 3: We enable selective salting for BIGCORP with four buckets, salting by order id. Each BigCorp order is keyed BIGCORP-0 through BIGCORP-3 depending on the order id. These four physical keys hash to up to four partitions, so BigCorp's eight thousand orders spread across several partitions and no single partition is hot. Ordinary customers keep their plain keys and their strict ordering.

Step 4: Because each individual order's events share the same order id, they still land in the same bucket, so order-level ordering is preserved, which is the ordering that actually matters for payments. What is given up is strict ordering across all of BigCorp's orders, which we did not need.

Step 5: A downstream consumer that wants a complete ordered view of BigCorp now reads all four buckets and merges them by a producer-stamped sequence number, reassembling the combined sequence. This is the consumer-side trade-off: more partitions and keys to read, plus a merge step, in exchange for eliminating the hot partition without downtime.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A hot partition from a skewed key happens because Kafka assigns a keyed record with the deterministic formula hash of the key modulo the number of partitions. If one enterprise customer produces eighty percent of the traffic, that single key always hashes to one partition, so that partition is overwhelmed while the rest sit nearly idle. The first instinct is to add partitions, and that is exactly the trap this question tests: adding partitions spreads the non-skewed traffic, but the dominant key is still one key, so it still maps to a single partition. The hot spot might move to a different partition, but it does not go away.

The real fix is to change the key so the hot logical entity no longer maps to one partition, which is key bucketing or salting. I pick a bucket count, say four, derive a bucket from a varying field such as the order id, and append it to the key, so the one customer BigCorp becomes BigCorp-0 through BigCorp-3. Those four physical keys hash to up to four partitions, so the load that was crushing one partition is now shared. In practice I salt selectively, only the keys that are actually hot, so ordinary customers keep their plain key and their strict per-customer ordering and pay no cost, and only the genuinely hot customer is split.

The deliberate detail is choosing the salt field so the ordering you must keep stays inside one bucket. On the National Bank of India corporate orders stream, what matters is ordering of events within a single payment order, not across all of BigCorp's orders, so I salt by order id. Every event for one order shares the order id and therefore the same bucket, so order-level ordering is preserved, while BigCorp's many different orders spread across buckets to kill the hot partition. The thing I consciously give up is strict ordering across all of BigCorp's orders, which we never needed.

That leads to the consumer-side trade-off, which is the second half of the answer. Before salting, all of a customer's records lived in one partition, so a single consumer read them in strict order for free. After salting, the hot customer's records are spread across several partitions and possibly several consumers, so to reconstruct a complete or ordered view of that customer the consumer must read all the buckets and merge them, typically by buffering and sorting on a producer-stamped sequence number. Finally, I do all of this without downtime by rolling out the new key logic going forward: I first deploy consumers that understand both the old plain keys and the new salted keys and can merge across buckets, then I flip the producers behind a feature flag, and the old plain-keyed records drain naturally with no gap. I never try to re-key existing data, because the fix is about new traffic, and I keep the hot-customer list in configuration so adding a newly hot customer is a config change rather than a code change.

answers.question: (Scenario) A Kafka partition reassignment is triggered for scaling/rebalancing and you observe spikes in consumer lag and latency — explain the five causes: (1) data copying saturates disk I/O and network on source/destination brokers, (2) throttling slows replication but keeps the pipe busy longer, (3) leader movement causes consumers to reconnect (NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION errors + metadata refresh), (4) cold page cache on the new broker forces disk reads instead of memory reads until cache warms, (5) coordination overhead from ISR changes and metadata propagation — and why you should monitor replication throughput, avoid reassignment during peak traffic, and throttle appropriately?
answers.shortTitle: (Scenario) A partition reassignment for scaling/rebalancing causes spikes in consumer lag and latency — explain the five causes and how to mitigate them.

s1_definition.profdef: A partition reassignment moves partition replicas from one set of brokers to another, which Kafka does to rebalance load, add or drain brokers, or recover from failures. Although it is an online operation, it causes transient consumer lag and latency spikes for five reasons: bulk data copying saturates disk and network on the source and destination brokers, replication throttling reduces the rate but extends the duration of contention, leader movement forces producers and consumers to reconnect and refresh metadata after NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION errors, the destination broker's page cache is cold so reads hit disk until it warms, and the coordination overhead of in-sync replica changes and metadata propagation adds churn. Mitigation is to monitor replication throughput, avoid reassignment during peak traffic, and apply appropriate throttles.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India is relocating the records for some accounts from one branch vault to another while the branch stays open. Moving boxes of ledgers ties up the loading dock and the delivery trucks, so normal deliveries slow down; that is disk and network saturation. To avoid blocking the dock completely, the movers go slower, but then the trucks occupy the dock for longer; that is throttling trading rate for duration. While an account's master ledger is being moved, tellers who try to use the old vault are told "that ledger moved, go to the new vault," and they have to look up the new location; that is leader movement and metadata refresh. At the new vault, the clerks have not memorized where anything is yet, so every lookup means walking to the shelves instead of recalling from memory; that is a cold cache. And the branch manager has to keep updating the master directory of which vault holds what, which itself takes effort; that is coordination overhead.
s1_definition.oneliner: Reassignment copies data online, so lag spikes come from disk and network saturation, throttling that trades rate for duration, leader moves that force metadata refresh, cold page cache on the destination, and coordination churn — mitigate by monitoring replication throughput, avoiding peak hours, and throttling appropriately.

**One line to remember:** Reassignment copies data online, so lag spikes come from disk and network saturation, throttling that trades rate for duration, leader moves that force metadata refresh, cold page cache on the destination, and coordination churn — mitigate by monitoring replication throughput, avoiding peak hours, and throttling appropriately.

sections.s2_technical:
Cause one is bulk data copying saturating disk and network. When a replica is reassigned to a new broker, that broker must fetch the entire partition log from the leader, which can be gigabytes. This replication competes with normal produce and consume traffic for the same disks and network links on both the source and destination brokers. Since consuming often reads from the page cache and produce writes sequentially, suddenly adding large sequential reads for replication and large writes for the new replica steals I/O bandwidth, slowing the foreground traffic and causing lag to rise.

Cause two is throttling that keeps the pipe busy longer. To protect foreground traffic you apply a replication throttle, which caps the bytes per second used for moving data. This genuinely reduces the instantaneous contention, which is good, but it also extends how long the reassignment runs. So instead of a short, sharp spike you get a longer, gentler elevation of lag. The lesson is that throttling is a trade between intensity and duration, and you must size it so the reassignment still finishes in a reasonable window rather than dragging on for hours while catching up is impossible.

Cause three is leader movement forcing reconnection and metadata refresh. Reassignment often changes which broker is the leader for a partition. When the leader moves, producers and consumers that were talking to the old leader get a NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION error, must refresh cluster metadata to discover the new leader, and reconnect. During that brief window, requests for the affected partitions fail and retry, which shows up as a latency spike and a momentary lag bump. Clients handle this automatically, but at scale many partitions moving at once can cause a burst of metadata refreshes across the fleet.

Cause four is the cold page cache on the destination broker. Kafka relies heavily on the operating system page cache so that consumers reading recent data are served from memory, not disk. A broker that just received a replica has none of that partition's data in its page cache, so once it becomes leader, consumer fetches for that partition initially miss the cache and hit disk, which is far slower. Latency for that partition stays elevated until enough data is read and the cache warms. This is why a partition can be fully in-sync yet still slow right after a move.

Cause five is coordination overhead. Every replica movement changes the in-sync replica set, which the controller must track, and the resulting metadata updates must propagate to all brokers and clients. In-sync replica shrink and expansion events, leader elections, and metadata epoch bumps all add bookkeeping that momentarily competes with serving traffic, especially when many partitions are reassigned simultaneously. Individually small, these add up into measurable churn during a large reassignment.

The three mitigations map onto these causes. You monitor replication throughput and the partition reassignment progress so you can see whether you are saturating links or falling behind, using broker metrics for replication bytes and the reassignment tool's verify mode. You avoid reassignment during peak traffic, scheduling it for low-traffic windows so the extra I/O and the cold-cache period overlap with spare capacity rather than competing with your busiest load. And you throttle appropriately, setting leader and follower replication rate limits high enough to finish in a reasonable time but low enough to protect foreground traffic, and you move partitions in small batches rather than all at once to bound leader movement, metadata churn, and the number of simultaneously cold replicas. Here is how you drive it:

```bash
# Generate and execute a reassignment plan, then verify progress.
kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 \
  --reassignment-json-file plan.json --execute \
  --throttle 50000000   # 50 MB/s cap on replication to protect foreground traffic

kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 \
  --reassignment-json-file plan.json --verify   # removes throttle when complete
```

Senior-level nuances: prefer moving a few partitions at a time so only a small fraction of clients see NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION at once; pre-warm or accept a warm-up window for the destination before relying on it as leader by delaying the preferred-leader election until the new replica has caught up and served some reads; set the throttle dynamically and raise it near the end when the cluster is calmer; and always run verify to ensure the throttle configuration is cleaned up, because a forgotten throttle silently caps replication forever and causes mysterious under-replication later.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India added two new brokers to the cluster and ran a partition reassignment to balance load onto them. During the move, the settlement consumer group showed sharp lag spikes and elevated end-to-end latency, alarming the on-call team. Rajesh and Priya transfers flow through this cluster.

Problem 1 — the reassignment copied several large partitions at full speed with no throttle, saturating disk and network on the source and destination brokers, so foreground consume slowed and lag jumped. This is causes one and two: raw copying contention, and the realization that we needed a throttle, which then trades rate for duration.

Problem 2 — as leaders moved to the new brokers, settlement consumers briefly got NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION, refreshed metadata, reconnected, and then hit a cold page cache on the new brokers, so even after catching up, latency stayed high for a while. This is causes three, four, and five: leader movement and metadata refresh, cold cache, and coordination churn.

Our runnable demo models a `ReassignmentPlan`, a `Broker` with disk and network budgets and a page cache warmth level, and a `ReassignmentSimulator` that runs the move with and without throttling and in peak versus off-peak windows, reporting the lag spike magnitude and duration. The classes are `ReassignmentDemo`, `Broker`, `Partition`, `ReassignmentPlan`, and `ReassignmentSimulator`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four large settlement partitions being reassigned to new brokers, run first unthrottled at peak and then throttled off-peak.

Step 1: The reassignment starts copying each partition's full log from the source leader to the destination broker. Unthrottled, this copying runs at full speed and consumes most of the disk and network bandwidth on both brokers, leaving little headroom for foreground consume. Lag begins to rise. This is cause one.

Step 2: We add a fifty megabyte per second throttle. Contention drops because replication no longer hogs the links, but the total copy now takes longer, so the elevated lag persists for a longer, gentler window instead of a short, sharp spike. This is cause two, the rate-versus-duration trade.

Step 3: As each partition's leader moves to a new broker, settlement consumers talking to the old leader receive NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION, refresh cluster metadata, find the new leader, and reconnect. Requests for those partitions briefly fail and retry, producing a latency bump. This is cause three.

Step 4: Immediately after a leader moves, the destination broker's page cache holds none of that partition's data, so consumer fetches miss the cache and read from disk, keeping latency high until the cache warms through repeated reads. This is cause four, and it explains why a partition can be in-sync yet still slow.

Step 5: Throughout, the controller tracks in-sync replica changes and propagates metadata updates across the cluster, which is extra bookkeeping competing with serving traffic, amplified when many partitions move at once. This is cause five. In the off-peak throttled batched run, all five effects overlap with spare capacity and are moved a few partitions at a time, so the lag stays contained and recovers quickly.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A partition reassignment is an online operation that moves replicas between brokers for scaling, rebalancing, or recovery, and even though clients stay up, it causes transient consumer lag and latency spikes for five distinct reasons. First, the destination broker must copy the entire partition log, often gigabytes, from the source, and that bulk transfer saturates disk and network on both brokers, stealing I/O from normal consume and produce. Second, if you add a replication throttle to protect foreground traffic, it genuinely lowers the instantaneous contention but extends how long the move runs, so you trade a short sharp spike for a longer gentle one. Third, when leaders move to the new brokers, producers and consumers hit NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION, refresh cluster metadata, and reconnect, which causes a brief failure-and-retry latency bump. Fourth, the destination broker's page cache is cold, so right after it becomes leader, consumer fetches miss memory and hit disk until the cache warms, keeping that partition slow even once it is in-sync. Fifth, every move changes the in-sync replica set and triggers metadata propagation, and that coordination overhead adds churn, especially when many partitions move at once.

On the National Bank of India cluster we saw exactly this when we added brokers and reassigned partitions onto them. Running unthrottled during peak hours, the copy saturated the links and settlement lag jumped, and as leaders moved, consumers briefly got not-leader errors, refreshed metadata, and then hit cold caches on the new brokers, so latency stayed elevated for a while even after catching up.

The three mitigations map directly onto those causes. I monitor replication throughput and the reassignment progress so I can see whether I am saturating links or falling behind, using the broker replication byte metrics and the reassignment tool's verify mode. I avoid reassignment during peak traffic and schedule it for a low-traffic window, so the extra I/O and the cold-cache warm-up period overlap with spare capacity instead of competing with the busiest load. And I throttle appropriately, setting the replication rate limit high enough to finish in a reasonable time but low enough to protect foreground traffic, while moving partitions in small batches rather than all at once so that only a few clients see not-leader errors at any moment and only a few replicas are cold simultaneously.

The senior details I always add are to delay promoting a freshly moved replica to leader until it has caught up and warmed a little, to raise the throttle near the end when the cluster is calmer, and to always run verify so the throttle configuration is removed afterward, because a forgotten throttle silently caps replication forever and causes mysterious under-replication later. The mental model is that reassignment is safe and online, but it is real work on finite disk, network, cache, and coordination resources, so you plan it like any capacity-sensitive operation rather than firing it off at full speed during your busiest hour.

answers.question: Why does Kafka retention cleanup (deleting expired log segments) cause spikes in disk I/O and temporarily degrade broker performance — deletion of many large segment files triggers metadata-heavy random I/O (inode updates, block deallocation) on top of normal sequential read/write traffic, disrupts the OS page cache (invalidated entries force consumers to read from disk), and runs in bursts (scan, batch delete, sleep, repeat) so monitoring shows periodic I/O spikes — and why is this worse on cloud disks like EBS (storage-layer amplification of delete operations)?
answers.shortTitle: Why does Kafka retention cleanup cause spikes in disk I/O and temporarily degrade broker performance, and why is it worse on cloud disks like EBS?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka stores each partition as a series of segment files, and retention cleanup deletes whole segments once they age out by time or size. Deleting many large segment files is not free: it triggers metadata-heavy random I/O for inode updates and block deallocation, it invalidates page cache entries so subsequent consumer reads miss memory and hit disk, and the cleaner runs in periodic bursts of scan, batch delete, and sleep, so the disk I/O graph shows regular spikes that momentarily degrade broker throughput and latency. On cloud block storage such as Amazon EBS, deletes are amplified at the storage layer because the virtualized device turns a logical delete into additional backend operations, making the spikes larger and longer than on local disks.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps daily ledgers in thick bound volumes on shelves, one volume per day, and the rule is to shred volumes older than seven days. Normally clerks just write new entries and read recent volumes, which is smooth, orderly work. But once a day the shredding crew arrives and pulls dozens of old volumes off the shelves at once, updates the shelf index for each removed volume, and reclaims the empty shelf space. All that pulling, indexing, and reshelving is jerky, scattered work that ties up the aisles, and while it happens the clerks who wanted to grab a recent volume find the aisles clogged, so their lookups slow down. If the shelves are actually a rented off-site storage service rather than the branch's own room, every shred request becomes several messages back and forth to the storage company, so the disruption is bigger and lasts longer.
s1_definition.oneliner: Retention cleanup deletes big segment files in periodic bursts, and those deletes are metadata-heavy random I/O that also evict page cache, so you see spiky disk I/O and latency; on EBS the virtualized storage amplifies each delete, making it worse, which you smooth with smaller segments, staggered deletes, and headroom.

All that pulling, indexing, and reshelving is jerky, scattered work that ties up the aisles, and while it happens the clerks who wanted to grab a recent volume find the aisles clogged, so their lookups slow down. If the shelves are actually a rented off-site storage service rather than the branch's own room, every shred request becomes several messages back and forth to the storage company, so the disruption is bigger and lasts longer.

**One line to remember:** Retention cleanup deletes big segment files in periodic bursts, and those deletes are metadata-heavy random I/O that also evict page cache, so you see spiky disk I/O and latency; on EBS the virtualized storage amplifies each delete, making it worse, which you smooth with smaller segments, staggered deletes, and headroom.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the file layout. A Kafka partition is a directory of log segment files, each typically up to one gigabyte by default, plus matching offset and time index files. New data is appended to the active segment sequentially, which is cheap. Retention, configured by `retention.ms` for time or `retention.bytes` for size, decides when a closed segment is too old or the partition is too large, and the cleanup process deletes whole segments, not individual records. So cleanup is fundamentally a file-deletion operation, and deleting a one-gigabyte file plus its index files has costs beyond just marking space free.

The first cost is metadata-heavy random I/O. Appending data is sequential and friendly to disks, but deleting files forces the filesystem to update inodes, free the blocks the file occupied, and update allocation metadata, which are scattered, small, random operations rather than one smooth stream. When retention removes many segments at once, the broker issues a burst of these random metadata operations on top of the steady sequential produce and consume traffic, and random I/O is far slower per operation than sequential I/O, so the disk's effective throughput for foreground work drops during the burst.

The second cost is page cache disruption. Kafka deliberately relies on the operating system page cache so that consumers reading recent data are served from memory. When a segment file is deleted, the page cache entries backing that file are invalidated and freed, and the churn of freeing and reallocating cache pages during a deletion burst reduces the cache's effectiveness for the data consumers actually want. Consumers that would have been served from memory now miss the cache and read from disk, which both slows them and adds yet more disk load precisely when the disk is already busy with deletes.

The third cost is the bursty schedule. The log cleanup thread does not trickle deletes continuously; it runs on an interval governed by `log.retention.check.interval.ms`, scanning for eligible segments, deleting a batch, then sleeping until the next cycle. This scan-delete-sleep rhythm means the I/O cost arrives in periodic spikes rather than as a smooth background load, which is exactly why monitoring shows regular saw-tooth spikes in disk utilization and latency aligned to the check interval.

Why it is worse on cloud disks like EBS comes down to storage-layer amplification. A local SSD handles a delete close to the hardware. An EBS volume is a network-attached, virtualized block device, so operations traverse a storage backend that must track and reclaim blocks across a distributed system. A delete that is one operation locally can expand into multiple backend operations, and EBS also enforces provisioned IOPS and throughput limits, so a burst of delete-driven random I/O can exhaust your IOPS budget and get throttled, stretching the spike into a longer period of degraded performance. The same burst that is a brief blip on local NVMe can become a sustained latency event on a modestly provisioned EBS volume.

The mitigations follow from the causes. You reduce segment size with `segment.bytes` or roll segments more often with `segment.ms` so each deletion removes a smaller file and the random-I/O burst per delete is smaller and more frequent rather than huge and rare, smoothing the curve. You tune `log.retention.check.interval.ms` and avoid aligning many topics to delete at the same instant, staggering retention so deletes do not all pile into one cycle across the broker. You provision cloud storage with enough IOPS and throughput headroom to absorb delete bursts, choosing a volume type and size whose baseline and burst limits comfortably exceed your steady load plus cleanup spikes. You keep spare disk capacity so cleanup is not forced to run aggressively when the disk is nearly full. And at the architecture level, tiered storage moves older segments to object storage so local deletes shrink, which both reduces local delete pressure and offloads the amplified operations from the hot block device. Here is how you tune a topic:

```bash
# Smaller segments => smaller, smoother delete bursts; staggered checks
kafka-configs.sh --alter --topic settlements --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 \
  --add-config segment.bytes=268435456,segment.ms=3600000,retention.ms=259200000
# Broker-level: how often cleanup scans (server.properties)
#   log.retention.check.interval.ms=300000
```

Senior-level nuances: this is deletion cleanup for `cleanup.policy=delete`; log compaction has its own cleaner with different but related I/O characteristics, so know which policy your topic uses. Watch the specific metrics, filesystem busy percentage, average I/O service time, and for EBS the volume queue length and burst-balance credits, because a draining burst balance is the early sign that delete bursts are exhausting your IOPS. And remember that larger segments improve steady-state append and read efficiency, so there is a trade-off: very small segments smooth deletes but add file-handle and index overhead, so you size segments to balance smooth cleanup against steady-state efficiency rather than minimizing them blindly.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs its Kafka brokers on EBS volumes. The `settlements` topic has one-gigabyte segments and three-day retention. Every few minutes the on-call dashboard showed sharp disk latency spikes, and settlement consumers briefly lagged in lockstep with them. Rajesh and Priya settlements flow through this topic.

Problem 1 — the retention cleaner woke on its interval, found several aged one-gigabyte segments across partitions, and deleted them in a batch, issuing a burst of metadata-heavy random I/O and evicting page cache, so foreground consume slowed and lag ticked up. This is the core cause: big deletes in bursts.

Problem 2 — because the volumes were EBS with a modest IOPS budget, each delete burst drained the burst-balance credits and got throttled, so the spike that would be a blip on local NVMe stretched into a visible latency event. This is the cloud-storage amplification.

Our runnable demo models a `PartitionLog` with segment files, a `RetentionCleaner` that scans, deletes a batch, and sleeps, and a `StorageDevice` abstraction with a local-SSD cost and an EBS cost that amplifies deletes and throttles on an IOPS budget. We run cleanup with large segments on EBS to show the spike, then with smaller segments and staggered checks to show it smoothed. The classes are `RetentionCleanupDemo`, `Segment`, `PartitionLog`, `RetentionCleaner`, and `StorageDevice`.
