sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a partition with eight one-gigabyte segments on an EBS volume with a modest IOPS budget, six of which have aged past retention, versus the same data stored as thirty-two smaller segments with staggered cleanup.

Step 1: During normal operation, producers append to the active segment sequentially and consumers read recent data from the page cache, so disk I/O is smooth and latency is low.

Step 2: The retention check interval fires. The cleaner scans the partition, finds six expired one-gigabyte segments, and deletes them in a single batch. Each delete issues metadata-heavy random I/O to update inodes and deallocate blocks, and all six at once is a large burst.

Step 3: Deleting those segments invalidates their page cache entries, so consumers that were being served recent data from memory now miss the cache and read from disk, adding more disk load exactly when the disk is already busy with the delete burst, and lag ticks up.

Step 4: Because this is EBS, each delete is amplified into several backend operations, and the burst drains the volume's IOPS burst balance, so the storage layer throttles I/O. The spike that would be a brief blip on local NVMe stretches into a longer latency event, and the saw-tooth pattern repeats every check interval.

Step 5: With smaller two-hundred-fifty-six-megabyte segments and staggered deletes a few per cycle, each cleanup cycle removes less data, so the random-I/O burst per cycle is small enough to stay within the IOPS budget, the cache churn is limited, and the latency stays contained. The contrast run on local NVMe shows even the large-segment burst staying within a huge IOPS budget, confirming the cloud-storage amplification is the aggravating factor.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka stores each partition as a series of segment files and retention cleanup deletes whole segments once they age out by time or size. The reason that causes disk I/O spikes and temporary performance degradation is that deleting large segment files is not the cheap sequential work that normal appends and reads are. A delete forces metadata-heavy random I/O, updating inodes and deallocating blocks, which is scattered and slow compared to Kafka's usual sequential pattern. Deleting a segment also invalidates the page cache entries backing that file, so consumers that would have been served recent data from memory suddenly miss the cache and read from disk, adding load exactly when the disk is already busy. And the cleaner runs on an interval in a scan, batch-delete, sleep rhythm, so the cost arrives in periodic bursts, which is why monitoring shows a regular saw-tooth of disk utilization and latency rather than a smooth line.

On cloud block storage like EBS this is worse because of storage-layer amplification. An EBS volume is a network-attached virtualized device, so a delete that is nearly free on local hardware expands into multiple backend operations, and EBS enforces provisioned IOPS and throughput limits. A burst of delete-driven random I/O can drain the volume's burst balance and get throttled, so the brief blip you would see on local NVMe stretches into a sustained latency event on a modestly provisioned EBS volume.

On the National Bank of India brokers, which run on EBS, we saw settlement latency and consumer lag spike every few minutes in lockstep with the retention check interval, because the cleaner was deleting several one-gigabyte segments at once and exhausting the volume's IOPS budget. The fixes we applied map directly onto the causes. We reduced the segment size so each delete removes a smaller file and the random-I/O burst is smaller and more frequent rather than huge and rare, which smooths the curve. We staggered retention so not every topic deletes in the same cycle, and we tuned the check interval. We provisioned the EBS volumes with enough IOPS and throughput headroom to absorb delete bursts, kept spare disk capacity so cleanup never runs in a panic near a full disk, and adopted tiered storage so older segments live in object storage and local deletes shrink.

The nuances I always mention are that this is the delete cleanup policy specifically, that compaction has its own cleaner with related but different I/O, and that I watch the right signals, filesystem service time and queue length and, on EBS, the burst-balance credits, because a draining burst balance is the early warning that delete bursts are outrunning the IOPS budget. I also point out the trade-off, since larger segments are more efficient for steady-state appends and reads, so I size segments to balance smooth cleanup against steady-state efficiency rather than making them as small as possible. The one-line principle is that retention cleanup is real, bursty, random disk work layered on top of smooth sequential traffic, and on virtualized cloud disks it is amplified, so you engineer for the spike rather than being surprised by it.

answers.question: In a compacted topic, when and why does data "disappear" even though compaction retains the latest value per key — (1) a tombstone (null value) marks the key for deletion and after `delete.retention.ms` it's removed completely, (2) if `cleanup.policy=compact,delete` BOTH compaction AND time/size retention apply so even the latest record can expire, (3) messages with null or wrong keys bypass compaction entirely and are subject to retention deletion, (4) aggressive compaction settings (small segment size + frequent cleaner runs) remove old records almost immediately — and why is each of these expected behavior, not a bug?
answers.shortTitle: In a compacted topic, when and why does data "disappear" even though compaction keeps the latest value per key?

s1_definition.profdef: Log compaction promises to retain at least the latest value per key, but that promise has well-defined exceptions, so data can legitimately disappear. A tombstone, a record with a null value, marks a key for deletion and is itself removed after the delete retention window, erasing the key entirely. If the cleanup policy is compact plus delete, ordinary time or size retention applies on top of compaction, so even the latest record for a key can expire. Records with a null key, or keyed incorrectly, are not compactable at all and are subject to plain retention deletion. And aggressive compaction settings, such as small segments and frequent cleaner runs, remove superseded records almost immediately. Each of these is the documented behavior of compaction, not a defect.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps one current notice per account on a board, and the rule is "always keep the newest notice for each account." People expect nothing ever vanishes, but four documented rules say otherwise. First, if a clerk pins a blank "cancelled" slip for Rajesh and a day passes, even that cancelled slip is removed, so Rajesh's account vanishes from the board completely. Second, if the board also has a "nothing older than seven days" rule, then even Rajesh's newest notice disappears once it is seven days old. Third, notices pinned without an account number written on them cannot be matched to any account, so the "keep newest per account" rule does not apply to them and they are simply thrown out on the age rule. Fourth, if the tidy-up crew is told to work constantly and aggressively, old superseded notices for an account are pulled almost the instant a newer one is pinned. None of these is the board malfunctioning; they are exactly the rules as written.
s1_definition.oneliner: Compaction keeps the latest value per key, but tombstones expire the key after delete.retention.ms, compact,delete adds time or size expiry to even the latest record, null or wrong keys are not compactable and get retention-deleted, and aggressive settings purge old records almost instantly — all expected, all documented.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Log compaction promises to retain at least the latest value per key, but that promise has well-defined exceptions, so data can legitimately disappear. A tombstone, a record with a null value, marks a key for deletion and is itself removed after the delete retention window, erasing the key entirely. If the cleanup policy is compact plus delete, ordinary time or size retention applies on top of compaction, so even the latest record for a key can expire. Records with a null key, or keyed incorrectly, are not compactable at all and are subject to plain retention deletion. And aggressive compaction settings, such as small segments and frequent cleaner runs, remove superseded records almost immediately. Each of these is the documented behavior of compaction, not a defect.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps one current notice per account on a board, and the rule is "always keep the newest notice for each account." People expect nothing ever vanishes, but four documented rules say otherwise. First, if a clerk pins a blank "cancelled" slip for Rajesh and a day passes, even that cancelled slip is removed, so Rajesh's account vanishes from the board completely. Second, if the board also has a "nothing older than seven days" rule, then even Rajesh's newest notice disappears once it is seven days old. Third, notices pinned without an account number written on them cannot be matched to any account, so the "keep newest per account" rule does not apply to them and they are simply thrown out on the age rule. Fourth, if the tidy-up crew is told to work constantly and aggressively, old superseded notices for an account are pulled almost the instant a newer one is pinned. None of these is the board malfunctioning; they are exactly the rules as written.

**One line to remember:** Compaction keeps the latest value per key, but tombstones expire the key after delete.retention.ms, compact,delete adds time or size expiry to even the latest record, null or wrong keys are not compactable and get retention-deleted, and aggressive settings purge old records almost instantly — all expected, all documented.

sections.s2_technical:
Reason one is the tombstone. In a compacted topic, you delete a key by producing a record with that key and a null value, which is the tombstone. Compaction keeps the tombstone long enough for consumers to observe the delete, specifically for at least `delete.retention.ms`, which defaults to twenty-four hours. After that window and a subsequent cleaning pass, the tombstone itself is removed, and at that point the key is completely gone from the log, including any trace that it ever existed. So if you look for a key after its tombstone has aged out, the data has disappeared, and that is precisely the designed behavior: the tombstone is a self-expiring delete marker. You produce it like this:

```java
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("account.profiles", "SAV2001", null)); // tombstone
// after delete.retention.ms + a cleaning pass, SAV2001 is fully gone
```

Reason two is the combined cleanup policy. A topic with `cleanup.policy=compact` only compacts and never expires the latest value per key. But a topic with `cleanup.policy=compact,delete` applies both compaction and ordinary time or size retention. That means a record can be removed because it is older than `retention.ms` or because the partition exceeded `retention.bytes`, even if it is the latest value for its key. People who assume a compacted topic keeps the latest value forever are surprised when the latest value for a rarely updated key expires purely on age. This combination is useful for things like a changelog that you want deduplicated by key but also bounded in time, and the expiry of a stale latest value is the intended effect, not a loss.

Reason three is non-compactable records. Compaction is keyed: it reasons about the latest record per key. A record with a null key has no key to deduplicate on, so compaction simply skips it, and such records are only ever removed by ordinary retention if the topic allows deletion, or they linger. Worse, if a producer accidentally sends records with the wrong key or a null key when you expected a real key, those records are not protected by the latest-per-key guarantee at all, so they can vanish under retention while you assumed compaction was keeping them. This is why discipline about always setting a correct key on a compacted topic matters, and why seeing null-keyed records disappear is expected given how compaction is defined.

Reason four is aggressive compaction settings. How quickly superseded records are removed depends on tunables. A small `segment.bytes` or short `segment.ms` rolls the active segment sooner so recent updates become eligible for cleaning quickly, a low `min.cleanable.dirty.ratio` makes the cleaner run even when only a small fraction of the log is stale, and a short cleaner backoff makes it run often. With all of these aggressive, an old value for a key can be purged almost immediately after a newer value is written. If you expected to still find a slightly older version for debugging or replay, it is already gone. That rapid removal is exactly what aggressive settings request, so it is expected behavior.

The unifying senior-level point is that compaction's guarantee is narrow and precise: it retains at least the latest value per key, subject to tombstone expiry, subject to any additional delete policy, only for properly keyed records, and on a schedule you control. Every case where data disappears is one of these rules operating as documented. The practical implications are: design consumers to treat null values as deletes so tombstone expiry does not leave them with stale state; choose compact versus compact,delete deliberately based on whether you want unbounded latest-per-key or bounded-plus-deduplicated; enforce non-null correct keys at the producer, ideally with a schema or validation, so nothing silently falls outside the compaction guarantee; and tune compaction aggressiveness to match how long you actually need superseded versions to remain, lengthening delete retention if slow consumers must observe deletes and relaxing the dirty ratio if you need older versions to survive longer. A subtle operational nuance is that because compaction runs per partition and lazily, the disappearance is also timing-dependent, so the same key may still be visible on one partition's uncleaned segment while gone from another, which again is expected given the lazy, partition-local cleaner.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India keeps account state in a compacted topic `account.state`, expecting the latest snapshot per account to always be available for cache rebuilds. Rajesh is SAV2001 and Priya is CUR3001. Over time, operators were surprised by data vanishing in four different ways and suspected bugs.

Problem 1 — after deleting a closed account with a tombstone, its key disappeared entirely a day later. Problem 2 — a topic mistakenly configured as compact plus delete expired the latest snapshot of a dormant account purely on age. Problem 3 — some events published with a null key vanished under retention while compaction never protected them. Problem 4 — on a topic with very aggressive compaction settings, the previous snapshot of an account was gone almost immediately after an update, breaking a debugging workflow that relied on the prior version. Each was actually documented behavior.

Our runnable demo models a `CompactedTopic` with a configurable policy and settings, and a `Cleaner` that applies all four rules, then shows each disappearance and labels it as expected with the governing setting. The classes are `CompactionDisappearanceDemo`, `Record`, `TopicConfig`, `CompactedTopic`, and `Cleaner`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four separate compacted topics, each configured to trigger one of the four disappearance reasons.

Step 1 (reason one): On a pure compact topic, we write a snapshot for SAV2001 then a tombstone. The cleaner runs twenty-five hours later. Because the tombstone is older than the twenty-four-hour delete retention, it is removed along with the key, so SAV2001 is entirely gone. The data disappeared exactly as the tombstone mechanism specifies.

Step 2 (reason two): On a compact plus delete topic with one-hour time retention, we write the latest snapshot for a dormant account and let two hours pass. The time-retention rule applies on top of compaction and removes the record despite it being the latest value for its key, because compact plus delete means both policies are in force. This is intended for bounded changelogs.

Step 3 (reason three): On a topic that allows deletion, we publish a record with a null key. Compaction cannot deduplicate it because there is no key, so it is governed only by retention, and after one hour it is deleted. It was never under the latest-per-key guarantee, so its disappearance is expected and is really a producer discipline problem.

Step 4 (reason four): On a topic with an aggressive dirty ratio and a tiny cleaner backoff, we write an old version then a new version for CUR3001. The cleaner runs almost immediately and removes the superseded old version at once. Anyone relying on finding the prior version for debugging finds it already gone, which is exactly what aggressive settings request.

Step 5: In every case the cleaner is doing precisely what its configuration specifies. The lesson is that compaction retains at least the latest value per key only within the bounds of tombstone expiry, any additional delete policy, correct keying, and the aggressiveness you configured, so each disappearance is documented behavior rather than a bug.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Log compaction guarantees that a compacted topic retains at least the latest value per key, but that guarantee is narrow and has four documented exceptions, so data disappearing is almost always compaction behaving exactly as specified rather than a bug. The first reason is the tombstone. You delete a key by producing a record with that key and a null value, and compaction keeps that tombstone only for the delete retention window, defaulting to twenty-four hours, so slow consumers can observe the delete. After that window and a cleaning pass, the tombstone and the key are gone entirely, which is the self-expiring delete marker working as designed.

The second reason is the cleanup policy. A topic set to compact only keeps the latest value per key forever, but a topic set to compact plus delete applies ordinary time or size retention on top of compaction, so even the latest value for a rarely updated key can expire purely on age. That is intended for a bounded, deduplicated changelog, and people are only surprised when they assumed compaction meant the latest value lives forever. The third reason is non-compactable records. Compaction is keyed, so a record with a null key or an accidentally wrong key is never under the latest-per-key guarantee and is governed only by retention, which means it can vanish while you thought compaction was protecting it. That is really a producer-discipline issue. The fourth reason is aggressive settings. Small segments, a low cleanable dirty ratio, and a short cleaner backoff make the cleaner remove superseded versions almost immediately, so an older version you hoped to still find for debugging is already gone, which is precisely what aggressive settings request.

On the National Bank of India account-state topic we chased all four of these as suspected bugs before realizing each was documented behavior. A closed account's key vanished a day after its tombstone, a dormant account's latest snapshot expired on a compact plus delete topic, some null-keyed events disappeared under retention, and on an aggressively tuned topic the previous snapshot was purged the instant a new one arrived.

The way I turn this understanding into correct design is concrete. I make every consumer treat a null value as a delete so tombstone expiry never leaves stale state behind. I choose compact versus compact plus delete deliberately, picking pure compact when I need an unbounded latest-per-key store and compact plus delete when I want deduplication with a time or size bound. I enforce non-null, correct keys at the producer, ideally with validation or a schema, so nothing silently falls outside the compaction guarantee. And I tune the aggressiveness, lengthening delete retention when slow consumers must observe deletes and relaxing the dirty ratio when I need older versions to survive longer. The one-line principle I give the team is that compaction keeps the latest value per key only within the bounds of tombstone expiry, any additional delete policy, correct keying, and the schedule you configured, so when data disappears, the first thing to check is the topic's exact configuration, not the code.

answers.question: (Scenario) Multiple independent teams share the same Kafka cluster (multi-tenant) and one team suddenly spikes traffic — how do you prevent the noisy-neighbor problem: (1) hard isolation via separate clusters for critical workloads, (2) topic-level isolation (separate topics per team, not one shared topic), (3) Kafka quotas (produce/consume byte-rate limits per client-id/user to throttle the noisy team without dropping messages), (4) partition-level isolation (key by team so hot traffic is contained to specific partitions), (5) retention isolation (different TTLs per topic), (6) broker-level isolation (assign topic partitions to dedicated broker groups), (7) consumer group isolation (independent groups with their own offsets so a slow consumer doesn't block others)?
answers.shortTitle: (Scenario) Multiple teams share one Kafka cluster and one team spikes traffic — how do you prevent the noisy-neighbor problem?

s1_definition.profdef: The noisy-neighbor problem in a multi-tenant Kafka cluster is when one tenant's traffic spike consumes shared resources such as broker CPU, disk I/O, network bandwidth, and page cache, degrading other tenants. You prevent it with layered isolation: hard isolation by giving critical workloads their own cluster, topic-level isolation so tenants do not share topics, Kafka quotas that cap per-client or per-user produce and consume byte rates without dropping data, partition-level isolation by keying so a tenant's load stays on specific partitions, retention isolation with per-topic time-to-live, broker-level isolation that pins certain topics to dedicated broker groups, and consumer group isolation so each tenant's group has independent offsets and a slow consumer cannot block others.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India runs one big shared operations floor used by several departments: retail transfers, corporate payments, and card settlements. One day the corporate payments team runs a huge batch and floods the shared counters, mail trays, and phone lines, so the retail team suddenly cannot get their transfers through. To stop this you use layers of separation. The most critical department gets its own separate floor entirely. Each department gets its own counters and mail trays instead of one shared set. A supervisor caps how fast any one department can submit forms so a surge is slowed rather than allowed to swamp everyone. Each department's forms go into its own labeled bins. Old forms are cleared on each department's own schedule. Some departments get dedicated staff who only serve them. And each department keeps its own queue and its own place marker so a department that is slow to process does not freeze the others.
s1_definition.oneliner: Multi-tenant noisy-neighbor is prevented by layered isolation — separate clusters for critical workloads, per-team topics, per-client quotas, partition and broker isolation, per-topic retention, and independent consumer groups — so one tenant's spike cannot starve the others.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The noisy-neighbor problem in a multi-tenant Kafka cluster is when one tenant's traffic spike consumes shared resources such as broker CPU, disk I/O, network bandwidth, and page cache, degrading other tenants. You prevent it with layered isolation: hard isolation by giving critical workloads their own cluster, topic-level isolation so tenants do not share topics, Kafka quotas that cap per-client or per-user produce and consume byte rates without dropping data, partition-level isolation by keying so a tenant's load stays on specific partitions, retention isolation with per-topic time-to-live, broker-level isolation that pins certain topics to dedicated broker groups, and consumer group isolation so each tenant's group has independent offsets and a slow consumer cannot block others.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India runs one big shared operations floor used by several departments: retail transfers, corporate payments, and card settlements. One day the corporate payments team runs a huge batch and floods the shared counters, mail trays, and phone lines, so the retail team suddenly cannot get their transfers through. To stop this you use layers of separation. The most critical department gets its own separate floor entirely. Each department gets its own counters and mail trays instead of one shared set. A supervisor caps how fast any one department can submit forms so a surge is slowed rather than allowed to swamp everyone. Each department's forms go into its own labeled bins. Old forms are cleared on each department's own schedule. Some departments get dedicated staff who only serve them. And each department keeps its own queue and its own place marker so a department that is slow to process does not freeze the others.

**One line to remember:** Multi-tenant noisy-neighbor is prevented by layered isolation — separate clusters for critical workloads, per-team topics, per-client quotas, partition and broker isolation, per-topic retention, and independent consumer groups — so one tenant's spike cannot starve the others.

sections.s2_technical:
The first and strongest layer is hard isolation with separate clusters. If a workload is business-critical, such as settlement, you give it a physically separate Kafka cluster so no other tenant can ever touch its resources. This is the most expensive option in hardware and operations, so you reserve it for the few workloads where any cross-tenant impact is unacceptable, and you accept the cost because full isolation is the only true guarantee.

The second layer is topic-level isolation. Tenants should not share a single topic; each team gets its own topics. Sharing a topic couples tenants in many ways, including partition contention, retention, access control, and schema evolution. Separate topics let you set per-topic configuration and access control lists, and they localize a tenant's traffic and failures. This is the baseline hygiene of multi-tenancy.

The third layer is Kafka quotas, which are the key tool for throttling a spike without losing data. You set a produce byte-rate and a consume byte-rate limit per client id or per authenticated user, and when a tenant exceeds its quota, the broker delays that tenant's requests rather than rejecting or dropping them, so the tenant slows down but its messages are not lost and other tenants keep their fair share of bandwidth. You configure it like this:

```bash
# Throttle the 'corp-payments' app to 10 MB/s produce and 20 MB/s consume
kafka-configs.sh --alter --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 \
  --add-config 'producer_byte_rate=10485760,consumer_byte_rate=20971520' \
  --entity-type clients --entity-name corp-payments
```

There are also request-rate quotas that cap the percentage of broker request-handling threads a tenant may use, which protects CPU, not just bandwidth. Quotas are the mechanism that converts a sudden spike into gentle back-pressure on the offender alone.

The fourth layer is partition-level isolation by keying. If tenants must share a topic for some reason, you key records by tenant so each tenant's traffic maps to a known subset of partitions, which contains a hot tenant's load to specific partitions rather than spreading its impact across all of them. More commonly, giving each tenant its own topic already gives each its own partitions, which is cleaner.

The fifth layer is retention isolation. Each topic can have its own retention time or size, so one tenant's need to keep data for thirty days does not force everyone else's disk usage up, and a tenant that writes huge volumes with short retention does not evict another tenant's longer-lived data. Per-topic retention keeps storage pressure contained to the tenant that creates it.

The sixth layer is broker-level isolation. Using replica placement and rack or broker-group assignment, you can pin a tenant's topic partitions to a dedicated set of brokers, so that tenant's load lands on its own brokers and does not compete for CPU, disk, and cache with others on the shared brokers. This sits between full cluster separation and pure quotas, giving physical resource separation within one logical cluster for tenants that need more than quotas but not a whole cluster.

The seventh layer is consumer group isolation. Each tenant, and ideally each application, uses its own consumer group with its own committed offsets. Because offsets are per group, a slow or stuck consumer in one group only grows that group's lag and never blocks another group from reading the same or different topics. This ensures that a tenant whose consumers fall behind suffers alone rather than holding up everyone.

The senior-level framing is that these layers are complementary and you choose a combination based on criticality and cost. Quotas plus per-team topics plus per-group consumers are the cheap default that handles most noisy-neighbor cases. Broker-group isolation is the middle tier for tenants that need resource separation without a dedicated cluster. A separate cluster is the top tier for the few truly critical workloads. You also add observability per tenant, tracking per-client byte rates, request-handler utilization, and per-group lag, so you can detect a noisy neighbor quickly and tighten its quota, and you codify tenant onboarding so every new topic gets sensible quotas, retention, and access control by default rather than inheriting unbounded shared defaults.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs one shared Kafka cluster used by three teams: Retail (Rajesh and Priya transfers), Corporate payments, and Card settlements. One morning the Corporate team ran a massive end-of-month batch and flooded the cluster, and Retail transfers slowed to a crawl.

Problem 1 — all three teams were sharing some topics and had no quotas, so Corporate's spike consumed the shared broker bandwidth and starved Retail. This is the classic noisy neighbor, and the immediate fix is per-client quotas plus per-team topics.

Problem 2 — Card settlements is business-critical and must never be affected by another team, so quotas alone were not enough reassurance. This is where broker-group isolation and ultimately a separate cluster come in.

Our runnable demo models a `Cluster` with shared bandwidth, `Tenant` producers with byte rates, a `QuotaEnforcer` that throttles an over-quota tenant without dropping messages, and shows the before-and-after effect on each tenant's effective throughput, plus a dedicated broker group for the critical tenant. The classes are `NoisyNeighborDemo`, `Tenant`, `QuotaEnforcer`, `Cluster`, and `ConsumerGroupIsolation`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a shared cluster with sixty megabytes per second of bandwidth and three tenants, Retail wanting twenty, Corporate spiking to one hundred, and Cards wanting fifteen.

Step 1: Without quotas, total demand is one hundred thirty-five against sixty available, so bandwidth is shared proportionally. Corporate's huge demand grabs most of the pipe, and Retail and Cards receive far less than they need. Retail transfers for Rajesh and Priya slow dramatically. This is the noisy neighbor starving its neighbors.

Step 2: We apply per-client quotas: Retail twenty, Corporate capped at ten, Cards fifteen. When Corporate exceeds its ten-megabyte-per-second quota, the broker delays its requests rather than dropping them, so Corporate's batch simply takes longer while its messages are preserved.

Step 3: With Corporate capped, total allowed demand now fits within the sixty-megabyte-per-second budget, so Retail gets its twenty and Cards gets its fifteen. No tenant is starved, and Corporate loses no data, it just runs slower. The spike has been converted into back-pressure on the offender alone.

Step 4: Because Cards is business-critical, we pin its topic partitions to a dedicated broker group, so even CPU, disk, and cache for Cards are physically separated from the shared brokers, and in the limit Cards would move to its own cluster for absolute isolation.

Step 5: Each tenant uses its own consumer group with independent offsets, so when Corporate's consumers fall far behind during the batch, only the Corporate group's lag grows; the Retail group keeps reading at its own pace and is never blocked. This confirms that offset isolation prevents a slow consumer in one tenant from affecting another.

```
  2. corporate app produces at 100 MB/s
  3. broker: rate > producer_byte_rate(10) -> add delay to responses
  4. corporate effective rate -> 10 MB/s (throttled, intact)
  5. retail + cards keep their quotas; no starvation
  6. each tenant consumer group commits its own offsets -> no cross-block
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The noisy-neighbor problem in a shared Kafka cluster is when one tenant's traffic spike consumes shared broker resources, CPU, disk I/O, network bandwidth, and page cache, and degrades everyone else. The way I prevent it is layered isolation, choosing how many layers based on how critical each workload is. The strongest layer is hard isolation: a business-critical workload gets its own physically separate cluster so no other tenant can ever touch its resources, which I reserve for the few cases where any cross-tenant impact is unacceptable because it is the most expensive option.

Below that, the baseline hygiene is topic-level isolation, giving each team its own topics rather than one shared topic, because separate topics let me set per-topic configuration, access control, and retention and localize a tenant's traffic and failures. The single most important runtime tool is Kafka quotas: I set per-client or per-user produce and consume byte-rate limits, and critically, when a tenant exceeds its quota the broker delays its requests rather than dropping them, so a spike becomes gentle back-pressure on the offender alone while everyone else keeps their fair share and no data is lost. There are also request-rate quotas that cap a tenant's share of broker request-handler threads, which protects CPU and not just bandwidth.

The remaining layers fill specific gaps. If tenants must share a topic I key records by tenant so a hot tenant's load stays on specific partitions, though giving each tenant its own topic usually makes that unnecessary. Per-topic retention isolation means one tenant's long retention does not inflate everyone's disk and a high-volume tenant does not evict another's data. Broker-level isolation pins a tenant's partitions to a dedicated broker group, giving physical resource separation inside one logical cluster for tenants that need more than quotas but not a whole cluster. And consumer group isolation, where each tenant and application has its own group with its own offsets, ensures a slow or stuck consumer only grows its own lag and never blocks another group.

On the National Bank of India shared cluster we hit this when the Corporate team's end-of-month batch starved Retail transfers. The immediate fix was per-client quotas plus per-team topics, which capped Corporate and restored Retail and Cards without losing any Corporate messages. Because Cards settlement is business-critical, we went further and pinned it to a dedicated broker group, with a separate cluster as the ultimate option. The way I summarize it for the team is that quotas plus per-team topics plus per-group consumers are the cheap default that solves most noisy-neighbor cases, broker-group isolation is the middle tier, and a dedicated cluster is the top tier, and alongside all of them I run per-tenant observability on byte rates, request-handler utilization, and lag so I can spot a noisy neighbor and tighten its quota before it hurts anyone, and I bake sensible quotas, retention, and access control into tenant onboarding so no new topic ever inherits unbounded shared defaults.

s1_definition.analogy: Imagine each type of account at National Bank of India has one designated master branch that handles all its transactions, with backup branches keeping copies. If the master branch for an account keeps changing from one branch to another every few minutes, chaos follows. The backlog of unprocessed transactions grows during each handover. Head office is constantly rewriting the master directory, which is extra work for everyone. sections.s2_technical:
First, understand the leader's central role. For each partition, exactly one replica is the leader, and all produce and consume requests go to the leader; followers only replicate. Clients cache cluster metadata that maps each partition to its current leader broker. When a leader moves, that cached mapping is stale, so the first impact is that a client sending to the old leader gets a NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION error, must fetch fresh metadata to learn the new leader, and then retry the request against it. Each such cycle adds latency and shows up as a transient error, and when leaders move constantly, clients spend a meaningful fraction of their time refreshing metadata and retrying instead of doing useful work.

Second, consumer lag increases during transitions. While a leader is moving, the affected partition is briefly unavailable for consumption, and consumers must reconnect to the new leader. During that window, no progress is made on that partition, so lag ticks up each time, and if leaders move frequently, these repeated small stalls accumulate into noticeable lag and latency. Producers similarly buffer and retry during the gap, which can cause bursts once the new leader is available.

Third, broker coordination load rises. Leadership is tracked by the controller, and every leader change triggers metadata updates that must propagate to all brokers and clients, plus any in-sync replica set changes that accompany the move. This bookkeeping is normally cheap but becomes significant when it happens repeatedly across many partitions, stealing broker capacity from serving traffic and sometimes feeding a vicious cycle where the load from churn causes more instability.

Fourth, and most seriously, durability risk. When leadership churns, especially if it is driven by brokers flapping in and out of the cluster, follower replicas can fall out of the in-sync replica set because they cannot keep up during the disruption. A partition that normally has three in-sync replicas can temporarily drop to two or one. If it drops to one and your durability relies on at least two in-sync replicas, writes are either rejected or, if misconfigured, acknowledged on a single copy, which is the durability hole covered by the acks and min-in-sync-replicas contract. So frequent leader movement is not just a latency problem; it can quietly erode your replication safety.

The stabilization steps follow the root causes. The first and most important is to fix the underlying instability rather than treating symptoms. Common root causes include brokers under memory pressure doing long garbage-collection pauses that make them miss heartbeats and get kicked out, undersized or saturated disks and network causing replication to fall behind, flaky hardware or network links, and misconfigured timeouts such as too-short ZooKeeper or controller session timeouts that evict healthy-but-slow brokers. You diagnose with broker logs, garbage-collection logs, and metrics for under-replicated partitions, in-sync replica shrink and expand rates, and leader election rate, then address the specific cause, for example by tuning the JVM heap and garbage collector, adding capacity, replacing bad hardware, or correcting timeouts.

The second stabilization step is to avoid unnecessary preferred-leader elections. Kafka has a notion of a preferred leader, the first replica in a partition's assignment, and it periodically rebalances leadership back to the preferred leader to keep load even. If auto leader rebalancing is too aggressive, or if you trigger manual preferred-leader elections carelessly, you cause avoidable leader movement. You can disable or tune the automatic rebalance and only run preferred-leader elections deliberately during calm windows, so leadership moves when you intend it to, not constantly. The relevant broker setting is auto leader rebalance enable and its imbalance threshold and check interval.

The third stabilization step is monitoring the leader count per broker. A healthy cluster has leadership spread fairly evenly across brokers. If you watch the leader count per broker over time, you can see churn as the counts bouncing around, spot a broker that keeps losing and regaining leadership (a sign it is flapping), and detect imbalance where one broker carries too many leaders and becomes a hotspot. This metric, together with the leader election rate and under-replicated partition count, tells you both that churn is happening and often which broker is at fault. Here are the commands:

```bash
# See leader distribution and which partitions are under-replicated
kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-replicated-partitions --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092

# Trigger a preferred-leader election DELIBERATELY, only when the cluster is calm
kafka-leader-election.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 --election-type preferred --all-topic-partitions
```

Senior-level nuances: set generous but correct session and heartbeat timeouts so a briefly slow broker is not evicted, which prevents a flap-and-recover loop; keep brokers' garbage collection pauses short because long pauses are a leading cause of spurious evictions; stagger maintenance so you never take down enough brokers to force mass leadership movement; and treat a rising leader election rate as a first-class alert, because it is the earliest signal that something is making leadership unstable before it turns into latency and durability problems.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India's cluster began showing frequent leader movement after a memory-pressure issue made one broker pause for long garbage collections, repeatedly missing heartbeats and getting evicted and re-added. Settlement producers and consumers suffered. Rajesh and Priya transfers flow through the affected partitions.

Problem 1 — every time the flapping broker lost and regained leadership, producers and consumers got NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION, refreshed metadata, retried, and lag bumped, so latency and error rates rose and settlement throughput dropped. This is the client-facing impact.

Problem 2 — during the churn, follower replicas fell out of the in-sync set, dropping some partitions to a single in-sync copy, which threatened durability. This is the durability-risk impact, and it forced us to prioritize stabilizing rather than just retrying harder.

Our runnable demo models a `Broker` that can flap, a `PartitionLeadership` tracker, and a `ClientImpact` model that counts NOT_LEADER errors, metadata refreshes, retries, lag, and in-sync replica shrink as leaders move, then shows the improvement after we stop the flapping and disable aggressive auto-rebalance. The classes are `LeaderChurnDemo`, `Broker`, `PartitionLeadership`, and `ClientImpact`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a cluster where broker-2 is the leader for several settlement partitions and keeps flapping due to long garbage-collection pauses.

Step 1: Broker-2 pauses for a long garbage collection, misses its heartbeats, and the controller declares it dead and moves leadership of its partitions to other brokers. Moments later broker-2 recovers and rejoins, and because it is the preferred leader, leadership often moves back. This bounce repeats.

Step 2: Each time leadership moves, settlement producers and consumers that were talking to the old leader get NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION, refresh cluster metadata, discover the new leader, and retry. This adds latency, raises the error rate, and wastes client time on metadata work.

Step 3: During each transition the affected partitions are briefly unavailable, so consumers make no progress and lag bumps up each cycle. Producers buffer and retry, then burst once the new leader is available, adding jitter to end-to-end timing.

Step 4: The controller does repeated metadata and in-sync replica bookkeeping for every move, loading the brokers, and during the churn some follower replicas fall out of the in-sync set, dropping partitions toward a single in-sync copy and threatening durability.

Step 5: After we fix the root cause by tuning the heap and garbage collector so broker-2 no longer pauses, and after disabling the overly aggressive automatic leader rebalancing, leadership stops moving. NOT_LEADER errors, refreshes, retries, lag bumps, and coordination operations all fall to near zero, and the in-sync replica set stays full, restoring both performance and durability.

answers.question: Why can Kafka sustain very high throughput on commodity disks — explain sequential append-only writes vs random I/O, zero-copy transfer (`sendfile`), and reliance on the OS page cache rather than an in-process cache.
answers.shortTitle: Why can Kafka sustain very high throughput on commodity disks?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka achieves very high throughput on ordinary disks through three design choices. It stores each partition as an append-only log and writes sequentially, which is dramatically faster than random I/O even on spinning disks and still much faster on SSDs. It serves consumer reads with zero-copy transfer using the operating system's sendfile system call, which sends bytes straight from the page cache to the network socket without copying them through application memory. And it relies on the operating system page cache rather than maintaining its own in-process cache, so recent data is served from RAM for free and the JVM heap stays small, avoiding garbage-collection pressure.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India records every transaction in a long ledger. Instead of flipping around the ledger to find a spot for each entry, which is slow, clerks always write the next entry on the very next line at the end, which is fast and smooth; that is sequential append. When head office asks for a copy of recent pages, instead of a clerk photocopying each page by hand and walking it over, the bank uses a direct pass-through chute that sends the pages straight from the shelf to the courier without the clerk touching them; that is zero-copy. And because the most recent pages are already lying open on the desk from being written, anyone who wants them just reads them off the desk instead of fetching them from the vault; that is the operating-system page cache serving recent data from memory for free.
s1_definition.oneliner: Kafka is fast on cheap disks because it writes sequentially to an append-only log, serves reads with zero-copy sendfile straight from page cache to the socket, and leans on the OS page cache instead of an in-process cache, keeping the JVM heap small and avoiding garbage-collection stalls.

sections.s2_technical:
The first pillar is sequential append-only writes versus random I/O. A Kafka partition is an ordered log, and producers only ever append to the end of the active segment. Appending sequentially means the disk head, on a spinning disk, barely moves, and even on an SSD the controller can write large contiguous blocks efficiently with minimal write amplification. Random I/O, by contrast, scatters small writes all over the disk, forcing seeks on spinning disks and expensive read-modify-write cycles on SSDs. The performance gap between sequential and random access is enormous, often one to two orders of magnitude, which is why Kafka's append-only design lets commodity disks sustain throughput that would be impossible with a random-access data structure like a B-tree updated in place. Kafka also batches many records into one write and relies on the operating system to flush, so individual small producer records coalesce into large sequential disk writes.

The second pillar is zero-copy transfer with sendfile. When a consumer fetches records, those bytes often already sit in the operating system page cache because they were recently written or read. Without zero-copy, serving them would require copying the data from the kernel page cache into the application's user-space buffer, then back into the kernel socket buffer, then out to the network card, which is multiple copies and multiple context switches per transfer. Kafka instead uses the sendfile system call, which tells the kernel to transfer bytes directly from the page cache to the network socket without ever copying them into the JVM. In Java this is exposed through `FileChannel.transferTo`, and conceptually the hot path is:

```java
// Conceptually how Kafka serves a fetch: kernel moves bytes file -> socket directly.
fileChannel.transferTo(position, byteCount, socketChannel); // sendfile under the hood
// No copy into JVM heap, far fewer context switches, saturates the NIC.
```

This removes the per-byte cost of user-space copies, so a single broker can push data to many consumers at close to network line rate using very little CPU.

The third pillar is reliance on the operating-system page cache rather than an in-process cache. Many systems build their own large in-memory cache inside the application process. Kafka deliberately does not; it lets the operating system cache file data in the page cache, which is memory the OS already manages. This has several compounding benefits. Recently written data is already in the page cache, so consumers reading the tail of the log, which is the common case, are served from RAM without any disk read at all. Because the cache lives in the kernel and not the JVM heap, the Kafka process can run with a small heap, which keeps garbage-collection pauses short and predictable, a major reliability win since long GC pauses are a leading cause of broker instability. The page cache also survives a broker process restart, so a restarted broker can serve hot data from a warm cache immediately. And by not duplicating data in both an app cache and the OS cache, Kafka avoids wasting memory on double buffering.

These three pillars reinforce each other. Sequential writes keep recent data contiguous and hot in the page cache; the page cache makes most reads hit memory; and zero-copy then ships those cached bytes to consumers without touching the heap. The net effect is that the common path, producers appending and consumers reading the tail, involves almost no random disk access, almost no user-space copying, and almost no JVM memory pressure, which is exactly why Kafka saturates commodity hardware so well.

Senior-level nuances worth stating. Zero-copy is bypassed when the broker must transform bytes, for example when TLS encryption is enabled or when the broker must recompress or down-convert message formats for an older client, because those require the data to pass through user space, so you preserve the fast path by keeping client and broker message formats aligned and by being aware that encryption adds CPU and copies. Durability still depends on replication and flush behavior: Kafka relies on the page cache and the operating system to flush to disk lazily, trading an fsync-per-message for throughput, and it gets durability from replication across brokers rather than from forcing every write to disk immediately, which is why replication factor and acks settings, not disk fsync, are your durability contract. Finally, because Kafka leans on the page cache, you should give the operating system plenty of free RAM for caching rather than sizing a huge JVM heap, and you should expect performance to depend on how much of your working set fits in the page cache.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India streams card-authorization events through Kafka on commodity servers with ordinary SSDs, and the platform team was skeptical that cheap disks could handle the volume. Rajesh and Priya generate authorizations alongside millions of others.

Problem 1 — the team feared that writing millions of small authorization records per minute would thrash the disks with random I/O. In reality Kafka appends them sequentially to the partition log and batches them, so the disk sees large contiguous writes and keeps up easily. This is the sequential-write advantage.

Problem 2 — the team worried that fanning out those events to many consumer services would saturate broker CPU with data copying. In reality zero-copy sendfile ships bytes from the page cache straight to each consumer's socket, and the hot tail of the log is served from RAM via the page cache, so a single broker feeds many consumers cheaply. This is the zero-copy and page-cache advantage.

Our runnable demo models the cost of sequential versus random writes, counts the copies and context switches for a naive user-space read versus a zero-copy transfer, and models page-cache hit rates for tail reads versus old reads, reporting the throughput difference. The classes are `ThroughputDemo`, `WritePattern`, `TransferPath`, and `PageCache`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one million card-authorization records produced and then fanned out to several consumer services.

Step 1: Producers send many small authorization records. The Kafka client batches them by size and a short linger, so instead of a million tiny disk operations, the broker receives large batches and appends them sequentially to the end of the active segment. The disk sees big contiguous writes, which commodity SSDs handle at high throughput with minimal write amplification.

Step 2: Compared with a hypothetical random-write data structure, the sequential append is roughly one to two orders of magnitude cheaper, as the demo's cost model shows, which is why cheap disks keep up with the write rate that the team feared would thrash them.

Step 3: Consumer services fetch recent authorizations. Because those records were just written, they are still in the operating-system page cache, so the broker reads them from RAM, not disk. The hot tail of the log is served from memory for free.

Step 4: To send those cached bytes to each consumer, the broker uses zero-copy sendfile, transferring the bytes directly from the page cache to the network socket without copying them into the JVM heap. The naive path would make four copies and several context switches per transfer; zero-copy collapses that to effectively one transfer with minimal CPU, so one broker feeds many consumers near network line rate.

Step 5: Because the cache lives in the kernel rather than the JVM, Kafka runs with a small heap, keeping garbage-collection pauses short and the broker stable, and the page cache stays warm across restarts. The three pillars together mean the common path, appending and reading the tail, involves almost no random disk access, almost no user-space copying, and almost no heap pressure, which is the whole reason commodity hardware sustains such high throughput.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka sustains very high throughput on commodity disks because of three deliberate design choices that reinforce each other. The first is sequential append-only writes. A partition is an ordered log and producers only ever append to the end, so the disk sees large contiguous writes instead of scattered random ones. Sequential I/O is often one to two orders of magnitude faster than random I/O, on spinning disks because the head barely moves and on SSDs because it avoids expensive read-modify-write amplification, and Kafka batches many small records into big writes, so even millions of tiny events become efficient sequential appends that ordinary disks handle easily.

The second is zero-copy transfer using the sendfile system call. When a consumer fetches data, those bytes are usually already in the operating-system page cache, and rather than copying them from the kernel into the application's user-space buffer and back into the socket buffer, Kafka asks the kernel to transfer them directly from the page cache to the network socket. In Java this is FileChannel.transferTo, and it eliminates the per-byte user-space copies and most context switches, so a single broker can feed many consumers at close to network line rate using very little CPU.

The third is relying on the operating-system page cache instead of an in-process cache. Kafka does not build its own big heap cache; it lets the OS cache file data in memory it already manages. Because recently written data is already in the page cache, consumers reading the tail of the log, which is the common case, are served from RAM with no disk read at all. Because the cache lives in the kernel and not the JVM heap, Kafka runs with a small heap, which keeps garbage-collection pauses short and the broker stable, and the cache even survives a process restart so a restarted broker serves hot data immediately.

On the National Bank of India card-authorization stream, this is exactly why cheap servers with ordinary SSDs kept up with millions of events. The writes were sequential batched appends rather than random thrashing, the hot tail was served from the page cache, and zero-copy let one broker fan those events out to the fraud scorer, the ledger updater, and analytics without saturating CPU. The nuances I always mention are that zero-copy is bypassed when the broker must transform bytes, such as with TLS encryption or message-format down-conversion for old clients, so I keep client and broker formats aligned and budget CPU for encryption; that durability comes from replication and the acks contract rather than forcing an fsync per message, since Kafka flushes lazily through the page cache; and that because Kafka leans on the page cache, you give the operating system plenty of free RAM instead of sizing a giant heap. The one-line principle is that Kafka wins by turning messaging into sequential log appends and cached, zero-copy reads, which is the pattern commodity hardware is best at.

answers.question: How is a partition stored on disk (segment files, offset index), and how does retention/compaction interact with segments?
answers.shortTitle: How is a partition stored on disk (segment files, offset index), and how does retention/compaction interact with segments?

s1_definition.profdef: A Kafka partition is stored on disk as a directory of log segment files. Each segment is a `.log` file holding a contiguous range of records by offset, accompanied by an offset index `.index` file that maps offsets to byte positions in the log, and a time index `.timeindex` file that maps timestamps to offsets. Only the newest segment, the active segment, is written to; older segments are closed and immutable. Retention and compaction operate at the granularity of these closed segments: time or size retention deletes whole aged segments, and compaction rewrites closed segments to keep only the latest record per key, while the active segment is left untouched.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps a partition's transaction history in a filing cabinet, where each drawer is a segment holding a block of consecutive entries. Each drawer has a small index card on the front that says "entry number so-and-so starts at this spot in the drawer," so a clerk can jump straight to an entry instead of reading the whole drawer; that is the offset index. There is also a second card mapping dates to entry numbers; that is the time index. Clerks only ever add new entries to the front drawer that is currently open; the older drawers are sealed and never changed. When it is time to clean up, the bank either throws out whole sealed drawers that are too old, which is retention, or rewrites sealed drawers to keep only the latest entry for each account, which is compaction, and in both cases they never touch the open front drawer.
s1_definition.oneliner: A partition is a directory of immutable closed segments plus one active segment, each segment paired with an offset index and a time index, and retention deletes whole aged segments while compaction rewrites closed segments to the latest-per-key, never touching the active segment.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Kafka partition is stored on disk as a directory of log segment files. Each segment is a `.log` file holding a contiguous range of records by offset, accompanied by an offset index `.index` file that maps offsets to byte positions in the log, and a time index `.timeindex` file that maps timestamps to offsets. Only the newest segment, the active segment, is written to; older segments are closed and immutable. Retention and compaction operate at the granularity of these closed segments: time or size retention deletes whole aged segments, and compaction rewrites closed segments to keep only the latest record per key, while the active segment is left untouched.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps a partition's transaction history in a filing cabinet, where each drawer is a segment holding a block of consecutive entries. Each drawer has a small index card on the front that says "entry number so-and-so starts at this spot in the drawer," so a clerk can jump straight to an entry instead of reading the whole drawer; that is the offset index. There is also a second card mapping dates to entry numbers; that is the time index. Clerks only ever add new entries to the front drawer that is currently open; the older drawers are sealed and never changed. When it is time to clean up, the bank either throws out whole sealed drawers that are too old, which is retention, or rewrites sealed drawers to keep only the latest entry for each account, which is compaction, and in both cases they never touch the open front drawer.

**One line to remember:** A partition is a directory of immutable closed segments plus one active segment, each segment paired with an offset index and a time index, and retention deletes whole aged segments while compaction rewrites closed segments to the latest-per-key, never touching the active segment.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the on-disk layout. For a topic partition, Kafka creates a directory named like `topicname-0` for partition zero. Inside it are groups of three files per segment, named by the base offset of the segment, for example `00000000000000000000.log`, `00000000000000000000.index`, and `00000000000000000000.timeindex`. The `.log` file is the actual record data, a sequence of record batches appended in offset order. The `.index` file is the offset index, and the `.timeindex` file is the time index. A partition therefore looks like a series of these triples, one per segment, with the highest-base-offset segment being the active one.

The offset index exists to make reads fast. The `.log` file can be a gigabyte, so to find the record at a given offset without scanning, Kafka keeps the offset index, which is a sparse map from a logical offset to the physical byte position in the `.log` file where that offset's batch begins. It is sparse, meaning it does not have an entry for every record but one roughly every few kilobytes, controlled by `index.interval.bytes`, so to read offset N, Kafka binary-searches the index for the nearest indexed offset at or below N, seeks to that byte position in the log, and scans forward a short distance to N. This makes a lookup cheap while keeping the index small. The time index similarly maps timestamps to offsets so that operations like "seek to the first message after this time" and time-based retention can work efficiently.

Now segment rolling. The active segment keeps growing as producers append. Kafka closes it and starts a new active segment when the active segment reaches `segment.bytes` in size or `segment.ms` in age, whichever comes first. When a segment is closed, it becomes immutable; nothing is ever appended to or modified in a closed segment. This immutability is what makes retention and compaction safe and simple, because they only ever operate on segments that will not change under them, and it is why the active segment is always excluded from cleanup.

Retention interacts with segments by deleting whole segments. With `cleanup.policy=delete`, Kafka checks closed segments against the retention policy: a segment is eligible for deletion when all its records are older than `retention.ms`, judged by the segment's largest timestamp, or when the partition's total size exceeds `retention.bytes` and the oldest segments must go to fit. Crucially, retention never deletes individual records; it deletes entire segment files, so retention granularity is the segment. This is why segment size matters for retention precision: smaller segments let retention trim data closer to the exact cutoff, while a large segment cannot be deleted until its very last record ages out.

Compaction interacts with segments by rewriting them. With `cleanup.policy=compact`, the log cleaner scans the closed segments, builds a map of the latest offset per key, and rewrites the closed segments into new, smaller segments that keep only the most recent record for each key, plus tombstones within their retention window. It processes the dirty portion of the log, the closed segments that have accumulated enough stale updates per the `min.cleanable.dirty.ratio`, and it never touches the active segment. Compaction preserves offsets, meaning the surviving records keep their original offsets even though intermediate offsets are now gone, so the log can have gaps in offset numbering after compaction, which consumers handle transparently. A topic can also be `compact,delete`, in which case both apply: the cleaner compacts closed segments and retention still deletes whole segments that age out.

Putting the interaction together: both retention and compaction are segment-oriented background operations that only touch closed, immutable segments and always skip the active segment. Retention is coarse, operating by deleting whole segments based on age or size. Compaction is finer within a key but still works segment by segment, rewriting closed segments to the latest value per key. The offset and time indexes are maintained alongside, rebuilt for the rewritten segments after compaction and deleted along with their segment on retention.

Senior-level nuances. Segment size is a central tuning knob with competing effects: smaller segments give finer retention and let compaction and cleanup run in smaller, smoother bursts, but they add file-handle and index overhead and more frequent rolling, while larger segments are more efficient for steady-state append and read but make retention coarser and cleanup burstier. The active segment is never eligible for retention or compaction, so a very low-traffic partition whose active segment rarely rolls can retain data far longer than `retention.ms` suggests, until `segment.ms` forces a roll. After a broker restart Kafka may rebuild or sanity-check indexes from the log, which is why index files are treated as reconstructable rather than authoritative. And compaction's offset-preserving rewrite is why you can rely on a specific key's latest value always being present while older offsets for that key simply vanish.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India stores two kinds of streams: the `account.ledger` topic for an append-only transaction history under delete retention, and the `account.state` topic for the latest balance per account under compaction. Rajesh is SAV2001 and Priya is CUR3001. The team needed to understand exactly how segments, indexes, retention, and compaction behave to tune disk usage and reason about what data survives.

Problem 1 — the ops team saw multiple `.log`, `.index`, and `.timeindex` files per partition and did not understand the layout or why some old data was deleted in chunks rather than record by record. This is the segment-and-index layout plus the fact that retention deletes whole segments.

Problem 2 — on the compacted `account.state` topic they noticed offset gaps and wanted to confirm that the latest balance per account was always retained. This is compaction rewriting closed segments to the latest-per-key while preserving and skipping offsets.

Our runnable demo models a `Partition` made of `Segment` objects each with a log, an offset index, and a time index, an active segment that cannot be cleaned, a `RetentionPolicy` that deletes aged segments, and a `Compactor` that rewrites closed segments to latest-per-key. It shows an offset-index lookup, a retention pass, and a compaction pass with resulting offset gaps. The classes are `SegmentStorageDemo`, `LogRecord`, `OffsetIndex`, `Segment`, `Partition`, `RetentionPolicy`, and `Compactor`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an `account.ledger` partition with two closed segments and one active segment, and an `account.state` compacted partition.

Step 1: On disk the ledger partition is a directory containing, for each segment, a `.log` file of records, a `.index` offset-index file, and a `.timeindex` time-index file, named by the segment's base offset. The highest-base-offset segment is the active one that producers are still appending to; the others are closed and immutable.

Step 2: To read offset four, Kafka finds the segment whose offset range contains four, binary-searches that segment's sparse offset index for the nearest indexed offset at or below four, seeks to that byte position in the `.log`, and scans forward a short distance to offset four. The sparse index keeps lookups cheap without storing an entry per record.

Step 3: A retention pass runs with a cutoff. Each closed segment is checked by its largest timestamp, and any segment whose records are all older than the cutoff is deleted as a whole file, along with its index and time index. Retention never removes individual records; its granularity is the whole segment, and the active segment is never eligible.

Step 4: On the compacted `account.state` partition, the compactor scans the closed segments, builds the latest record per key, and rewrites the closed segments to keep only those latest records. SAV2001 had three versions across offsets zero, two, and three; only offset three survives, so offsets zero and two disappear and the log now has gaps in offset numbering, which is normal because compaction preserves the surviving records' original offsets.

Step 5: Throughout, the active segment is left untouched by both retention and compaction, which is why both operations are safe and simple, and it also means a low-traffic partition can keep data longer than its retention time suggests until the active segment finally rolls. The combination gives the ledger a bounded, segment-granular history and the state topic a guaranteed latest-value-per-key store.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Kafka partition is stored on disk as a directory of log segment files. Each segment is a dot-log file holding a contiguous range of records in offset order, and it is paired with a dot-index offset index and a dot-timeindex time index, all named by the segment's base offset. Only the newest segment, the active segment, is written to; all older segments are closed and immutable. That immutability is the foundation that makes everything else safe.

The offset index exists so reads are fast without scanning gigabyte files. It is a sparse map from logical offset to the physical byte position in the log, with one entry roughly every few kilobytes controlled by the index interval, so to read a given offset Kafka binary-searches the index for the nearest indexed offset at or below it, seeks to that byte position, and scans forward a short way. The time index does the same for timestamps, which is what powers time-based seeks and time retention. Kafka rolls the active segment into a closed one when it hits the configured segment size or segment age, and from that moment the segment never changes.

Retention and compaction both operate at segment granularity on closed segments and always skip the active segment. Delete retention deletes whole segments: a closed segment is removed when all its records are older than the retention time, judged by its largest timestamp, or when the partition exceeds its size limit and the oldest segments must go. It never deletes individual records, which is why retention is coarse and why segment size controls how precisely you can trim data. Compaction instead rewrites closed segments: the log cleaner builds the latest record per key across the dirty closed segments and rewrites them to keep only those latest records plus tombstones within their window, preserving the surviving records' original offsets, so after compaction the log legitimately has gaps in offset numbering. A topic can be both compact and delete, in which case the cleaner compacts closed segments and retention still deletes whole aged ones.

On the National Bank of India systems this maps cleanly: the append-only ledger topic uses delete retention so old history is trimmed by dropping whole aged segments, and the account-state topic uses compaction so the latest balance per account is always retained while older versions vanish, which is exactly the offset-gap behavior we saw and confirmed was correct. The nuances I always mention are that segment size is a trade-off, since smaller segments give finer retention and smoother cleanup bursts but more file and index overhead, while larger segments are more efficient but coarser; that the active segment is never cleaned, so a low-traffic partition can hold data longer than its retention time until the segment finally rolls; and that index files are treated as reconstructable from the log, which is why a broker can rebuild them on restart. The one-line principle is that a partition is a sequence of immutable segments plus one active segment, each with a sparse offset and time index, and all cleanup is segment-oriented, which is what makes Kafka's storage both fast to read and simple to clean.
