sections.s6_takeaway:
Solace hierarchical routing lets a publisher put meaning directly into a slash-separated topic string such as a news category, a country, and a city, and lets subscribers express interest using level-aware wildcards, where a single-level wildcard matches exactly one level and a multi-level wildcard matches one level and everything below it. The defining characteristic is that the broker itself evaluates every message's topic against every active subscription, usually with an efficient trie, and delivers each message only to the subscribers whose pattern matches. The routing intelligence lives in the broker, so consumers stay thin and receive only what they asked for.

A concrete example is a news system that publishes to a topic built as news, then category, then country, then city. The Brazil operations desk subscribes with a country-pinned multi-level pattern that reads as any category, Brazil, then anything below, so it receives every Brazilian event regardless of category or city. The global sports desk subscribes with a category-pinned pattern that reads as sport, then anything below, so it receives every sport event in every country. A Sao Paulo sport event matches both and is delivered to both; a United States markets event matches neither and the broker simply drops it.

This is hard in Kafka because Kafka's broker is deliberately simple. A Kafka topic is a flat, pre-created, partitioned log, the broker never interprets structure in the topic name or looks inside the message, and a consumer subscribes to a whole topic and reads every record in its partitions. To reproduce the Brazil-only or sport-only behaviour you have three choices, each with a cost. You can create a separate topic for every combination, which makes publishing route the data but explodes the number of topics and partitions you must create and manage. You can publish everything to one broad topic and filter inside each consumer with simple field checks, which is easy but wastes network and consumer CPU because every consumer downloads and scans everything. Or you can add a stream-processing layer such as Kafka Streams or ksqlDB that reads the broad topic, branches by field, and republishes narrower topics that consumers read cleanly, which is precise but adds infrastructure to operate.

At National Bank of India I used exactly this trade-off. Desks that wanted finely sliced live feeds, like the Brazil desk and the sports desk, used Solace subscriptions and let the broker deliver only matching events, while the same feed flowed into a single Kafka topic for seven-year compliance retention and analytics, where a consumer filtered in application code. The senior point I make is that Solace moves routing CPU into the broker, which you must size for it, while Kafka pushes that cost to consumers in exchange for enormous throughput, durable retention, and replay, so the right answer is usually to use each where its model fits rather than forcing one to behave like the other.

---

answers.question: What is the topic proliferation problem in Kafka — as routing needs grow (by type × country × city), the number of flat topics grows very fast, each needing creation, partition sizing, and management — and how does Solace avoid this (one hierarchical topic space, consumers just change their subscription pattern)?
answers.shortTitle: What is the topic proliferation problem in Kafka, and how does Solace avoid it?

s1_definition.profdef: Topic proliferation is the operational problem in Kafka where, because the broker can only route at the granularity of a whole flat topic, the number of topics you must create grows multiplicatively with the number of routing dimensions. If you want to route by three dimensions such as type, country, and city, you end up needing roughly type times country times city topics, each of which must be explicitly created, sized for partitions and replication, monitored, retained, and governed. Solace avoids this because its topic space is a single hierarchical namespace and routing is a subscription-time concern, so adding a new routing need is just a new subscription pattern, not a new broker object.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India wants a separate physical mailbox for every combination of transaction type, branch city, and amount band. With three types, fifty branches, and four amount bands you suddenly need six hundred mailboxes, each installed, labelled, locked, and inspected by the facilities team. That is Kafka topic proliferation. Solace instead has one smart sorting room: every letter is addressed hierarchically, and a desk that wants a new slice just tells the sorting clerk a new address pattern. No new mailbox is ever built; the clerk simply matches addresses on the fly.
s1_definition.oneliner: In Kafka routing lives in the number of topics, so routing dimensions multiply topics; in Solace routing lives in the subscription pattern, so dimensions cost nothing structurally.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Topic proliferation is the operational problem in Kafka where, because the broker can only route at the granularity of a whole flat topic, the number of topics you must create grows multiplicatively with the number of routing dimensions. If you want to route by three dimensions such as type, country, and city, you end up needing roughly type times country times city topics, each of which must be explicitly created, sized for partitions and replication, monitored, retained, and governed. Solace avoids this because its topic space is a single hierarchical namespace and routing is a subscription-time concern, so adding a new routing need is just a new subscription pattern, not a new broker object.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India wants a separate physical mailbox for every combination of transaction type, branch city, and amount band. With three types, fifty branches, and four amount bands you suddenly need six hundred mailboxes, each installed, labelled, locked, and inspected by the facilities team. That is Kafka topic proliferation. Solace instead has one smart sorting room: every letter is addressed hierarchically, and a desk that wants a new slice just tells the sorting clerk a new address pattern. No new mailbox is ever built; the clerk simply matches addresses on the fly.

**One line to remember:** In Kafka routing lives in the number of topics, so routing dimensions multiply topics; in Solace routing lives in the subscription pattern, so dimensions cost nothing structurally.

sections.s2_technical:
Kafka routes at topic granularity. The broker does not look inside a record, so the only way for a consumer to receive just a subset of data without downloading everything is for that subset to already be its own topic. This forces the routing decision to publish time: the publisher must decide which fine-grained topic a record belongs to and write it there.

The moment you have more than one routing dimension, the topic count becomes a product. Suppose you route transactions by type (credit, debit, transfer), by country (IN, BR, US, UK), and by amount band (small, medium, large). That is three times four times three, which is thirty-six topics, and it was only three small dimensions. Real systems have dozens of branches and many categories, so the count reaches hundreds or thousands quickly. Each topic is not free: it needs a creation step (often gated by a platform team), a partition count chosen for its expected throughput, a replication factor, retention settings, ACLs, and monitoring for under-replicated partitions and consumer lag. A cluster has a practical ceiling on total partitions because each partition consumes broker memory, file handles, and controller metadata, so uncontrolled topic growth can destabilise the cluster.

There is a second pain: change. If the business adds a fourth amount band or a new country, you must create a new set of topics, update producer routing logic, update ACLs, and tell consumers to subscribe to the new topics. Routing logic is now baked into topic structure, which is the hardest thing to change in a running Kafka estate.

Teams mitigate this in several ways, none free. One mitigation is to keep topics coarse, such as one `transactions` topic, and filter in consumers; this trades topic sprawl for consumer CPU and network waste, since every consumer reads everything. Another is to add a stream-processing layer with Kafka Streams or ksqlDB that reads a coarse topic and dynamically branches into narrower topics, which centralises the routing but adds a stateful service you must operate and scale. A third is a hybrid where a few high-value slices get their own topics and the long tail is filtered client-side.

Solace avoids the problem by making the topic a publish-time string in a single hierarchical namespace rather than a pre-created broker object. There is no `createTopic` step for each combination; the publisher just writes a richly structured topic string like transaction, then country, then type, then band. Routing is entirely a subscriber concern expressed with wildcards. A desk that wants Brazil large transactions subscribes with a pattern pinning the country and band levels; a desk that wants everything from Mumbai subscribes with a multi-level wildcard under Mumbai. Adding a new routing need is a new subscription pattern registered by the consumer, and adding a new dimension value such as a new country requires no broker change at all because any topic string is instantly routable. The broker's trie-based matcher handles arbitrary combinations without any pre-provisioning.

The senior nuance is that this is a genuine trade-off, not a free win. Solace pays with broker-side matching CPU and with the fact that its hierarchical persistence and replay story is different from Kafka's partitioned log. Kafka's flat log gives it unmatched sequential throughput, ordered partitions, long retention, and replay, which are exactly why banks keep Kafka as the durable backbone even when Solace handles the live fan-out. So the practical answer to proliferation is often not to force Kafka to route finely, but to let Solace route and let Kafka store.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India wants to distribute its live transaction feed to many desks, each wanting a different slice defined by transaction type, country, and amount band.

Problem 1 — The platform team notices that giving every desk its own Kafka topic means creating type times country times band topics. When the business opened operations in two new countries, the number of topics jumped again, and each new topic needed partitions, replication, ACLs, and a dashboard. This is exactly the topic proliferation problem: routing dimensions multiply topic count, and every topic is an operational object.

Problem 2 — A new compliance rule arrives mid-quarter: a "very large" amount band must be tracked separately. In the Kafka-per-combination design this means creating a whole new row of topics across every type and country and rewiring producers. This is exactly why routing baked into topic structure is painful to change.

Problem 3 — The architecture team asks: what if routing were a subscription pattern instead of a topic? Then a new band is just a new subscription string, no broker objects created. This is exactly how Solace's single hierarchical namespace avoids proliferation.

The demo models both worlds. A `KafkaTopicPlanner` computes and "creates" the cartesian set of topics for given dimensions and reports the count and the operational cost. A `SolaceNamespace` publishes into one hierarchical space and lets desks register patterns, showing that adding a dimension value or a new desk costs zero new topics. The `main` method first sizes the Kafka topic explosion for three dimensions, then adds a fourth band and shows the explosion grow, then shows Solace absorbing the same requirements with only new subscription strings.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three transaction types, four countries, three amount bands, plus a later fourth band for compliance.

Step 1: The Kafka planner walks the cartesian product of three types, four countries, and three bands. It "creates" three times four times three, which is thirty-six topics. Each topic is logged with its partition and replication settings.

Step 2: The planner reports that thirty-six topics need thirty-six times six, which is two hundred and sixteen partitions provisioned, each consuming broker metadata and file handles.

Step 3: Compliance adds a fourth band. The planner reruns with four bands and now produces three times four times four, which is forty-eight topics, a jump of twelve new topics. The demo logs a warning because this also means rewiring producers, adding ACLs, and creating dashboards for the new topics.

Step 4: The Solace path starts. Three desks register subscription patterns: Brazil large, everything India, and a new very-large monitor. The namespace reports zero topics created and three subscriptions registered.

Step 5: A message with topic `txn/BR/transfer/large` is published. The namespace tests each pattern: the Brazil-large desk matches on country BR and band large, so it is delivered; the India desk fails on country; the very-large monitor fails on band. One matching desk receives it, and no topic had to exist beforehand.

Step 6: A message with topic `txn/IN/credit/veryLarge` is published. The India desk matches via its multi-level wildcard; the very-large monitor matches via its band pin. Two desks receive it. The brand-new band value `veryLarge` worked instantly with zero broker changes, which is the whole point.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Topic proliferation is the operational problem in Kafka where the number of topics you must create grows multiplicatively with your routing dimensions. Because the Kafka broker only routes at the granularity of a whole flat topic and never looks inside a record, the only way a consumer can receive just a slice without downloading everything is for that slice to already be its own topic. So if you want to route by type, country, and amount band, you end up needing roughly type times country times band topics, which for even small dimensions becomes dozens, and for real systems becomes hundreds or thousands.

The cost is not just the count. Every Kafka topic needs an explicit creation step that is usually gated by a platform team, a partition count chosen for its throughput, a replication factor, retention settings, access-control lists, and monitoring for under-replicated partitions and consumer lag. Partitions consume broker memory, file handles, and controller metadata, so a cluster has a practical ceiling and uncontrolled topic growth can destabilise it. Worse, routing is now baked into topic structure, so when the business adds one new amount band or one new country you must create a whole new set of topics, rewire producer routing, update ACLs, and tell every consumer about the new topics. Routing structure is the hardest thing to change in a running Kafka estate.

Solace avoids this because its topic is a publish-time string in a single hierarchical namespace rather than a pre-created broker object. There is no per-combination creation step; the publisher simply writes a structured topic such as transaction, then country, then type, then band, and routing is entirely a subscriber concern expressed with level-aware wildcards. A desk that wants Brazil large transactions registers one subscription pattern, and a brand-new amount band required by compliance is just one more subscription string, with zero new topics created and no producer rewiring, because any topic string is instantly routable by the broker's matcher.

At National Bank of India I used this distinction directly. When desks wanted finely sliced live feeds across many combinations of type, country, and band, forcing Kafka to route them would have meant creating and governing hundreds of topics and rebuilding them every time the business added a dimension value, so we let Solace route those live slices through one hierarchical namespace where new needs are just new subscriptions. The senior point I always add is that this is a trade-off rather than a free win: Solace pays with broker-side matching CPU, while Kafka's flat log is exactly what gives it unmatched throughput, ordered partitions, long retention, and replay. So in practice the cleanest answer to proliferation is not to make Kafka route finely but to let Solace route the live fan-out and keep Kafka as the durable, replayable backbone.

answers.shortTitle: When should you choose Kafka over Solace, and when should you choose Solace over Kafka?

s1_definition.profdef: The choice between Kafka and Solace is a choice between two different core models. Kafka is a durable, partitioned, append-only log that excels at long-term retention, deterministic replay, event sourcing, and a rich stream-processing ecosystem through Kafka Streams and ksqlDB, scaling horizontally by partition. Solace PubSub+ is a broker-centric message router whose strength is broker-native hierarchical topic routing with wildcard subscriptions, letting consumers with diverse and changing routing needs filter dynamically without anyone creating new topics. You choose Kafka when the dominant requirement is durable streaming, replay, and stream processing; you choose Solace when the dominant requirement is flexible, broker-side, content-shaped routing to many heterogeneous consumers.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of Kafka as National Bank of India's permanent ledger vault: every transaction is written down in order and kept for years so you can replay the exact history, rebuild any report, and feed analytics. Think of Solace as the bank's smart internal mail room: it does not keep letters forever, but it is brilliant at instantly sorting each letter to exactly the desks that asked for that kind of letter, even as desks keep changing what they want. If your need is "remember everything and replay it", you want the vault. If your need is "deliver the right slice to the right desk right now, and the desks keep changing", you want the mail room.
s1_definition.oneliner: Choose Kafka when you must store and replay the event history; choose Solace when you must route live events flexibly to ever-changing consumers.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The choice between Kafka and Solace is a choice between two different core models. Kafka is a durable, partitioned, append-only log that excels at long-term retention, deterministic replay, event sourcing, and a rich stream-processing ecosystem through Kafka Streams and ksqlDB, scaling horizontally by partition. Solace PubSub+ is a broker-centric message router whose strength is broker-native hierarchical topic routing with wildcard subscriptions, letting consumers with diverse and changing routing needs filter dynamically without anyone creating new topics. You choose Kafka when the dominant requirement is durable streaming, replay, and stream processing; you choose Solace when the dominant requirement is flexible, broker-side, content-shaped routing to many heterogeneous consumers.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of Kafka as National Bank of India's permanent ledger vault: every transaction is written down in order and kept for years so you can replay the exact history, rebuild any report, and feed analytics. Think of Solace as the bank's smart internal mail room: it does not keep letters forever, but it is brilliant at instantly sorting each letter to exactly the desks that asked for that kind of letter, even as desks keep changing what they want. If your need is "remember everything and replay it", you want the vault. If your need is "deliver the right slice to the right desk right now, and the desks keep changing", you want the mail room.

**One line to remember:** Choose Kafka when you must store and replay the event history; choose Solace when you must route live events flexibly to ever-changing consumers.

sections.s2_technical:
Kafka's defining property is the durable log. Records are appended to partitions and retained for a configured time or size, often days, weeks, or indefinitely with compaction. Because the log persists and each consumer tracks its own offset, a consumer can rewind and replay from any point. This is what makes event sourcing possible: the log of events is the source of truth, and you can rebuild state by replaying. For example, a settlement service can reset a consumer group's offset to the start of the `trade.events` topic and recompute every position, which you would express operationally with `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets --to-earliest --execute`. Solace is a messaging broker whose persistence and replay model is different and generally not aimed at long-horizon reprocessing of an entire history.

Kafka's second property is the stream-processing ecosystem. Kafka Streams lets you write a topology in the application that reads a topic, does joins, windowed aggregations, and stateful transforms, and writes results back to Kafka, all with exactly-once semantics. ksqlDB lets you express the same with SQL. For instance, a fraud service can use a Kafka Streams aggregation over a five-minute hopping window to count transactions per account and flag spikes. Solace does not offer this native streaming-compute ecosystem; you would pair it with an external processor.

Kafka's third property is partitioned horizontal scale with ordering. A topic is split into partitions, each an ordered log, and ordering is guaranteed within a partition keyed by, for example, account id, so all events for one account stay ordered while the topic as a whole scales across brokers and consumers. This gives very high sequential throughput, which is why banks use Kafka as the firm-wide event backbone.

Solace's defining property is broker-native hierarchical routing. The broker understands structured topic strings and wildcard subscriptions and does the matching itself, so a consumer with a specific or changing interest just adjusts its subscription pattern and immediately receives exactly the matching slice, without anyone creating a topic. This is the right tool when you have many heterogeneous consumers whose routing needs are diverse and keep changing, such as trading desks each wanting a different cut of a market feed. Solace also supports multiple delivery models including direct low-latency fan-out and persistent queues, and multi-protocol access such as JMS, MQTT, AMQP, and REST, which matters in mixed enterprise estates.

So the decision rules are as follows. Choose Kafka when you need durable event streaming kept for a long time, deterministic replay, event sourcing where the log is the source of truth, the Kafka Streams or ksqlDB processing ecosystem, and partitioned log scalability with per-key ordering at very high throughput. Choose Solace when consumers have diverse and frequently changing routing needs, when you want the broker itself to do hierarchical, content-shaped routing with wildcards, when you need dynamic filtering without creating new topics (avoiding topic proliferation), and when low-latency fan-out and multi-protocol access to many consumers matter more than long-term replay.

The senior nuance is that these are not mutually exclusive and are frequently complementary. A common bank architecture uses Solace for real-time, finely routed, low-latency distribution to desks and uses Kafka as the durable, replayable backbone for retention, analytics, and event sourcing, sometimes bridging the two so an event flows through Solace for live routing and lands in Kafka for history. The wrong move is to force one tool into the other's job: forcing Kafka to route finely causes topic proliferation, and forcing Solace to be your seven-year replayable ledger fights its design.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India must handle two very different requirements for its trade and transaction events, and the team must pick the right tool for each.

Problem 1 — Compliance requires that every trade event be stored for seven years and be replayable, so that at any time the settlement ledger can be rebuilt by replaying the full history from the beginning. This is exactly what Kafka's durable, offset-based log gives you: retain forever, reset offsets, and replay to reconstruct state, which is the essence of event sourcing.

Problem 2 — Multiple trading desks each want a different, frequently changing slice of the live market and transaction feed, and they must not wait for a platform team to create a new topic every time their interest changes. This is exactly what Solace's broker-native hierarchical routing gives you: each desk sets a wildcard subscription and the broker delivers the matching slice instantly, with no topic creation.

Problem 3 — The architecture team wants a decision helper that, given a requirement's characteristics, recommends Kafka or Solace with a clear reason, so that engineers stop forcing the wrong tool and causing either topic proliferation or a broken replay story.

The demo models this with a small decision engine. A `Requirement` carries flags such as needsLongReplay, needsStreamProcessing, needsFlexibleRouting, and routingChangesOften. A `BrokerAdvisor` applies the decision rules and returns a recommendation with a reason. The `main` method runs the compliance-replay requirement and the changing-desk-routing requirement through the advisor and prints the recommendation, then shows a tiny illustration of Kafka replay (offset reset) and Solace dynamic subscription (pattern change) to make the trade-off concrete.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two requirements, one for seven-year compliance replay with stream processing, one for many trading desks whose routing changes often.

Step 1: The compliance requirement enters the advisor with needsLongReplay and needsStreamProcessing both true. The advisor's first rule checks durability and replay; both are set, so it scores durability as dominant.

Step 2: The advisor returns a recommendation of Kafka, with the reason that a durable partitioned log gives long-term retention, deterministic replay, event sourcing, and the Kafka Streams and ksqlDB ecosystem with per-key ordering. This is logged at info.

Step 3: The desks requirement enters the advisor with needsFlexibleRouting and routingChangesOften both true, and the durability flags false. The first rule does not fire because durability is not needed.

Step 4: The second rule checks flexible or changing routing; both are set, so it scores routing as dominant and returns a recommendation of Solace, with the reason that broker-native hierarchical wildcard subscriptions let diverse, changing consumers filter dynamically with no new topics.

Step 5: The demo prints two concrete illustrations. For Kafka it shows that rebuilding the ledger means resetting the trade.events consumer group to the earliest offset and recomputing, which only a durable replayable log can do. For Solace it shows a desk changing its subscription live from a narrow pattern to a broad multi-level wildcard, receiving a different slice immediately with no topic creation.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The choice between Kafka and Solace comes down to which core model your dominant requirement needs. Kafka is a durable, partitioned, append-only log, so you choose it when you need long-term event retention, deterministic replay, event sourcing where the log is the source of truth, the Kafka Streams and ksqlDB stream-processing ecosystem, and partitioned horizontal scalability with per-key ordering at very high throughput. Because each consumer tracks its own offset against a retained log, you can rewind and replay history to rebuild state, which is exactly what event sourcing and firm-wide analytics depend on.

Solace PubSub+ is a broker-centric message router whose defining strength is broker-native hierarchical routing with wildcard subscriptions. You choose Solace when consumers have diverse and frequently changing routing needs, when you want the broker itself to do content-shaped hierarchical routing, and when you need dynamic filtering without creating new topics, which avoids the topic proliferation that Kafka suffers when routing dimensions multiply. Solace also shines for low-latency fan-out to many heterogeneous consumers and for multi-protocol access such as JMS, MQTT, AMQP, and REST in mixed enterprise estates.

The key senior insight is that these are not competitors forced into one slot; they are usually complementary. A common bank architecture uses Solace for the real-time, finely routed, low-latency distribution of market and transaction feeds to trading desks whose interests keep changing, while Kafka acts as the durable, replayable backbone that retains every event for years for compliance, analytics, and event sourcing. Events can flow through Solace for live routing and land in Kafka for history, so each tool does the job its design is best at.

At National Bank of India I applied exactly this split. Compliance needed seven-year trade retention and the ability to rebuild the settlement ledger by replaying the whole history, so that went to Kafka, where we could reset a consumer group to the earliest offset and recompute. Meanwhile many trading desks each wanted a different and often-changing slice of the live feed and could not wait for a platform team to create a topic each time, so that went to Solace, where each desk simply adjusted its wildcard subscription and received the new slice instantly. The mistake I always warn against is forcing one tool into the other's role: pushing fine routing onto Kafka explodes topic counts, and making Solace your long-horizon replayable ledger fights its design, so I match the tool to the dominant requirement and let them work together.

answers.question: What is Apache Pulsar — a distributed messaging system that combines Kafka-like durable log (BookKeeper storage) with RabbitMQ-like queue features (shared subscriptions, per-message ack) + multi-tenancy + geo-replication built-in — and when would you consider Pulsar over Kafka (multi-tenancy, simpler geo-replication, combined queue + streaming in one system)?
answers.shortTitle: What is Apache Pulsar, and when would you consider Pulsar over Kafka?

s1_definition.profdef: Apache Pulsar is a distributed messaging and streaming platform that combines a Kafka-like durable, append-only log with RabbitMQ-like queue semantics in a single system. Its storage and serving are separated: brokers are stateless and serve traffic, while Apache BookKeeper provides the durable, replicated log storage. Pulsar natively supports multiple subscription types including exclusive, failover, shared, and key-shared, giving both streaming fan-out and work-queue distribution with per-message acknowledgement. It also ships with first-class multi-tenancy through tenants and namespaces and with built-in geo-replication across clusters.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India wants one messaging platform that behaves like a permanent ledger when needed and like a shared work queue when needed, and that can safely host many independent departments on the same infrastructure. Kafka is great as the ledger but its work-queue behaviour and tenant isolation need extra effort. RabbitMQ is great as the work queue but is not the durable replayable ledger. Pulsar is the single platform that tries to be both: the ledger lives in a dedicated vault service (BookKeeper), the clerks at the counter (brokers) are interchangeable because they hold no state, each department gets its own walled area (tenant and namespace), and the same message can be either replayed like a log or shared out like a queue depending on how you subscribe.
s1_definition.oneliner: Pulsar is a log and a queue in one system, with stateless brokers over BookKeeper storage, native multi-tenancy, and built-in geo-replication.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Apache Pulsar is a distributed messaging and streaming platform that combines a Kafka-like durable, append-only log with RabbitMQ-like queue semantics in a single system. Its storage and serving are separated: brokers are stateless and serve traffic, while Apache BookKeeper provides the durable, replicated log storage. Pulsar natively supports multiple subscription types including exclusive, failover, shared, and key-shared, giving both streaming fan-out and work-queue distribution with per-message acknowledgement. It also ships with first-class multi-tenancy through tenants and namespaces and with built-in geo-replication across clusters.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India wants one messaging platform that behaves like a permanent ledger when needed and like a shared work queue when needed, and that can safely host many independent departments on the same infrastructure. Kafka is great as the ledger but its work-queue behaviour and tenant isolation need extra effort. RabbitMQ is great as the work queue but is not the durable replayable ledger. Pulsar is the single platform that tries to be both: the ledger lives in a dedicated vault service (BookKeeper), the clerks at the counter (brokers) are interchangeable because they hold no state, each department gets its own walled area (tenant and namespace), and the same message can be either replayed like a log or shared out like a queue depending on how you subscribe.

**One line to remember:** Pulsar is a log and a queue in one system, with stateless brokers over BookKeeper storage, native multi-tenancy, and built-in geo-replication.

sections.s2_technical:
Pulsar's first distinguishing idea is the separation of compute and storage. In Kafka a broker both serves clients and owns the partition data on its local disk, so adding capacity or recovering from a failed broker involves moving large amounts of partition data. In Pulsar the broker is stateless: it serves produce and consume traffic but the actual durable data lives in BookKeeper, a separate distributed log store made of nodes called bookies. A topic's data is a sequence of ledgers striped and replicated across bookies. Because brokers hold no data, you can add or restart a broker quickly and it simply picks up serving topics; scaling storage and scaling serving are independent decisions. This is powerful operationally but means you run and tune two systems, BookKeeper and the brokers, plus ZooKeeper or an equivalent for metadata.

Pulsar's second distinguishing idea is unified messaging through subscription types. A subscription is how consumers attach to a topic, and the type decides the delivery semantics. Exclusive means one consumer only. Failover means one active consumer with hot standbys. Shared means messages are distributed round-robin across many consumers like a classic work queue, with per-message acknowledgement so individual messages can be acked or redelivered independently, which Kafka does not do natively because Kafka tracks a single offset per partition per group. Key-shared means messages with the same key always go to the same consumer, preserving per-key order while still sharing load. For example, a settlement worker pool can subscribe in shared mode to pull trades one at a time and ack each as it finishes, while an audit consumer subscribes exclusively and reads the whole stream in order. This gives you RabbitMQ-style queues and Kafka-style streaming from the same topic.

Pulsar's third distinguishing idea is first-class multi-tenancy. The hierarchy is tenant, then namespace, then topic. A tenant is an isolated organisational unit, a namespace groups topics and carries policies such as retention, quotas, backlog limits, and access control, and topics live inside namespaces. This lets many teams share one Pulsar cluster with real isolation and per-namespace policy, whereas in Kafka multi-tenancy is achieved more loosely with naming conventions, ACLs, and quotas rather than a built-in tenant model.

Pulsar's fourth distinguishing idea is built-in geo-replication. You can configure a namespace to replicate across multiple clusters in different regions, and Pulsar handles asynchronous cross-region replication natively. In Kafka cross-region replication is typically done with separate tooling such as MirrorMaker 2 or a commercial replicator, which is capable but is an additional component to operate.

So when would you consider Pulsar over Kafka? Consider Pulsar when you need strong multi-tenancy because many independent teams or clients must share one platform with isolation and per-namespace policy. Consider it when you want simpler built-in geo-replication across regions without bolting on separate tooling. Consider it when you genuinely need both queue semantics (shared, per-message ack, work distribution) and streaming semantics (ordered replayable log) in one system, so you do not run both RabbitMQ and Kafka. Consider it when independent scaling of storage and serving, via the stateless-broker and BookKeeper split, is operationally attractive.

The senior nuance is the honest trade-off. Kafka has a far larger ecosystem, more mature tooling, Kafka Streams and ksqlDB, broad client and connector support, and more widely available operational expertise. Pulsar's architecture is elegant but has more moving parts (brokers, bookies, metadata store), so it can be more complex to run well. The decision should weigh Pulsar's native multi-tenancy, unified queue-plus-stream model, and built-in geo-replication against Kafka's ecosystem maturity and operational familiarity.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India is consolidating messaging platforms and evaluating Pulsar.

Problem 1 — Today the settlement team runs RabbitMQ for its work queue (distribute trades one by one to a worker pool, ack each when done) and separately runs Kafka for the durable, replayable event log for compliance. Operating two platforms is costly. This is exactly where Pulsar's unified model helps: one topic can be consumed in shared mode as a work queue with per-message ack and simultaneously in exclusive mode as an ordered replayable stream.

Problem 2 — Several independent departments (retail payments, trading, cards) must share one messaging platform but must be isolated so one noisy department cannot affect another's quotas or data. This is exactly what Pulsar's tenant and namespace multi-tenancy provides, with per-namespace retention and quota policy.

Problem 3 — The bank runs in Mumbai and a disaster-recovery region, and transaction events must replicate across regions without bolting on separate tooling. This is exactly what Pulsar's built-in geo-replication provides at the namespace level.

The demo models a simplified Pulsar. A `PulsarTopic` stores an append-only log (BookKeeper-like) and supports attaching subscriptions of different types. A `Subscription` has a type (EXCLUSIVE, SHARED, KEY_SHARED) that decides how messages are dispatched to its consumers, with per-message ack for SHARED. A `Namespace` groups topics under a tenant and carries a retention policy, demonstrating multi-tenancy, and a `geoReplicateTo` method illustrates cross-cluster replication. The `main` method publishes trade events, consumes them as a shared work queue and as an exclusive ordered stream from the same topic, shows two tenants isolated in namespaces, and shows a namespace replicating to a DR cluster.

Input data: a trading namespace under tenant nbi with seven-year retention, three trade events T-1, T-2, T-3 in the trade.events topic.

Step 1: The trading namespace is created with seven-year retention. The topic trade.events is created under it. These are isolated by tenant and namespace from any other department.

Step 2: Three trade events are appended to the topic's ledger, which is the BookKeeper-like durable log. Nothing is routed yet; the data is simply persisted and replicated in storage.

Step 3: A SHARED subscription named settle-workers is attached with two consumers, worker-A and worker-B. Step 4: An EXCLUSIVE subscription named audit is attached with a single consumer. Dispatch delivers all three messages in order to the one consumer. This is classic ordered streaming from the same topic that was just used as a queue.

Step 5: The audit subscription replays from the start, re-reading all three events in order, which is possible only because the data is a durable retained log rather than a consumed-and-gone queue.

Step 6: A second namespace, payments, is created under the same tenant with a different thirty-day retention policy, demonstrating that two departments share one platform with isolated policy.

Step 7: The trading namespace is geo-replicated to the dr-pune cluster, demonstrating built-in cross-region replication without extra tooling.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Apache Pulsar is a distributed messaging and streaming platform that combines a Kafka-like durable, append-only log with RabbitMQ-like queue semantics in one system. Its most distinctive architectural choice is the separation of compute and storage: brokers are stateless and serve produce and consume traffic, while the durable data lives in Apache BookKeeper, a separate replicated log store whose nodes are called bookies, with a metadata store such as ZooKeeper or etcd tying it together. Because brokers hold no data, you can scale and recover serving capacity quickly and independently of storage.

What makes Pulsar unified is its subscription types. A topic can be consumed as an exclusive or failover subscription, which gives a single ordered, replayable stream like Kafka, or as a shared subscription, which distributes messages round-robin across a pool of consumers with per-message acknowledgement like a classic work queue, or as a key-shared subscription, which keeps all messages of a given key on one consumer so you preserve per-key order while still sharing load. This means you get both queueing and streaming from the same topic, instead of running RabbitMQ and Kafka side by side. On top of this, Pulsar has first-class multi-tenancy through a tenant, namespace, and topic hierarchy with per-namespace retention, quota, and access policy, and it has built-in geo-replication that replicates a namespace across clusters in different regions natively.

You would consider Pulsar over Kafka in a few specific situations. You consider it when you need strong multi-tenancy because many independent teams or clients must share one platform with real isolation and per-namespace policy rather than Kafka's looser convention-and-ACL approach. You consider it when you want simpler built-in geo-replication across regions without bolting on separate tooling like MirrorMaker. You consider it when you genuinely need both queue semantics and streaming semantics in one system so you can retire a separate queue broker. And you consider it when independent scaling of storage and serving through the stateless-broker-over-BookKeeper design is operationally attractive.

At National Bank of India the evaluation was concrete. The settlement team was running a separate queue broker to hand trades one by one to a worker pool with per-message ack, and separately running a durable log for seven-year compliance replay, so Pulsar's ability to serve the same trade topic as a shared work queue and as an exclusive replayable stream was attractive for consolidation, while its tenant and namespace model let retail payments, trading, and cards share one cluster with isolated retention policies, and its built-in geo-replication covered the Mumbai-to-DR requirement. The honest senior caveat I always give is that Kafka still has the larger ecosystem, more mature tooling, Kafka Streams and ksqlDB, and more widely available operational expertise, whereas Pulsar's elegant architecture has more moving parts to run well, so the choice weighs Pulsar's native multi-tenancy, unified queue-plus-stream model, and geo-replication against Kafka's ecosystem maturity.

answers.question: Can Kafka and Solace be used together — yes, many companies use Kafka as the durable system of record for long-term event retention and replay, and Solace for dynamic event distribution and selective routing to consumers — they solve different problems and are often complementary?
answers.shortTitle: Can Kafka and Solace be used together, and why are they often complementary?

s1_definition.profdef: Yes, Kafka and Solace are frequently used together because they solve different problems and complement each other. Kafka serves as the durable system of record: a partitioned, append-only log that retains events for the long term and supports deterministic replay, event sourcing, and stream processing. Solace serves as the dynamic distribution layer: a broker-native hierarchical router that delivers precisely filtered slices to many heterogeneous consumers with low latency and without creating new topics. A common pattern bridges them, so an event flows through Solace for real-time selective routing while also landing in Kafka for durable retention and later replay.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India using two services together. Solace is the smart mail room that instantly sorts each incoming letter to exactly the desks that asked for that kind of letter, as desks keep changing their requests. Kafka is the permanent records vault where a copy of every letter is filed in order and kept for years, so auditors can replay the entire history whenever they need. The mail room makes sure the right person gets the right letter now; the vault makes sure nothing is ever lost and everything can be reconstructed later. You want both: fast, flexible delivery today and a durable, replayable record forever.
s1_definition.oneliner: Solace routes live events flexibly to the right consumers now; Kafka durably stores every event for replay later, and bridging them gives you both.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Yes, Kafka and Solace are frequently used together because they solve different problems and complement each other. Kafka serves as the durable system of record: a partitioned, append-only log that retains events for the long term and supports deterministic replay, event sourcing, and stream processing. Solace serves as the dynamic distribution layer: a broker-native hierarchical router that delivers precisely filtered slices to many heterogeneous consumers with low latency and without creating new topics. A common pattern bridges them, so an event flows through Solace for real-time selective routing while also landing in Kafka for durable retention and later replay.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India using two services together. Solace is the smart mail room that instantly sorts each incoming letter to exactly the desks that asked for that kind of letter, as desks keep changing their requests. Kafka is the permanent records vault where a copy of every letter is filed in order and kept for years, so auditors can replay the entire history whenever they need. The mail room makes sure the right person gets the right letter now; the vault makes sure nothing is ever lost and everything can be reconstructed later. You want both: fast, flexible delivery today and a durable, replayable record forever.

**One line to remember:** Solace routes live events flexibly to the right consumers now; Kafka durably stores every event for replay later, and bridging them gives you both.

sections.s2_technical:
The reason they combine well is that their design centres are different. Kafka optimises for a durable, ordered, partitioned log with long retention, offset-based replay, per-key ordering, and a stream-processing ecosystem. Solace optimises for broker-side hierarchical routing with wildcard subscriptions, low-latency fan-out, multi-protocol access, and dynamic filtering without topic creation. When a system needs both durable history and flexible live routing, using each for its strength is cleaner than forcing one to do both.

There are a few concrete integration patterns. The first is a bridge or connector that moves events between the two. Solace provides bridging capabilities, and Kafka has Kafka Connect, so you can run a connector that consumes from Solace and produces to Kafka, giving every routed event a durable home, or the reverse, publishing Kafka events into Solace for selective fan-out. For example, a transaction event can be published once, selectively delivered to desks via Solace wildcard subscriptions, and simultaneously captured into a Kafka `transactions` topic for seven-year retention.

The second pattern is Solace-in-front, Kafka-behind. The producer publishes to Solace, where the broker routes slices to live consumers such as trading desks, and a sink bridge persists the full stream into Kafka. Live consumers get only their slice with low latency; Kafka holds the complete ordered record for compliance and analytics. This avoids topic proliferation on the Kafka side because the fine routing happens in Solace, and it avoids consumer-side waste because desks do not each read everything.

The third pattern is Kafka-as-source, Solace-as-distribution. Events are produced into Kafka as the system of record, and a bridge republishes selected streams into Solace for dynamic, content-shaped distribution to many consumers whose interests change. Here Kafka guarantees durability and replay while Solace handles the flexible last-mile delivery.

The senior nuances matter in a bank. First, think about ordering and delivery guarantees across the bridge: Kafka gives per-partition ordering keyed by, say, account id, and you must decide how that maps to Solace delivery and whether the bridge preserves ordering and handles duplicates idempotently. Second, think about the system of record principle: pick one source of truth, usually Kafka, so that if the two diverge you know which one is authoritative and can replay Kafka to rebuild. Third, think about back-pressure and retention mismatches: Solace may drop or age out messages faster than Kafka retains them, so the durable copy must be the long-horizon one. Fourth, monitor the bridge itself as a first-class component, because a stalled bridge silently breaks either durability or live delivery.

So the answer is a clear yes, and the reason is that they are complementary rather than competing. Solace handles dynamic event distribution and selective routing to changing consumers; Kafka handles durable long-term retention, replay, event sourcing, and stream processing. Many enterprises run exactly this split, often with a bridge connecting them, choosing one as the authoritative system of record.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India publishes a firm-wide transaction event stream and needs two outcomes at once.

Problem 1 — Many trading and operations desks each want a different, often-changing slice of the live transaction feed delivered immediately, such as all Mumbai transactions or all large transactions, and they must not trigger a new topic every time their interest changes. This is exactly Solace's job: publish into a hierarchical namespace and let each desk's wildcard subscription receive its slice with low latency.

Problem 2 — Compliance requires that every transaction event be stored durably for seven years and be replayable so the full ledger can be rebuilt at any time. This is exactly Kafka's job: append every event to a retained, ordered log that supports offset-based replay.

Problem 3 — The bank does not want to publish twice or maintain two divergent truths. It wants one publish that both routes live and persists durably, with Kafka as the single authoritative system of record. This is exactly the bridge pattern: an event enters Solace for routing and a sink bridge captures the same stream into Kafka.

The demo models this complementary architecture. A `SolaceRouter` publishes events into a hierarchical namespace and delivers matching slices to subscribed desks. A `SolaceToKafkaBridge` observes every event Solace receives and persists it into a `KafkaSystemOfRecord`, which retains events in an append-only log and supports replay from the beginning. The `main` method publishes several transactions, shows desks receiving only their slices live, shows the bridge persisting every event, and then shows compliance replaying the full ordered history from Kafka to rebuild the ledger.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two desk subscriptions (Mumbai operations on everything under Mumbai, and a large-transaction monitor on any large transaction) and four transaction events, keyed by account id for ordering.

Step 1: Both desks register their subscription patterns in Solace. Kafka's transactions topic is empty. The bridge is wired so that every event Solace receives will be captured into Kafka.

Step 2: The first event, a small Mumbai debit for Rajesh, is published once. Solace tests the patterns: Mumbai operations matches on the Mumbai branch, so it is delivered live to that desk; the large monitor does not match because the band is small. The same event is then handed to the bridge, which appends it to Kafka at offset zero.

Step 3: The second event, a large Mumbai transfer for Rajesh, is published. Mumbai operations matches on branch and the large monitor matches on band, so both desks receive it live. The bridge appends it to Kafka at offset one, keyed by Rajesh's account so his events stay ordered.

Step 4: The third event, a large Sao Paulo credit for Priya, is published. Mumbai operations does not match because the branch is not Mumbai, but the large monitor matches on band, so only the monitor receives it live. The bridge appends it to Kafka at offset two.

Step 5: The fourth event, a small London fee for Priya, matches neither desk, so no live delivery happens, but the bridge still appends it to Kafka at offset three. This is the crucial point: Solace filtered it out for live delivery, yet the durable record kept it anyway.

Step 6: Later, compliance replays Kafka from the start. All four events are re-read in offset order, regardless of which desks saw them live, allowing the full ledger to be rebuilt deterministically. Solace gave the right slice to the right desk in real time; Kafka kept the complete, replayable truth.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, Kafka and Solace are very commonly used together, and the reason is that they solve different problems and complement each other rather than compete. Kafka is the durable system of record: a partitioned, append-only log that retains events for the long term and supports deterministic offset-based replay, event sourcing, and a stream-processing ecosystem. Solace is the dynamic distribution layer: a broker-native hierarchical router that delivers precisely filtered slices to many heterogeneous consumers with low latency and without anyone creating new topics as consumer interests change.

The way they fit together is usually a bridge. A single transaction event is published once, Solace routes it live to exactly the desks whose wildcard subscriptions match, and a sink bridge, often built with Kafka Connect or Solace's own bridging, captures the same stream into a Kafka topic that is retained for years. Live consumers get only their slice with low latency and without topic proliferation, while Kafka keeps the complete, ordered, replayable record for compliance, analytics, and ledger reconstruction. A key design point is that even events that matched no live subscription are still persisted to Kafka, so the durable record is complete regardless of who was listening at the time.

The senior nuances I always raise are, first, choose one authoritative system of record, normally Kafka, so that if the two ever diverge you know which is the source of truth and can replay Kafka to rebuild. Second, decide how ordering maps across the bridge, keying Kafka by something like account id so per-account order is preserved, and make the bridge idempotent against duplicates. Third, watch for retention mismatches, since Solace may age messages out faster than Kafka retains them, which is precisely why the durable copy belongs in Kafka. And fourth, monitor the bridge as a first-class component, because a stalled bridge silently breaks either durability or live delivery.

At National Bank of India this was the exact architecture we used. Trading and operations desks wanted diverse, frequently changing slices of the live transaction feed, such as all Mumbai activity or all large transactions, delivered immediately and without spawning new topics, so Solace handled that selective, low-latency routing. At the same time compliance needed every transaction stored durably for seven years and replayable to rebuild the ledger, so a bridge captured the same stream into Kafka, which we treated as the authoritative system of record. Solace made sure the right desk got the right event now; Kafka made sure nothing was ever lost and the whole history could be replayed later. That complementary split is why the two platforms so often live side by side in a bank.
